full_judgment:
Md Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: At the instance of the defendant No 2 in Title Suit No, 29 of 1994, this appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 7-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari decreing the suit.
2. The salient facts relating to the case of the parties that stemmed from the impugned judgment are:
The predecessor of present respondent Nos. 1(a)-1(g), Panna Lal Agorwala as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit praying for declaration of title as well as partition in the suit land so described in the schedule to the plaint measuring a total area of 1.79 + 16½ = 1.95½ acres of land.
3. The case of the plaintiffs described in the plaint in short is that, one, Hira Lai Agorwala belonged to part of the suit land measuring an area of 1.79 acres by virtue of several registered deeds dated back to 1936 and 1953 and accordingly, his name was prepared in the RS record and thereby he acquired title and possession over the said property. Apart from that, the said Hira Lal Agorwala and his cousin named, Gourishankar Agorwala purchased 22 decimals of land from RS Plot No. 953 by registered kabala dated 18-6-1988 and thereby, they started enjoying title and possession over that 22 decimals of land proportionately by erecting homestead thereon. Subsequently, Hira Lala Agorwala sold out 5½ decimals of land out of his share of 11 decimals of land in RS Plot No. 953 to Gourishankar Agorwala by way of gift. It has further been stated that, the wife of Hira Lal Agorwala, Fulia BieAgorwala took defendant No. 2 as her adopted son. While Hira Lal Agorwala had been enjoying title and possession over 1.79 acres of land he proposed be settle (pattan) the same to the predecessor of the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 3-5, Gourishankar fixing the consideration (salami) at Taka 6,001 and the yearly rent at Taka 28 and it was executed on 4th Ashar, 1360 BS through amalnama and dakhila. Subsequently, Gourishankar Agorwala died leaving behind the plaintiff, the predecessor of the opposite-parties as well as defendant Nos. 3-5. It has further been stated that, after getting that 1.79 acres of land, Gourishankar Agorwala started enjoying title and possession over that property by giving rent to different tenants where there remained several shops and thus acquired indefeasible title and possession over the settled land. It has also been stated that, Shib Lal Agorwala, defendant No. 2 is not the adopted son of Hira Lal Agorwala and Hira Lal Agorwala was older than that of Gourishankar Agorwala when Gourishankar Agorwala devolved the responsibility upon Hira Lal Agorwala to get his name prepared in the SA record in respect of the suit land but ultimately it has not been recorded in his name in spite of taking settlement from Hira Lal Agorwala and therefore, the suit land was wrongly prepared in the name of Hira Lal Agorwala in SA record alone. The defendant No. 2 has never acquired any property left by Gourishartkar Agorwala and in the aforesaid way plaintiff is entitled to 1/4 share left by his father, Gourishankar Agorwala and when the plaintiff requested the defendants to partition the suit property on 2nd Chaitra, 1399 BS corresponding to 16-5-1992 AD, the defendants denied to partition the same and hence the suit.
4. The predecessor of the present petitioners as defendant No. 2 filed written statement denying all the material averments so made in the plaint. It has mainly been asserted in the written statement, his predecessor, Hira Lal Agorwala took him as adopted son though he died in the year 1971 and then he became dependent on the income of the wife of the Him Lal Agorwala named, Fulia Bie Agorwala. The suit property is located in the Pangsha Bazar which is very valuable one. After the demise of Hira Lal Agorwala, the plaintiff and the defendants kept on living jointly and the plaintiff, Parma Lal Agorwala used to look after the suit property though fact remains the plaintiff and the defendant No. 2 are full-brothers. It has further been stated that only to grab the entire property left by Hira Lal Agorwala and then acquired by him that is, the present defendant No. 2, the plaintiff out of greed filed the instant suit which is liable to be dismissed.
5. In order to dispose of the suit, the learned Joint District Judge framed as many as four different issues. The plaintiff examined five witnesses and produced several documents which were marked as exhibits 1-8 series while the present defendant No. 2 examined three witnesses and also produced several documents which were also marked as Exhibits ‘ka’ to ‘ja’ series. However, after conclusion of the trial, the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit in-part against the defendant No. 2 declaring title of the plaintiffs in respect of 38 decimals of land and also gave saham for the same land in his favour.
6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and part decree, the defendant No. 2 as appellant then preferred this appeal and during pendency of the rule, he died leaving behind the present appellants as his heirs.
7. Mr Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, the learned counsel appearing for the defendant No. 2- appellants upon taking us to the impugned judgment as well as other documents so appeared in the paper book at the very outset submits that, admittedly the suit land has been recorded in the name of Hira Lal Agorwala in SA khatian and though the learned Joint District Judge has not touched upon the very vital question giving any observation as to what prevented the plaintiff in recording his name in the SA khatian in spite of the fact that, his predecessor took settlement of the suit land by virtue of amalnama in the year 1953 AD and thereby erred in law in decreing the suit.
8. The learned counsel next contends that, the trial court ought to have dismissed the suit holding that, at the time of alleged settlement in the year 1360 BS neither Gourishankar nor his heirs were found to have paid any consideration claiming to be at Taka 6,001 as well as yearly rent at Taka 28 and though the said transaction could not be proved by any PWs yet the learned Joint District judge decreed the suit without discussing any evidence to that effect and therefore, the impugned judgment is liable to be set-aside.
9. The learned counsel goes on to submit that, the court below should have dismissed the suit holding that, the plaintiff has totally failed to prove that, Hira Lal Agorwala received any salami or any rent from Gourishankar Agorwala and that very transaction though has not been proved by any PW yet the learned Joint District Judge has erroneously decreed the suit.
10. The learned counsel next contends that, the leaned Joint District Judge rightly observed that, Hira Lal Agorwala has not transferred homestead land which has been described in schedule-‘ta’ to the plaint by way of oral gift to Gourishankar Agorwala yet the learned Joint District Judge has erred in law by not holding that, Hira Lal Agorwala also did not transfer suit property measuring 1.79 acres of land to Gourishankar Agorwala by way of alleged amalnana.
11. The learned counsel by referring to the cause title of the plaint also contends that, in its plaint the name of the father of the defendant No. 2 has been asserted as "Hira Lal Agorwala" and, as such, the plaintiff himself admitted that Shib Lal Agorwala, the defendant No. 2 is the adopted son of Hira Lal Agorwala and, as such, the positive case of the plaintiff that, Shib Lal Agorwala is the adopted son of Fulia Bie Agorwala stood disproved and the learned Joint District Judge should have disbelieved the case of the plaintiff to that effect as well.
12. The learned counsel further submits that, in a suit filed for confirmation or declaration of title, the plaintiff is to prove his/her own case to the hilt but in the instant case, the plaintiff has measurably failed to prove the said legal proposition and, as such, the trial court ought to have dismissed the suit.
13. By quoting the provision of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act as well as sections 17 and 19 of the Registration Act, the learned counsel next submits that, through alleged amalnama no title of the suit land has been conferred upon the father of the plaintiff as admittedly it was not registered one as per those provision of law.
14. To substantive the said contention, the learned counsel has then placed his reliance in the decision reported in 3 ALR (AD).70 and 15 ADC 859.
15. The learned counsel wrapped up his submission contending that, in spite of the legal provision for registering such kind of amalnama yet the alleged amalnama since is an unilateral deed so until and unless, any kabuliat is furnished by the recipient/lessee against that amalnama in favour of the lesser no right, title can be acquired in favour of its lessee, the predecessor of the plaintiff.
16. With those submissions, the learned counsel finally prays for allowing the appeal on setting aside the judgment passed by the learned Joint District Judge.
17. In contrast, Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned senior counsel along with Mr SM Tariqul Islam, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent No, 1(a)-1(g) very robustly opposes the contention so have been taken by the learned counsel for the appellants and contends that, mere recording the name of the predecessor of the present appellants in the SA khatian does not ipso facto confer/create right, title and ownership of the present appellants in the suit property because it has been settled as soon as invasion over title is made, then the aggrieved party can bring a suit and hence in the instant suit, the plaintiff was not required to challenge the preparation of the latest record though stands in the name of the predecessor of the defendant No. 2-appellants, Hira Lal Agorwala.
18. The learned counsel next contends that, there had been no necessity to execute any kabuliat against the amalnama by the predecessor of the plaintiff to become it effective.
19. The learned counsel in that respect further adds that, even an amalnama was not required to be registered under section 107 as well as sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act.
20. The learned counsel by relying upon a decision reported in 11 BLT (BCD) 131 also contends that, in view of the principle so have been followed by a Hindu in accordance with Dayabhag School of Hindu Law, certain conditions have to be fulfilled to take adoption of any Hindu and since that very precondition set forth therein has not been fulfilled in taking defendant No. 2 as adopted son by Hira Lal Agorwala, the defendant No. 2-appellants has not acquired any property left by Hira Lal Agorwala.
21. The learned counsel in that respect further contends that, it has clearly been stipulated therein that to take adoption to any Hindu son or daughter, his/her biological father and mother must give consent but in the instant case, nothing sort of this is found to have happened and in that sense, the case of the plaintiff respondent is that, since the condition has not been fulfilled so the alleged adoption of  the predecessor of the appellants, taken by Hira Lal Agorwala cannot be sustained in law.
22. The learned counsel in his next breath also contends that, it is not Hira Lal Agorwala rather after the demise of Hira Lal Agorwala his wife, Fulia Bie took adoption of the defendant No. 2 and since Fulia Bie has not acquired any land left by her husband, Hira Lal Agorwala so invariably, the defendant No. 2, predecessor of the appellants did get nothing on the demise of Hira Lal Agorwala.
23. The learned counsel by referring to the decision reported in 73 DLR (AD) 119 also contends that, since the amalnama is 30 years old so under the provision of section 90 of the Evidence Act that very document would be treated as genuine one.
24. The learned counsel wrapped up his submission contending that, a title deed always prevails over the record-of-right and since the plaintiff has been able to prove acquiring title over the suit property through amalnama, a proven title deed so the preparation of SA record in the name of the predecessor of the present appellant will not made any deviation in acquiring and enjoying title by the plaintiff-predecessor of respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(g) in the suit property and finally prays for dismissing the appeal.
25. We have considered the submission so advanced by the learned counsels for the appellants and that of the respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(g) at length.
26. It is not denying that, the plaintiff filed the suit claiming the suit land on two different counts, firstly, for declaration of title and secondly, for partition claiming to be undivided one, In order to address those core issues, we would like to look at the plaint in the first place in particular, the cause of action which has been described in paragraph No. 8 to the plaint. In paragraph No. 8, it has clearly been asserted that, on 2nd Joistha, 1399 BS corresponding to 16-5-1992, the defendants denied title of the plaintiff in the suit land as well as denied to partition the same in his favour. In regard to acquiring title over the suit property, the plaintiff has fully based his title on the execution of amalnama. For such obvious reason, we would like to take a glance of the contents of amalnama which has been marked as Exhibit 7 by the plaintiff. On going through the amalnama, we find that, Hira Lal Agorwala as the vendor or the lesser of the suit property measuring an area of 1.79 acres of land took Taka 6,001 as salami (consideration) and then settled the suit property in favour of his cousin, Gourishankar Agorwala.
27. Now we would like to look at how the said transaction can be proved by the plaintiff by adducing and producing evidences. At the first instance, from the trend of depositions, we find that, the PW 2 claimed to have knowledge about the execution of amalnama as his brother-in-law that is, Ajit Kumar Gosh stood as ascribe of that amalnama and he knew the signature of his said brother-in-law and therefore, he marked the amalnama and dakhila as 7-7ka though those very two documents were taken into evidence with objection raised by the defendant No. 2-petitioner when it was marked as exhibits. But in the cross-examination, that very PW 2 very candidly submitted that, since he was not present at the time of execution of amalnama so he has got no knowledge about any transaction alleged to have asserted in the body of the amalnama.
28. Now in regard to the transaction, we find the evidence of PW 5 to be vital who claimed to have remained present at the time of execution of that amalnama. He stated in his examination-in-chief that Taka 6,001 was taken by Hira Lal Agorwala by fixing yearly rent at Taka 28 in respect of 1.79 acres of land. He also claimed that, Hira Lal Agorwala put his signature in Hindi and he also marked the said amalnama as well as flak/sib (twice) as Exhibits 7 and 7-1. Though he claimed to have witnessed the transaction on that very date but while cross-examining that PW 5 by the defendant, he could not give the particulars of some vital information happened in his life that is, in regard to his marriage, date of birth of his son and even he asserted that he could not read the arnalnama and identified the signature put by attesting witnesses in it which alternatively proves that very PW 5 is none but a hired and tutored witness. In regard to enjoying possession none of the five witnesses even PW 5 could utter a single word that, the predecessor of the plaintiff, Gourishankar Agorwala ever took possession from Hira Lal Agorwala either after the alleged date of execution of amalnama or after the death of Hira Lala Agorwala in the year 1971.
29. On top of that, in that amalnama, there has been clear stipulation in the last part of it saying "recipient would register a "kaidiat" accepting the very amalnama". But fact remains, no kabithat was found to have given by the recipient that is, Gourishankar Agorwala in favour of the vendor or lesser, Hira Lal Agorwala leaving the execution and carrying out of the alleged amalnarna as concocted one.
30. Now we would like to further turn to the cause of action to see how invasion on title of the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 over the suit land has been made. As we have earlier observed by quoting paragraph No 8 of the plaint that, on 2nd Joishta, 1399 13S corresponding to 16-5-1992 since the defendant denied title of the plaintiff, he had then compelled to file the suit. But in the said paragraph, there has been no assertion in whose presence, the defendants denied title of the plaintiff. So in absence of any such case, the alleged case of the plaintiff in regard to invasion of title cannot stand rather proves to be a invented one having no basis. We see neither the plaintiff deposed as PW 1 nor the other plaintiff's witnesses in their respective evidence ever asserted when the title of the plaintiff was denied and on which circumstances that denial was made. So mere claiming that as soon as invasion is made over the title, the aggrieved party herein the plaintiff can file a suit having no necessity to challenge the propriety of preparation of any record-of-right simply does not hold water. So from the above, it is clear that, the plaintiff has hopelessly failed to make out his case of "invasion" on title in the suit property. Curiously enough, ongoing through the entire judgment, we don't find that, that very point has ever been discussed by the trial court though he decred the suit in-part. Rather what we found from the impugned judgment in regard to address the point of title of the plaintiff is, since the plaintiff's witnesses have been able to prove possession in the suit land by producing several rent receipts which were marked as exhibit-8 series, the plaintiffs have got title in the suit property. Mere having possession in any land does not confer title over it. In that regard, we can profitably rely on a decision passed by our Appellate Division so have been reported in 4 BLT (AD) 150 where it has been propounded that:
"Section 42—in a suit for declaration of title mere possession of the property is not sufficient unless the plaintiff can produce a document of title showing his acquisition of right, title and interest in the suit property."
31. So we find the above decision is squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.
32. Funnily enough, the learned Judge of the trial court admitted the title and possession in respect of 'ta' schedule land of the defendant No. 2-appellants asserting that he got 50% share out of 22 decimals of land and had it been so, there has been no rational not to find 1.79 acres of land in favour of the present appellants as the heirs of Hira Lal Agorwala but the learned Judge of the trial court has clearly misdirected himself on that very point and made out a third case providing 1/5 share out of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff even though, it is the definite case of the plaintiff that he is entitled to have ¼ share in the suit property claiming of having no share of the defendant No. 2 in the suit land. But it seems, the learned Judge in an over enthusiastic manner passed the impugned judgment.
33. Further, ongoing through judgment, we also find that, the learned Judge of the trial court has given much emphasis on the weakness of the defendant's case by discussing the evidence so adduced and produced by the defendant's witness and thereby declared title and gave saham to the plaintiffs by overlooking the settled and universal proposition that, the plaintiff is to prove his/her own case without depending on the weakness of the defendant's case by sidetracking universal proposition laid down in 9 BLT (AD) 66 = 6 BLC (AD) 41 where it has been held:
"There may be thousands of defects in the documents of the defence as well as their case but that will not entitle the plaintiff to get a decree as the plaintiff has to prove his case independent of the weakness of the defence case. From the materials on record, it appears that the plaintiff has failed to prove genuineness of their documents and also their possession which escaped the notice of the High Court Division and it only discussed the evidence of the defence and finding fault dismissed the defence case and restored the decree passed by the trial court in favour of the plaintiff which is not sustainable."
34. Though the learned counsel appearing for the appellants put much emphasis in regard to the genuineness of the alleged amalnama in acquiring title by referring to the provision of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and those of sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act asserting that, until and unless, that very amalnama is registered it will never confer any title upon its recipient though that very amalnama carries no legal value in absence of any kabuliat set to be furnished by the recipient leaving the amalnama unilateral deed and it cannot be acted upon. In that respect, the learned counsel has then placed his reliance in a slew of decisions which we earlier observed reported in 3 ALR (AD) 70 and 15 ADC 859. We have also gone through those very decisions and find substance in the submission as the very compulsion of registration such kind of document came into being in the year 1929. When admittedly alleged amalnama was registered in the year 1360 BS corresponding to 1953 AD. Though the learned counsel for the respondent opposes the said contention in regard to the legal necessity but could not provide any authority to controvert the said submission of the learned counsel for the defendant No. 2-appellants,
35. On top of that, in the amalnama which was marked as exhibit-7 by the plaintiffs, there has been clear stipulation that, in order to give effect of the amalnama, the recipient must furnish a 'kabuliat' and it is admitted position that, amalnama is an unilateral deed and until and unless, that very deed is accepted by the recipient through issuing kabuliat, the said amalnama can never be acted upon nor any title can be passed thereby. In that respect, we can also rely on a decision reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 232 where though kabuliat was given by the recipient to his landlord but against that no settlement or amalnama was given in favour of the lessee so the ratio in regard to the effectiveness of an unilateral deed will squarely be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as well.

36. Furthermore, in order to prove the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land, the learned Judge has given much stress on Exhibit 8 series which was produced at the instance of the plaintiffs in particular, PW 2, 3 and 4 who happened to be the tenants both under the plaintiff as well as defendant No. 2-appellants and from the evidence of those very witnesses it could not be clear who has actually been in possession in the suit shops standing on the suit land. Because, the defendant No. 4 who appeared in favour of the present defendant No. 2-appellant and full-brother of the defendant No. 2-appellant and the plaintiff as well, has clearly asserted that, the appellants have been enjoying title and possession over the suit property by building a Cinema Hall named, 'Nupur Cinema Hall' and the rent was given in respect of that very Cinema Hall to the defendant No. 2-predecessor of the appellants. He has also stated in his examination-in-chief that, before the demise of Hira Lal Agorwala, all the tenants had given rent to him and after his demise, the plaintiff used to collect the said rent and presently, the defendant No. 2- appellant has now been collecting rent and he again very strenuously stated that, the plaintiff has got no title and possession over the suit property. In the cross-examination, that very DW-3 clearly asserted “পান্না, শিব লাল কে ভাড়ার টাকা দিতে দেখিয়াছি”. It has been found from the materials on record that, after the demise of Hira Lal Agorwala, the plaintiff used to collect rent from the shops located in the suit land and handed the same to his wife, Fulia Bie. So, in regard to possession, it cannot be clear from the testimony of the plaintiff that he has got exclusive possessing over the suit land and he alone collected rent from the tenants of the suit property, still the learned Joint District Judge solely relying upon the evidence of PW 2, 3 and 4 found the plaintiff to be in possession over the suit property which is not based on materials on record as discussed above.
<u>37. Another tipping point is that, we came to learn from the argument so advanced by the learned counsel for the appellants and the respondent Nos. 1(a)-1(g) that, after preparation of the SA record in the respective area, the latest record that is, BS record was also prepared in the name of the present defendant No. 2-predecessor of the appellants as the heir of Hira Lal Agorwala and that very fact has been proved not by the defendant-appellants rather by the plaintiff himself who in his deposition as PW 1 clearly asserted “শিব লাল আগারওয়ালার নামে হাল রেকর্ডে ২টি ঘর হইয়াছে। শিব লাল পৌরসভার ট্যাক্স দেয়”. So since two consecutive records was prepared in the name of the predecessor of the present appellants so until and unless, that very record is declared inoperative no title can accrue in favour of the plaintiff, the predecessor of the respondent Nos. 1 (a)-1(g) even though the plaintiff has utterly failed to make out any case of "invasion" which is his core issue in claiming title over the suit property.</u>
38. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances, we don't find any iota of substance in the impugned judgment and decree which is vitiated by non-consideration of the evidence and materials on record let alone the legal provision involved in the matter as observed and discussed hereinabove.
39. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed however without any order as to costs.
40. The judgment and decree dated 7-8- 2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 29 of 1994 is hereby set-aside.
41. In regard to Cross Objection being No. 3 of 2004, we also don't find any iota of substance in regard to preferring thereof and the learned Joint District Judge in the impugned judgment has rightly disbelieved the case of the plaintiffs-respondents and found the defendant No. 2 to be entitled 50% of share and we thus don't find any illegality in the same.
42. In the result, the Cross Objection being No. 3 of 2004 is dismissed.
Let a copy of this judgment along with the lower court records be communicated to the court concerned as well as the respondents forthwith.
End.

full_judgment:
This Application under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 ("Act") is premised on the facts as set out below.

 

2. The petitioner, Mr Pankaj Roy and the Respondents are promoters-shareholders of Alliance Securities & Management Limited ("the Company"). At the 58th Meeting of the Company's Board of Directors ("HOD") held on 29-4-2013, the petitioner was elected as Chairman for two years "or until decision otherwise is taken unanimously by all members" of the BOD.

 

3. It is contended that the Respondent No. 1, Mr Tapan Krishna Podder failed to attend five consecutive BOD meetings without any leave of absence and by operation of section 108(1)(f) of the Act ceased to be a director of the Company. The petitioner served a notice dated 18-6-2015 on all the directors for holding a BOD meeting on 22-6-2015 pursuant to section 95 of the Act. The petitioner also served a notice on the Respondent No. 1, given that the primary issue raised at that BOD meeting of 22-6-2015 was the cessation of directorship of Respondent No. 1 by operation of law. It so transpired at the meeting that the Respondent Nos. 1-3 refused to accept the proposition that a director's post may become vacant by operation of section 108(1)(f). Resulting heated exchanges between all present led the petitioner, as Chairman, to adjourn the meeting and leave the premises. The petitioner contends that, therefore, the Respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3, in a mala fide manner, conducted another meeting that very day termed in the facts as the "Second Board Meeting". It was decided at that Meeting that the Respondent No. 3, Mr Partha Pratim Das shall be the new Chairman and the Respondent No. 1 the new Managing Director.

 

4. It is submitted by the petitioner that the Second Board Meeting was a new BOD meeting which ought to have been called and conducted by serving notice afresh on all the directors as per section 95. Furthermore, the Respondent No. 1 having ceased to be a director by operation of section 108(1)(f) well before the meetings of 22-6-2015, he, in particular, was not entitled to hold and attend any BOD meeting in the manner that he did. The minutes of the Second Board Meeting were signed by the Respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3. The petitioner submits, however, that since the Respondent No. 1 had ceased to be a director by that date by operation of law, the Second Board Meeting was held and resolutions passed therein without a quorum of three directors attending and voting as otherwise prescribed under Article 39 of the Articles of Association ("Articles").

 

5. Given the reasoning above the absence of a notice for the Second Board Meeting is submitted to manifest mala fide intention. It is submitted that both the calling of the said Meeting and the resolution adopted therein are now liable to be declared null and void. The intervening illegal election of a new Chairman and the appointment of a disqualified director as Managing Director have, according to the petitioner, made it impracticable to call and hold further BOD meetings. Consequentially, the petitioner has been constrained to file this Application under section 85(3) of the Act under which this Court has adequate judicially endorsed powers to cancel or modify BOD resolutions and pass any Order as deemed fit.

 

6. The Respondents' general contention in opposition is that the Respondent No. 1 was not absent consecutively from three HOD meetings. It is asserted that the Respondent No. 1 never failed to attend three consecutive BOD meetings (i.e. the 65th to 67th meetings) given that he duly attended the 66th ROD meeting. It is argued that section 108(1)(f) is, therefore, not applicable against the Respondent No. 1 and, as such, the instant Application is liable to be rejected.

 

7. It is noted at the outset that an Application as this under section 85(3) in the above facts and circumstances tests the limits of this Court's jurisdiction in its many facets. That is an issue raised by the Respondents that this Court most first address. As in several other instances, so here, there is merited reiteration of this Court's view that its intervention generally sought under the Act has to be predicated at the very outset of this Court's reading of its jurisdiction under section 3 of the Act. This Court finds that section 3 incorporates the essence of the exclusivity of this Court's jurisdiction under the Act subject, however, to the proviso therein. Evidently, the Government till date has had no cause to invoke its power under the proviso to empower any other court to exercise jurisdiction under the Act retaining intact, therefore, the exclusivity of this Court's jurisdiction under section 3 (Moqbul Ahmed us Ahmed Impex reported in 48 DLR (AD) 82, paragraph 11 at page 84). That being the case, this Court fully subscribes to Mr Justice KM Hasan's view, as he was then, in the High Court Division's Judgment in Abdul Muhit vs SIBL. reported in 54 DLR 306, in paragraph 19 at page 309 thus:

 

"I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates, perused the applications, affidavits-in-opposition and papers annexed to them. It is settled by a long line of decisions reported in 19 DLR 735, 20 DLR (SC) 335, 28 DLR 101, 44 DLR 452, AIR 1936 (Allahabad), (Fun Bench) 830, 79 Company Cases 830, AIR 947 Madras 322 that unless jurisdiction is provided in the Companies Act the petitioners cannot come to this Court for violation of any provision of the Act. The Company Court has a special company jurisdiction and that jurisdiction has to be found from specific provisions of the Act. Some of the specific provisions giving this court jurisdiction may be found in sections 12, 60, 43, 81, 85(3), 156, 197, 233 and 241. The "Court" referred to in these sections has been defined in section 2(d), according to which the "court" means court having jurisdiction under this Act, section 3(1) of the Act while giving jurisdiction to the court states "The court having jurisdiction under this Act shall be the High Court Division."

 

8. It is that special "Company Jurisdiction" that constitutes the starting point of considering the maintainability of this Application as raised by the Respondents along with the more substantive grounds raised by both parties. Indeed, this special statutory jurisdiction as attaches to this Court through specific provisions of the Act, inclusive of section indeed 85(3), came to be endorsed by the Appellate Division in Abdul Mohit Major (Retd) Dr. Rezaul Haque vs Social Investment Bank Ltd, reported in 2 ADC 492 = 67 DLR (AD) 82, The Appellate Division's findings on the exclusivity of this Court's statutory jurisdiction under the Act, therefore, anticipated and paved the way for the provisions of Rule 9 of the Companies Rules, 2009. Locating such jurisdiction within the perimeter of section 85(3) has also led this Court to delve into the maintainability of this Application given that this is a case not of an ordinary general meeting or an EGM not held but rather of DOD meetings purportedly held without conformity to law. The question posed, therefore, is with regard to this Court's authority to deliberate in matters already transacted at various BOD meetings including two meetings held on 22-6-2015. That dilemma has been addressed in a Judgment of the Appellate Division. In disposing of CPLA No. 3176 of 2013 on 25-5-2014 (Md Rafiqul Islam and others vs Mostafa kmal Mohiuddin and others), the Appellate Division addressed the challenge mounted against the High Court Division's intervention in BOD meetings under section 85(3). The Appellate Division found no reason to interfere with the High Court's Judgment given its interpretation of the breadth of the High Court Division's jurisdictional reach under section 85(3). The Appellate Division categorically held that section 85 brings within its purview all company meetings i.e. annual general meetings, BOD meetings and other meetings. Accordingly, a judicial justification was found by the Appellate Division for the matter of impracticability in holding BOD meetings to equally fall within this Court's jurisdiction for consideration and disposal.

 

9. The other objection raised concerning this Court's authority to reevaluate and revisit business already transacted in any meeting has been favorably addressed in a catena of decisions of which Satish Chandra Barak vs Dhaka Jute Mills Ltd. reported in PLD 1968 (Dac) 610 as well as in 19 DLR 280 and Ghyastuidin Ahmed vs Faruque reported in 38 DLR (AD) 296 are noteworthy. These authorities affirm this Court's ample powers under section 85(3) to give ancillary directions to call hold and conduct meetings in such manner as it deems fit and expedient. The ratio decidendi of these two cases has been the basis further for this Court's decision in ABM Khaliquzzaman & others vs United Commercial Bank Ltd. & another reported in 2 LCLR [2013] Vol 2 HCD 101 as well as 2008 BLD HCD 635 as affirmed by the Appellate Division in Reazaul Karim vs ABM Khalequzuman reported in 62 DLR (AD) 411.

 

10. Furthermore, in revisiting these cases in Mazakat Ali Harun vs EX1M Bank Ltd. reported in 18 BLC (AD) 68 the Appellate Division in reaffirmation of its pervious judgment in the Reazaul Karim Case confirmed this Court's entrenched authority to revisit the proceedings of any AGM or any company meeting to examine the legality of business already previously transacted therein. Any finding of illegality in such a context has been found as ground enough for this Court to nullify any transaction and require and direct meetings to be held afresh regardless of the fact of a previous meeting held. The Appellate Division in the Mazakat Ali, Harun Case delved extensively into a catena of precedents to arrive at the following decision at paragraph 17 at page 77 thus:

 

"Thus this Division has already laid down the law that even if AGM of a company is held and if it is found that any business was not transacted in accordance with law the Company Court can very much given ancillary directives in the matter of holding AGMs under section 85(3) of the Act, 1994 including the power to order a meeting of the company to be called, held and conducted in such manner as it thinks fit and expedient."

 

11. This Court, in the facts and circumstances, finds no reason to digress from that finding of the Appellate Division in the Mazakat Ali Harun Case and holds that the ratio therein by analogy amply and aptly covers the facts and circumstances arising in the present instance. The Respondents' preliminary objections as above are, therefore, dismissed as being without merit.

 

12. Focal to the petitioner's case is the application of section 108(1)(f) of the Act and the automatic vacation of office of a director. section 108(1)(f) allows for the office of a director to fall vacant if: "he absents himself from three consecutive meeting (sic) of the directors or from all meetings of the directors for a continuous period of three months, whichever is the longer, without leave of absent (sic) from the Board of Directors"

 

13. Five BOD meetings dating between 21-12-2014 and 19-2-2015, being the 65th, 66th, 67th, 68th and 69th meetings, are focal to the petitioner's case. Crucial further is the fact, as per the petitioner's contention, of the failure on the part the Respondent No. 1 to attend meetings reflecting absence continuously over a certain period of time without leave of absence from the BOD. Such period is roughly coextensive with a three-month period computed from 21-12-2014 and culminating approximately on 21-3-2015. The parties notably take opposing stands on the validity of two other subsequent meetings including the Second Board Meeting, both held on 22-6-2015.

 

14. The petitioner brings on record a table of attendance of each of these 130D meetings and attestations of attendance by individual signatures appended that establishes the continued absence of the Respondent No. 1 starting from the 65th down to the 69th meeting. It is noted that attendance of BOD meetings is to be deduced from an "Attendance Sheet" to which any director's signature would be affixed signifying actual attendance and/or by specific mention of such attendance reflected in the body of the meeting's minutes. Minutes, as a norm, should contain a record of members present. A practice has evolved in Bangladesh, as also, for example, in India, in the case of a Board Meeting to procure the members' signatures at the head of the first or top sheet to be used for the minutes. As A. Ramaiya notes, this practice obviates the need of having a separate book for recording the attendance of members and at the same time furnishes a record which can be used as evidence of the presence of any particular person at the meeting (See, "Guide to the Companies Act", Part-1, page 1811: 16th Edition, Reprint 2008). The absence of the signature of the Respondent No.1 in the relevant attendance sheets has, accordingly, been the decisive factor in the petitioner's case to establish the absence of the Respondent No. 1 from five consecutive BOD meetings held within a specified period of time. The Table below referred to and remarked upon by the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Reshad Imam sufficiently charts the holding of various BOD meetings and the fact of the Respondent No. 1 not having his presence registered particularly at the 65th down to the 69th BOD meetings by either signing the Attendance Sheet and/or having his presence acknowledged in the minutes of any such BOD meeting:

15. Indeed the Respondents contend that though the Respondent No. 1 did not attend 65th and 67th meetings he did in fact put in an appearance at the 66th BOD meeting, the appearance of the name of the Respondent No. 1 on the Attendance Sheet is relied upon to establish that fact.

 

16. The starting point of weighing the divergent views of the parties may indeed be Regulation 76(2) of Schedule (1) to the Act that requires directors attending any meeting to sign their names in a book kept for that purpose. That requirement gets varied in practice, and as acknowledged, for example, by Mr Pankaj Roy signed the Minutes as Chairman of the Board the meeting was adjourned by the Chairman, Mr Pankaj Roy. It is reflected in the Minutes that the other Directors were present in the Meeting. A. Ramaiya by directors' signatures appearing at the head of the top sheet of the minutes of BOD meetings to signify actual attendance. That is a practice prevalent in this jurisdiction as followed by the instant Respondent No. 4, Company itself. The Table above reflecting such practice in relation to the Company's BOD meetings beginning with the 62nd meeting reveals that attending directors have signed their names on the Attendance Sheets at the 62nd, 64th, 65th, 66th, 67th, 68th and 69th meetings. Additionally, the minutes of the 64th, 65th and 67th meetings reflect the presence, absence or partial attendance of the Respondent No. 1

 

17. The Respondent No. 1 contends that he attended the 66th BUD meeting as indicated by his name typed in the Attendance Sheet. The Company's consistent practice of additionally requiring signatures of attending directors, however, indicates otherwise. The Respondent No. 1 not having signed the Attendance Sheet for the 66th BOD meeting leads this Court to find that his office of a director stood vacant automatically under section 108(1)(f) around the third week of March, 2015, as computed from the date of the 65th BUD meeting.

 

18. This Court finds, therefore, that the Respondent No. 1 was absent without leave of absence from five consecutive BOD meetings beginning with the 65th and culminating in the 69th meeting and part of a period of three months eventually ending 21-3-2015, This was considerably before the spate of disputed BOD meetings held back-to-back under the aegis of rival groups on 22-6-2015. That leads this Court to question the standing of the Respondent No. 1 as of 21-3-2015 to continue as a Company director and attend the Second Board Meeting of 22-6-2015. That Meeting was held at the heels of an earlier meeting that very day presided over by the petitioner as Chairman to record that the office of director of the Respondent No. 1 had already been vacated. It is asserted that certain aggravated circumstances caused that First Board Meeting of 22-6-2015 to be adjourned and that at the Second Board Meeting held that day in the petitioner's absence the Respondent No. I was appointed Managing Director.

 

19. This Court finds that the automatic vacation of office under section 108(1)(f) is predicated on a minimum of administrative action in effecting the same. There is no requirement for the departing director like the Respondent No. 1, Mr Tapan Krishna Podder to additionally tender resignation to reinforce that which has transpired by operation of law. Mr Podder's office stood vacated as soon as the

 

Legal infirmity under section 108(1)(f) attached to him. As noted in Bharat Shushan vs FIB Portfolio Leasing Ltd. reported in (1992) 74 Comp Cas 20 Delhi, the vacation of office is automatic as soon as a director is found to have incurred the disability under the law. In this regard the law does away with the formality of any Board resolution confirming such vacancy. Nor does it envisage an opportunity given the affected director to show cause against imposition of such penalty (Shekhar Mehra vs Kilpess (P) Ltd, reported in (1986) 3 Comp LI 234 (MP)). The minimality of administrative action in this regard is also endorsed in Tanveerul Haque vs Unistar Shipping reported in 52 DLR 215. These cases obviate the necessity for any action extraneous to the law to reinforce that which has transpired automatically. This Court finds that anything nevertheless additionally done will be considered to be an act superfluous and redundant, but the absence of such external act shall not in any way negate the penalty imposed by law.

 

20. Given the above scenario this Court deduces that by the time that the 70th BOO meeting/First Board Meeting was called upon notice issued on 18-6-2015, the Respondent No. 1, Tapan Krishna Podder had already vacated office as director and, thereby, was shorn of all capacity to act qua director and assume office as Managing Director at the Second Board meeting of 22-6-2015.

 

21. The parties have deliberated at length on the adequacy of the agenda of the First Board Meeting of 22-6-2015. The agenda was simply of discussing a few matters pertaining to the Company. Here again, good practice appears to have filled a vacuum in the law to ensure preparedness and transparency in the conduct of Board meetings upon prior notification of specific agenda of such meetings. The law appears not to require prior notice of specific agenda but good corporate practice does. Even given that scenario, however, the absence in a specific instance, as in the case in the First Board Meeting, of a prior declaration of agenda cannot be considered to be a mandatory legal requirement failing which the business conducted at such meeting shall be deemed to be irregular. This view has been specifically stressed upon in cases like Abnas Kaur vs Lord Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd. reported in (1974), 44 Corn Cases 390, 413 (Del) and Sunil Dev vs Delhi District Cricket Association reported in (1994) 80 Corn Cases 174 (Del). A summing up of the judicial view with regard to a prior declaration of agenda of Board Meetings was succinctly done in Ferrucio J Koyaji vs Shanta G P Parulekar reported in (1998) 93 Corn as 750, (1994) 1 of LJ 345 (Del) (and as quoted in Halsbury Laws of India, 2007, 1701.27, 2007, Page 312 Para: 40, 483) thus:

 

 "The Companies Act 1956 does not provide that agenda of matters to be discussed and decided at a board meeting must be given in or along with the notice of the meeting, although it is customary and a good corporate practice to do that. The law does not require, as a general rule, agenda for the meetings of the directors and therefore, a meeting of which no agenda was given not be held to be an irregular meeting.

 

22. That ratio gets reflected further in Abnas Kaur vs Lord Krishna Sugar Mills Ltd., reported in (1974), Com Cases 390, 413 (Del) (and as quoted in Ramaiya Part 2, 16th Edition, Page 2760) where it was held that a Board of Directors can indeed transact business even without a formal agenda.

 

23. All parties are agreed that the 70th BOD meeting/First Board Meeting of 22-6-2015 was adjourned under unusual circumstances. The Respondents question, however, the petitioner Chairman's intent to so adjourn that meeting. It is noted that the 70th Meeting at that first instance centered on the automatic vacation of office by the Respondent No. 1. It is also acknowledged by all that the Respondent No. 1 was present at such First Board Meeting where events took a turn for the worse and further transaction of business had to be adjourned. Article 40 of the Articles recognizes the directors' capacity to adjourn meetings as deemed fit and an inherent authority necessarily reposes in the Chairman to so adjourn meetings. The very fact that the Second Board Meeting was held on 22-6-2015, but with the Respondents Nos. 1, 2 and 3 only being present to the petitioner's exclusion, bears testimony to the earlier meeting of that date being adjourned in less than amicable terms. But the very fact of adjournment of the previous meeting necessitated any subsequent meeting to only transact business that may have been left unfinished at the meeting from which the adjournment took place. There remains no scope from transacting any other business afresh. But that is preciously what happened in the Second Board Meeting. There is noted a marked deviation between the two successive Meetings of 22-6-2015 in that before the day was out the BOD had sanctioned a complete overhaul of the Company's management at the Second Board Meeting. This was accomplished in a manner not reflected in the notice of 18-6-2015 and was indeed not in the contemplation of the meeting from which the adjournment took place. That delinking of the two Meetings, in this Court's view, represents a meeting held afresh in the petitioner's absence without adequate notice. It was also a meeting, this Court finds, in which the Respondent No. 1 had no qualification in law to attend, deliberate and vote at in his capacity qua director. He had long been deprived of such capacity under the law since March, 2015. The Second Board Meeting of 22-6-2015 is, therefore, found to be a fresh one held not only in violation of the notice requirements in section 95 but also in blatant disregard of section 108(1)(f) of the Act. There is also the quorum requirement under Article 39 of the Articles that is attracted in the facts. It is found that business was purportedly transacted at that Second Board Meeting by only two directors qualified so to attend and vote.

 

24. For the reasons above this Court declares all proceedings of the Second Board Meeting and the business transacted therein null and void. No legal consequences resultantly are to be deemed to have flown at any material time from the purported decisions taken at that Meeting.

 

25. Consequentially, it is ordered that the Company's record shall henceforth aptly show the holding of a single 130D meeting, i.e., the 70th BOD meeting, called and adjourned on 22- 6-2015 under the Chairmanship of the petitioner. Such adjourned meeting may be convened at any date in the future but upon prior notice specifying the business to be transacted therein. Care should be taken to ensure that no business can be transacted at such adjourned meeting other than that left unfinished at the meeting from which the adjournment took place.

 

26. The findings and observations above do indeed, therefore, establish a scenario of the element of impracticability that had been introduced in the Company's affairs pending a final legal determination of the status of the Second Board Meeting purportedly held on 22-6-2015. That impracticability is seen to arise from the usurpation of office as director as well as that of Managing Director by the Respondent No. 1 on that date in a manner and circumstance wholly beyond the pale of the law.

 

27. Given that scenario, it is well within this Court's authority and jurisdiction to have entertained this Application and determined on the status of that particular Meeting as above. The Second Board Meeting of 22-6-2015 is, therefore, declared to be a nullity in the eye of law from which no legal consequence is found to have followed.

 

28. Accordingly, the Respondent No. 1, Mr Tapan Krishna Podder's continued holding of office as director beyond 23-1-2015 and arrogation of authority as Managing Director subsequently are found to be illegal and without any legal effect. It would now be open to the petitioner as the incumbent Chairman to call, hold and conduct the adjourned BOD meeting of 22-6-2015 upon due service of notice under section 95 of the Act upon all existing directors. Such meeting shall be held positively within 3(three) weeks computed from the date of the drawing up of this Order.

 

29. The learned Advocate for both parties confirm that no statutory filings were made pursuant to the BOD resolution passed in the Second Board Meeting of 22-6-2015 and, therefore, there is merited no additional direction from this Court to the Respondent No. 5, Registrar Joint Stock Companies and Firms to consider such filings, if any as a nullity and to have these expunged from the Registrar's records.

 

30. The petitioner and the Company are alerted to the fact that any failure to hold the adjourned meeting within the time frame signified above shall necessarily require the BOD to call a fresh meeting at any date thereafter fulfilling of course the notice requirements under section 95 of the Act.

 

31. In light of the above, this Application is allowed subject to the directions and observations above.

 

32. Let a certified copy of this Judgment and Order be specifically issued and served upon the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission at the cost of the petitioner.

 

There is no Order as to costs.

 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27.10.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2532 of 1996)
full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman J. This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 27.10,2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2532 of 1996, discharging the Rule, and, thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 23.05.1996 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd court, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No.74 of 1990, and, thereby, reversing the judgment and decree dated 19.06.1990 passed by the Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge, Narayangonj) in Title Suit No.9 of 1981 dismissing the suit. 

2. The present respondent No.1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.148 of 1977 in the Court of subordinate Court, (now Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Dhaka for specific pence of contract against the present respondent No.2 in the said suit, and, also for setting aside the exparte judgment and decree dated 03.03.1978 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Narayanganj in Title Suit Noi.148 of 1977 which was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Narayangonj and renumbered the same as Title Suit No.9 of 1981. 

3. Facts, leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that, one Omiya Narayan Ghosh, the owner of the suit land who transferred the suit land to the respondent No.1, Nirendra Chandra Das on 24.10.1973. Nirendra Chandra Dash entered into an agreement to transfer the suit land to the plaintiff and executed a Bainapatra on 29.10.1974, and, paid earnest money of Tk.17,000/-. But, sub-sequently, said Nirendra Chandra Das did not come to execute the sale deed on receipt of the balance amount of money. Thus, the plaintiff was compelled to file the suit. The respondent No.3 and her husband were aware of the Bainapatra, but, fraudulently, filed Title Suit. No.148 of 1977 for cancellation of the sale deeds of the year 1973 which was executed by Omiya Narayan Ghosh in favour of. Nirendra Chandra Dash, and, got an exparte decree during pendency of the instant suit. Hence the suit. 

4. In the aforesaid suit, one Chapala Rani Dash, the predecessor of the petitioner added herself as defendant No. 3 on 10.09.1981, and, filed written statement on 08.12.1981 contending, inter alia, that, her husband Sree Pati Kutner Das and Omiya Narayan Ghosh purchased the 3.15 acres of land including the suit land in equal share in auction, and, sub-sequently, the said Omiyatransferred his entire shares in the said undivided 3.15 acrer4 of land in favour of the defendant No.3 by a registered deed of sale dated 04.10.1976. Thereafter, it was transpired that, Omiya Narayan Ghosh fraudulently sold his 8 (eight) annas share in 3.15 acres of land which was executed and registered by the three deeds o sale of the year of 1973 in favour of defendant No. 1. Omiya never possessed the suit land, and, he never delivered possession of any part of the suit land to Nirendra Chandra Dash. 

5. After filing of the written statement on behalf of the defendant No. 3, the plain-tiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint on.-24.02.1990 by adding a prayer for declaration, that, the exparte decree dated 03.03.1978 passed by the learned Munsif, 4th Court, Narayangong in Title No.148 of 1977 is void, fraudulent and not binding upon plaintiff. The aforesaid prayer for amending was allowed by the order dated 29.03.1990. 

6. After amending of the plaint, the defendant No.3 filed an additional writ-ten statement stating, inter alia, that, she filed Title Suit No of 1977 on 07.07.1977, and, as such, the decree passed in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 is not hit: by the principal of lispendence, and, she had no Knowledge about the so called Bainapatra of the plaintiff before filing of the Title Suit No.148 of 1977. Moreover, the plaintiff was not a party in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977, and, as such, he has no locus standi to challenge the same. 

7. On conclusion of the trial, the Trial Court, considering the evidences and documents on record, dismissed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 19.06.1990. 

8. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the plain-tiff as appellant preferred Title Appeal No.74 of 1990 before the learned District Judge, Narayangonj. On transfer, the said appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.2, Narayangonj who by the judgment and decree dated 23.05.1996 allowed the appeal, and, thereby, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit. 

9. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree dated 23.05.1996 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, the heirs of the defendant No.3 as petitioners preferred Civil Revision No.2532 of 1996 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. 

10. In due course, a Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties discharged the Rule by the impugned judgment and order dated 27.10.2008, and, thereby, affirmed the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below. 

11. Feeling aggrieved, by the impugned judgment and order dated 27.10.2008 passed by the High Court Division, the defendants as petitioners herein preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.445 of 2009 before this Division, and, obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

12. Md. A. M. Aminuddin, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that, Chapala Rani Das, predecessor of the defendant-appellant before filing the instant suit for specific performance of contract filed a suit for declaration of her title in the entire suit land and for further declaration that sale deed by Omiyo to Mirendar is void, inoperative and fraudulent, the Court of appeal below in decreeing the instant suit for specific performance of contract wrongly set aside the decree obtained by Chapala in Title Suit No.148 of 1977 and the High Court Division committed an error in affirming the said decree passed by the Court of appeal below. He further submits that, before institution of the instant suit for specific performance of contract filed by Md. Alauddin Mia, plaintiff of the instant suit, Omiyo having transferred her share to Chapala Rani in the year 1976, relinquishing his entire share in the suit property, the Court of appeal below wrongly exercised its discretion in decreeing the instant suit, and, the High Court Division committed an error in affirming the said decree. He next submits that, both the appellate Court and the High Court Division railed to apply their mind to the evidence on record, misread it, and, thereby, arrived at an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that, the lower Appellate Court was wrong in decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract, when, clearly the plaintiff failed to perform his part of the contract, and, the. High Court Division on misreading of the material evidence on record affirmed the decision of the Court of appeal below. He further submits that, the High Court Division was wrong in upholding the decision of the Appellate Court without noticing that, the Appellate Court did not properly advert to the reasons assigned by the Trial Court. He also submits that, for non-service of summons Title Sit No.148 of 1977 revise and Nirendar's title remaining subjudice, the respondent No.1 cannot get a decree of specific per-formance. He finally submits that, the suit specific performance of contract suffers from the defect of multifariousness due to inclusion of prayer declaration that decree in title suit No. 148 of 1977 is not binding on the respondent No.1, and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed.

13. Mr. Khair Ejaj Masood, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He submits that, on 19.08.1977, the respondent No.1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.117 of 1977 for Specific Performance of Contract. According to the contract, Exhibit-1, the price was fixed at Tk.l8,800/- of which Tk.17,000/- was paid as earnest money, and, the rest was fixed to be paid within two years, and, the agreement also contain a default clause. The plaintiff in his deposition has clearly stated that, he made the offer of the rest of the contract money within the stipulated time of two years and, thereafter, issued a written notice on 01.08.1977, and, on the refusal by the defendant No.1, Nirendra. Chandra Das, the suit was filed. In deposition, the P.W.1 categorically stated that, he made the offer within the stipulated period, and, this statement of the P.W. 1 was not challenged by cross-examination, hence, this statement remained uncontroverted, and, would be deemed to have been admitted. Under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, the period of limitation in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract is 3 years from the date fixed for performance. This view finds support from the case reported in 42 DL R (AD)63. Moreover, in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, time is not the essence of contract specially when the suit was filed within time, and, this view finds support from the 5 MLR AD 189 case. He further submits that, the plaintiff has filed the original Kabla executed by Omiva in favour of the plaintiff and these registered kabalas carry a presumption of their correctness and the documents (Exhibits 2-4) filed from the custody of the plaintiff lend support to the genuineness of the agreement. From Exhibit-6, it appears that, the decree was obtained against the defendant No.1, Nirendra Chandra as by suppression of summon, and, the same is apparent from the service return (Exhibit-10) which shows Omiya Ghosh has remained untraced, and, the application for service of summon under Order 5 Rule 20 was prayed for, but, order sheet (Exhibit-9) shows that, the, Court passed no order, and order dated 09.02.197 further shows that, the suit was fixed for Service Return which was not received, and, by the same order, the Court found that, the service return has been received, and, fixed on 03.03.1978 for exparte hearing without giving any chance for filing written statement. The Court was not competent to proceed for an exparte decree. In such circumstances, thus, fraud is apparent in bringing about the exparte decree. Hanes, the, High Court Division rightly passed the impugned judgment. Therefore, he prays for dismissal of the instant appeal. 

14. We have heard the learned Senior Counsels for the respective parties. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

15. Leave was granted to examine the following submissions of the learned Senior Advocate for the appellants as to that-
"(1) Because, both the Appellate Court and the High Court Division failed to apply their mind to the evidence on record, misread it and thereby arrived at an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. 
(II) Because, the High Court Division was wrong in upholding the decision of the Appellate Court without noticing that the Appellate Court did not properly advert to the reason assigned by the trial Court. 
(III) Because, that the Appellate Court was wrong in decreeing the suit of specific performance of when clarify the plaintiff failed to perform his part of the contract in making payment of balance money and the High Court. Division affirmed the decision of the Appellate Court upon complete misreading of the oral evidence. 
(IV) Because, the decree in T. S. No. 148/1977 being binding on Nirendra until it is set aside, respondent No. 1 claiming through Nirendra was bound by it and cannot claim decree for specific performance. 
(V) Because, for non-service of summons Title Suit No.148/77 revives and Nirendar's title remaining subjudice respondent No. I can-not get a decree of specific performance. 
(VI) Because, the suit for specific performance suffered from the defect of multifariousness due to inclusion of a prayer for declaration that the decree in T.S. No. 148/77 is not binding on respondent No. 1." 

16. At this moment let us weigh up the evidence on record, state of affairs of the cases, and decisions of the three (03) Courts below, whether judgment and order of High Court. Division is justified or erred which calls for interference by this Division. 

17. For obtaining a decree meant for specific performance of contract, in addition to the execution of an agreement fairly and without any inducement, coercion or fraud and the question of limitation, the following questions are sine qua non: 
"Whether there subsists a legitimate and concluded contract amid the parties for sale/purchase of the property; 
Whether the Plaintiff was prepared and willing to carry out his portion of contract and whether he is still ready and willing to perform his part as mentioned in the contract; 
Whether the Plaintiff has, in fact, performed his part of the contract and, if so, how and to what extent and in what manner he has per-formed and whether such performance was in conformity with the terms of the contract; 
Whether it will be equitable to grant the relief of specific performance to the plaintiff against the defendant in relation to suit property or it will cause any kind of hardship to the defendant and if so, how and in what manner and the extent if such relief is eventually granted to the plaintiff; 
Whether the plaintiff is entitled for grant of any other alternative relief, namely refund of earnest money, etc. and if so, on what grounds.

18. In the instant case there is no iota of controversy about subsisting of a legitimate contract amid the parties for sale/purchase of the suit property. However, question remains whether the contract has been concluded or not there was a condition precedent in the contract and that is, the vendee should have to pay the rest amount and thereby conclude the happening of the execution and registration of the Kabala intended to. The concerned portion is as follows: 
".. অদ্য তারিখে বায়না বাবদ নগদ মং ১৭,০০০.০০ সত্তর হাজার টাকা বুঝিয়া পাইয়া অত্র বায়না পত্র লিখিয়া দিয়া স্বীকার ও অঙ্গীকার করিতেছি ��ে, অদ্য হইতে আগামী ২ দুই বৎসরের মধ্যে আপনি আমার প্রাপ্য বক্রী মং ১৮০০.০০ এক হাজার আটশত টাকা আমাকে বুঝাইয়া দিয়া আপনার নিজ খরচে আমার দ্বারা সাফ কবলা সম্পাদন ও রেজিস্ট্রারী করিয়া নিতে বাধ্য রহিলেন। যদি উক্ত সময় মধ্যে আমার পাওয়ানা বক্রী টাকা আমাকে বুঝাইয়া না দেন বা সম্পত্তি নিতি অস্বীকৃত হন তবে আপনার বায়না দেওয়া উক্ত টাকা বাজেয়াপ্ত হইবে, আর ষদি আমিও আমার পাওয়ানা উক্ত বক্রী টাকা আমি গ্রহণ না করি বা আপনার আপনি উপযুক্ত আদালতে আমার প্রাপ্য উক্ত বক্রী টাকা দাখিল করিয়া দিয়া আদালত যোগে সাফ কবলা সম্পাদন ও রেজিষ্টারী করিয়া নিতে পারিবেন, ইহাতে আমি কিংবা আমার পুত্র পোত্রাদি ওয়ারিশানগণের যে কোন প্রকার গুজরাপত্তি আইনতঃ আদালতে অগ্রাহ্য ও নামঙ্জুর হইবে ।”

19. In this juncture the Respondent-plaintiff as PW 1, in his examination in chief asserted that: 
“বায়না পত্রের পরে আমাকে নালিশা ভূমির দখল বুঝাইয়া দেয়। বায়না পত্রের মেয়াদ ছিল ২ বৎসর। কথা হয় যে বাদী টাকা দিলে দলিল রেজিস্ট্রি করিয়া দিবে। আমি অবশিষ্ট টাকা ম্যাদ মধ্যে নাই। তৎপর বাকী টাকা নিয়া দলিল রেজিস্ট্রী তারিখ মনে নাই। নোটিশ আদালতে দাখিল করি। ১নং বিবাদী নোটিশ রাখে নাই। করলা না দেওয়ার কারণে আমি চুক্তি প্রবালে কবলা পাওয়ার মামলা করিয়াছি। আসি বক্রী টাকা আদালতে দাখিল করিতে প্রস্তুত আছি। আমি চুক্তি মুলে কবলা সম্পাদনের ডিক্রী চাই।”

20. In his Cross-examination he admitted that:
"দলিল করার জন্য ২ বছর নেয়। বিক্রেতা কেন ঐ সময় নেয় বলিতে পারি না। ২ বছর কবে শেষ হয় খেয়াল নাই। ২ বছর মধ্যে লিখিত নোটিশ দেন নাই। বায়নাপত্রে শর্ত আছে যে দুই বৎসর মধ্যে দলিল করিয়া না নিলে বায়নার টাকা বাজেয়াপ্ত হইবে? ম্যাদ মধ্যে আমি নোটিশ দেই নাই। ১৯-৮-৭৭ ইং মামলা পায়ের সময় বায়না পত্র বলবৎ ছিল না। মামলাটি তদবীরের অভাবে ৩ বার খারিজ হয়। নিরেন্দ্রকে টাকা সাধার তারিখ বলিতে পারি না। কার মোকাবেলায় সাধি খেয়াল নাই । নিরেন্দ্র কোথায় থাকে জানি না। কবে কোথায় শেষ দেখি খেয়াল নাই ।”

21. On meticulous reading of the aforementioned statements it is as clear as daylight that though the PW 1 claimed that he offered his vendor the rest amount within the stipulated time enumerated in the very contract, nevertheless, there is no corroboration of this statement. In addition, he admitted that he did not give notice within time; pm 19-8-77, the time of filing of the suit the Bainapatra was not in force; he can't tell the date of offering the rest amount to Nirendra; couldn't say on whose presence he offered the rest amount; he don't know where Nirendra lives and when and where he last saw him. The obvious inferences from these statements any person of ordinary prudence should make are that PW 1 didn't offer the rest amount to Narendra, his vendor inside required timeframe as such, as per the condition precedent of the contract itself, not only the earnest money paid by the PW 1 to his vendor became confiscated but also there existed no valid contract between them to be specifically performed. 

22. Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 of the 4th Court of learned Munsif, Narayanganj was decreed on 03.03.1978. Defendant No. 3 filed an application under Order 1, Rule 10 CPC to be added as a party in the instant suit mentioning therein of that decree, with copy to the plaintiff, on 02:04.1981. And the plaintiff filed the application for smendment of plaint to include Prayer for declaration in respect of the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 on 24.02.1990. That is, almost 9 years after plaintiffs knowledge of the ex parte decree in Title Suit Nb. 148 of 1977 on 24.02.1990. 

23. Article 120 in the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908- Period of limitation for the suit for which no period of limitation provided elsewhere in this schedule is 6 year from the date of the right to sue accrues. It is apparent that the instant suit so far it relates to relief against ex parte decree dated 03.03.1978 in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

24. After inclusion of the relief in respect of ox part e decree dated 03.03.1978 in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977, Omiya Narayan Ghush, defendant No, 2 of the said suit was a necessary party to the suit, and the plaintiffs application for amendment of the plaint ought to have been coupled with a prayer for addition of Omiya Narayan Ghosh as a defendant in the suit, and that having been not done, the suit became bad for defect of parties too. 

25. The suit suffers from defect of multifariousness for adding the prayer for declaration in respect of ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 in a suit for specific performance of contract. In Golaw Fader Vs. Abdul Khaleque Choukder, 43 DL R (AD) 107 (Para-8], it has been held by this Divinitsn-
"In a suit for specific performance of contract, the real question to be determined is whether the contract for sale between the parties was genuine, whether on the basis thereof the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree. Nothing is permissible in law in such a suit which will convert the suit for specific performance of contract into a suit for determination for title." 

26. The claim of the plaintiff is based on the title of Narendra. The decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 being binding on Nirendra until it is set aside, the plaintiff too bound by it and cannot claim decree for specific performance of contract. In this regard, the arguments advanced on behalf of the respondent is of no sub-stance for the simple reason that the appellate court while declaring the decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 is not binding on the plaintiff, did not dismiss that Title Suit No. 148 of 1977. In view of the above ratio decidendi, a suit for specific performance of contract cannot be converted into a suit for any other purposes that affects title of the suit land. 

27. The findings of the appellate court and the High Court. Division on service of summons in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977, and the submissions made on behalf of the respondents in this regard are totally misconceived and wrong which is apparent from the entire Order Sheet of Title Suit No. 148 of 1977. Order No. 6 dated 29.09.1977 Order No. 8 dated 19.12.1977 and Order No. 10 dated 09.02.1978 clearly show that service of summons was effected by Registered Post with AD, and AD was received by the court. This manner of service has presumption of due service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 which contemplates as follows: 
"27. Where any Act of Parliament Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing prepaying and posting by registered post a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 

28. Substituted service under Order 5,  Rule 20, CPC was also done, and Service Return was received by the court. Rule 20 of Order 5, CP provides 
"Substituted Service. (1) Where the Court if satisfied that there reason to believe that the defendant is keeping out of the way for the purpose of avoiding service, or that for any other reaon the summons cannot be served in the ordinary Way, the Court shall order the summons to be served by affixing a copy thereof in some conspicuous place in the Court house, and also upon some conspicuous part of the house, if any) in which the defendant is known to have last resided, or carried on business, or personally worked for gain, or any such other manner as the Court thinks fit." 
Effect of Substituted Service. (2) Service substituted by order of the Court shall be as effectual as if it has been made on the defendant personally. 
Where Service Substituted, time for appearance to be fixed. (3) Where service is substituted by order of the Court, the Court shall fix such time for the appearance of the defendant as the case may require." 

29. Substituted service was effected in the last known address of Nirendra Chandra Das as per requirement of Order 5, Rule 20, CPC which is apparent from the Bainapatra, (Exhibit-1), and the plaint of Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 (Exhibit-10) in both places the address of Nirendra Chandra Das is same. So, as per Rule 20(3), Order 5, CPC, the service is effectual as if it has been made, on the defendant personally. 

30. Submission on behalf of the respondent with reference to Order 2, Rule 7, CPC is of no substance inasmuch as it is evident from the additional written statement that defendant No.3 took objection against inclusion of Prayer (1) in the plaint in respect of ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 148 of 1977 at the earliest: possible opportunity, that is, immediately after allowing amendment of plaint. So, there is no waiver against inclusion of Prayer (0 in the plaint within the meaning of order 2, Rule 7, CPC. 

31. In paragraph No. 5 of the plaint, it was stated- "he also executed a Bainapatra on 29.10.1974 corresponding to 11 Kartik, 1381 B.S. in favour of the plaintiff acknowledging the payment of said amount of Tk. 17,000/00 (Seventeen thousand) only as advance, and also surrendered physical possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff on the same date." 

32. But in Prayer (e) (o) of the plaint, it was prayed- "e) Put the plaintiff into physical possession in the suit, property through Court by removing all obstacle, if any, into the suit property." 33. The plaintiff as PW 1 stated in his examination-in-chief: 
বায়না পত্রের পরে আমাকে নালিশা ভূমির দখল বুঝাইয়া দেয়।”
In cross-examination, PW I stated: 
“আরজীর বিবরণ সত্য । আমি আরজীতে নালিশা ভূমির দখল চাই। সত্য নহে যে, নালিশা ভূমিতে আমার দখল নাই এই জন্য আদালতে যোগে দখল চাই। .... ১৯.৮.৭৭ ইং মামলা দায়ের সময় বায়নপত্র বলবৎ ছিল না।”

34. On the other hand, all the defendant's witnesses DW 1, 2, 3 and 4 credibly and consistently supported the case of writ-ten statement, and additional written statement. 

35. In civil suit/eases the established principle of proving facts is preponderance of evidences. In this case it is palpable evident that the respondent-plain-tiff failed to prove the vital facts affecting the very result of the suit. Rather, to this Division the case of the appellants-defendants deems to be proved believably. Apart from all other aspects of the case, the inherent vital contradictions in the plaint and the testimony of the plain-tiff as PW 1 are enough for dismissal of the suit. 

36. Our considered view is that, the Appellate Court on misconception of law, and misreading and wrong appreciation of evidence on record committed error of law resulting in erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice in allowing the appeal and decreeing the suit, and the High Court Division while sat on judgment of reversal, totally failed to appreciate evidence on record in order to arrive at its own independent decision, as such, was wrong in affirming the same by discharging the Rule. 

37. Accordingly, we find merit in the submissions- of the learned Counsel for the appellants. 

38. In view of the above the discussions the decision of the Appellate Court in decreeing the suit as a whole is found to be based upon total non-application of judicial mind and not been supported by evidence. As such, it should be reversed. The suit be dismissed. 

39. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 27.10.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2532 of 1996 and judgment of Court of appeal below dated 13-05-1996 are hereby set aside. 

End.
