case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29.01.2006 passed by the high court division in Civil Revision No. 2597 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Krishna Debnath J. This Civil Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 29.01.2006 in Civil Revision No. 2597 of 1997 passed by the high court division making the Rule absolute in part after reversing the judgment and decree dated 21.01.1997 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Bagerhat (in-charge) in Title Appeal No. 145 of 1994 and affirming those dated 31.05.1994 passed by Assistant Judge, Kachua in Title Suit No. 36 of 1991 dis-missing the suit. 

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are that respondent Nos. 1 & 2. instituted Title Suit no.36 of 1991 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Kachua for declaration of title in 2.96 acres of land out of 4.44 acres appertaining to CS khatian No. 145, Mouza Badhai, PS Kachua, District-Bagerhat and also for a further declaration that the enlistment of the suit property as vested property to be illegal, void, ultra vires not binding upon the plaintiffs and also for a decree restraining the defendants permanently from dispossessing the plaintiffs from the suit property and also for a further relief for setting aside the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No 511 of 1983 of the First Munsifs Court. Bagerhat contending, inter alia, that the entire land of CS khatian No.145 measuring an area of 4.44 acres belonged to Darikanath and Rajkumar in equal shares. Darikanath died leaving behind only son named Krishnalal. Thereafter Rajkumar died leaving behind 2(two) sons named Mohendra and Dhirendra. It is the further case of the plaintiffs that 8(eight) annas share belonged to Mohendra and Dhirendra sold in auction in Money Execution Case No. 6 of 1950 and that auction was purchased by Krishnalal. This way Krishnalal became the owner and possessor in 16 annas share in the land of CS khatian No.145. Thereafter Krishnalal died leaving behind 3(three) sons, the plaintiff Nos. 1, 2 and the defendant No.9. The S.A. record was wrongly recorded in the name of Mohendra and Dhirendra. The plaintiffs came to know about the said fact when the defendant No. 1 disclosed about the same on 06.01.1990 and also about the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No. 511 of 1983. It is the further case of the plaintiffs that the defendant No.1 claimed that he got lease of eight annas share in the jote from the vested property authority vide lease case No.11(Ka)of 72-73 and as such the suit. 

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaintiffs case contending, inter-alia, that the land of CS khatian No. 145 belonged to Darikanath and Rajkumar in equal shares. The entire land of that khatian was put to auction in Title Execution Case No.133 of 1944 and that auction was purchased by Sharaswati, the wife of Darikanath. The sale certificate was issued to her on 01.08.1945. Thereafter she sold 2.22 acres of land by a kabala dated 08.02.1946 in favour of Mohendra and Dhirendra. She again transferred 0.55 acres of land by a patta dated 21.02.1951 in favour of defendant No.7 and again transferred 1.05 acres of land by another patta dated 25.04.1953 in favour of said defendant No.7. After those transfers she had possession in 0.62 acres of land but that land was wrongly recorded in the name of Mohendra and Dhirendra. The said Sharaswati sold that 0.62 acres of land by a kabala dated 06.10.1983 in favour of Nirmalkanti. Thereafter she filed the Title Suit No. 511 of 1983 for correction of the SA record in respect of 0 .62 decimals impleading the plaintiffs to be defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and got an exparte decree on 27.04.1955. It is his further case that Mohendra and Dhirendra left for India in 1965 and their shares were declared as Enemy Property. The plaintiff No.1 had taken lease of 2.37 acres from the Enemy Property Authority vide the Miscellaneous Case No.11(Ka) of 7273. That lease was continued till 1990 and thereafter the defendant no. 1 took lease of said land from the Enemy Property Authority. It is the further case of the defendant no.1 that he purchased .77 decimals of land from the defendant No.7. 

4. The defendant No.3 contested the suit stating, inter-alia that one Siddiqur Rahman purchased o.15 decimals of land from the co-sharers and thereafter sold that land by a kabala dated 15.06.1983 to him. 

5. The defendant No.8, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter-alia, that 8(eight) annas share of CS khatian No. 145 belonged to Mohendra and Dhirendra and that share was declared as enemy property. That land was leased out with the plaintiffs and after expiry of lease term the same was leased out with the defendant No. 1. That land again was leased out with the plaintiffs. The Vested Property Authority had been in possession in the said 8(eight) annas share of the land appertaining to CS khatian No.145. 

6. Trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit on 31.05.1994. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs filed Appeal No. 145 of 1994 which was heard by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court Bagerhat and dismissed on 21.01.1997. 

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree, the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 2597 of 1997 where the high court division making the Rule absolute in part after reversing the judgment and decree dated 21. 01.1997 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Bagerhat (in-charge) in Title Appeal No. 145 of 1994 and that dated 31.05.1994 passed by Assistant Judge, Kachua in Title Suit No. 36 of 1991 dismissing the suit. 

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 29.01.2006 passed by the high court division, the defendant petitioners preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 427 of 2006 before this Division and a leave was granted considering the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant. 

9. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Advocate for the appellant submits that entire land of CS khatian No. 145 was purchased by Saraswati in Title Execution Case No. 133 of 1945 and the sale certificate was marked as exhibit "Uma". 

10. He further submits that the plaintiffs' predecessors' share was totally exhausted by the auction sale held vide Title Execution Case No. 133 of 1944. Lastly he submits that the high court division without pointing to any legal error in the findings arrived at by the courts below made the Rule absolute and as such the impugned judgment and order of the high court division shall be set aside. 

11. On the other hand Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submits that respondents are admittedly co-sharers in respect of 8(eight) annas share in the suit jute, in absence of any document of Title Execution Case No. 133 of 1944 no title can pass in favour of Saraswati. He supports the judgment and order of the high court division and prays for dismissal of the appeal. 

12. We have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and have considered their submissions, perused the records and others. 

13. It is admitted that the total land measuring an area of 4.44 acres of khatian No. 145, mouja Badhal belonged to Darikanath and Rajkumar in equal shares. It is the plaintiffs' case that Rajkumar died leaving behind 2(two) sons named Mohendra and Dhirendra and their shares were sold in auction in money. Execution Case No. 6 of 1950. It is their further case that by that auction purchase, Krishnalal became the absolute owner and possessor in 4.44 acres and thereafter he died leaving behind the plaintiff Nos. 1 & 2 and the defendant No. 9 as his 3(three) sons. It is their case that amicably the plaintiffs have possession in 2.96 acres and the defendant No. 9 has possession in the rest 1.48 acres. Lastly their case is that the order treating of 2.22 acres as vested property is illegal in view of the fact that long before the promulgation of the law of Enemy Property, the shares of Mohendra & Darikanath were sold in auction. 

14. On the otherhand the defendant No. l's case is that the entire land of the jote was sold in auction in Title Execution Case No, 133 of 1944 and that was purchased by Saraswati. It is his further case that Saraswati was exhausted by the transfers made by kabala dated 08.02.1946, 06.10.1983 and by patta dated 21.02.1951 and 25.04.1953. Lastly his case is that the plaintiffs have neither title nor possession in the suit land. 

15. The high court division found that the defendant has failed to produce any paper in support of Title Execution Case No. 133 of 1944. The high court division also found that both the courts below have failed to consider this important fact.
 
16. But it appears from the record that the court of Appeal below as the last court of facts concurred with the findings of the Trial Court that the Saraswati acquired the title and possession in respect of entire 4.44 acres of land belonging to predecessors of the plaintiffs by way of auction purchase in Execution Case No. 133 of 1944 and that this defendant No. 1 submitted: the writ of delivery of possession vide exhibit "Uma" in support of title of said Sharaswati. The high court division was wrong in finding that no title passed in favour of transferees from Sharaswati by kabala deed dated 04.02.1946, by patta dated 21.02.1951, 25.04.1953 and the deed dated 06.10.1983 upon an erroneous view that the auction purchase by Sharaswati is not supported by any delivery of possession. 

17. It further appears from the record- that plaintiff respondents did not challenge or filed any case against the Execution Case No. 133 of 1944 or against the exparte decree passed in. Title Suit No. 511 of 1963. The high court division without any legal footing found that the exparte judgment and decree was collusively obtained.
 
18. In view of the above, we found that the high court division upon an erroneous view made the rule absolute in part and hence the judgment and order of the high court division is liable to be interfered. 

19. In the result the appeal is allowed. 

20. The impugned judgment and order of the high court division is hereby set aside. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 1st November, 20] 8 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10919 of 2011)
full_judgment:
M. Enayetur Rahim J. This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 01.11.2018 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.10919 of 2011 making the Rule absolute. 

2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that the writ petitioners-respondents filed the writ petition No.10919 of 2011 in the High Court Division challenging the letter communicated under memo No. মপ্রাম/ম-১/ডিপিসি-০১/১১/৮৫৯ তারিখ ১৫/১২/২০১১ issued by the Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, and for a direction upon the respondents to finalize the amendment of the schedule of B.C.S. (Fisheries), Recruitment Rules, 1981 as per recommendation dated 17.12.2003 under Memo No. প্রঃশা-১৫-৮৫ (৫ম খন্ড)/১৯৭৯ and decision taken by the authority dated 24.11.2001, 14.11.2001 and 25.08.1992 to provide 1/3rd appointment by promotion to the entry level cadre post from the feeder post of the 2nd Class Gazetted Officers according to seniority of the gradation list, Directorate of Fisheries (Annexure-C to the writ petition) and resolution dated 28.07.1987 and 17.05.1999 taken by the Ministry of Fisheries and livestock and Resolution dated 11.11.2001 taken by the Ministry of Public Administration. 

3. In the writ petition, it is contended that the writ- petitioners getting appointment as Fishery Survey Officers, Assistant Firm Managers, Technical Assistants, have been serving in their respective services for about 15 to 27 years but they did not get any promotion. On 28.07.1987, a meeting was held presided over by the Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock with an agenda to amend B.C.S (Fishery) Recruitment Rules, 1981 and it was decided that in entry level, 2/3rd post should be recruited directly and the rest 1/3rd post should be filled up by way of .promotion. Accordingly, the proposal of amendment of B.C.S. Recruitment Rules was sent to Public Service Commission. On 25.08.1992, the Public Service Commission sent a letter to the Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration stating that the proposal of the amendment of the Rules has been accepted with some modification. On 10.11.2001 another meeting was held presided over by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration and it was decided in the said meeting to amend the schedule of the Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing the provision that 1/3rd post should be appointed in the entry level by way of pro-motion from the feeder post. On 24.11.2001, Ministry of Public Administration issued a letter addressing the Ministry of Fishery and Livestock requesting them to execute the decision of the Ministry of Public Administration held on 10.11.2001. On 17.12.2003, the Director General, Department of Fishery issued a letter addressing the Secretary, Ministry of Fishery and Livestock stating that the schedule of the B.C.S (Fishery) Recruitment Rules, 1981 has been amend-ed. Accordingly, it was provided to appoint 1/3rd to the entry level from the feeder post by way of promotion. But the Ministry of Fisheries failed to take any positive step. In such view of the matter, the writ-petitioners, compelled to file the writ petition. 

4. The High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order, made the said Rule absolute. 

5. Thus, the Government and others had filed civil petition for leave to appeal No.43 of 2011 and leave was granted. 

6. Hence, the present appeal. 

7. Mr. Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, learned Additional Attorney General appearing with Mr. Md. Mujibur Rahman, Assistant Attorney General submits that the writ petitioners are public servants and the instant dispute is in respect of the terms and conditions of their service in the Republic and the same is to be adjudicated by the Administrative Tribunal, so the writ petition was not maintainable, He further submits that the writ petitioners having appointed in the project and subsequently regularized in the revenue set up in 2001 and the service of the writ petitioners having guided by Gazetted and Non-Gazetted Employees (Department of Fisheries) Recruitment Rules, 1984 and according to the said Rules a gradation list has already been prepared and some of the writ petitioners have already been promoted to the upper post and as such the writ-petitioners had no locusstandi to file the writ petition. He further submits that the High Court. Division while making the Rule absolute failed to consider that the impugned recommendation dated 17.12.2003 along with other letters are internal communications of the Government and those do not confer any right to the writ petitioners, the High Court Division exceeded its limit in directing the Government to amend the B.C.S. (Fisheries) Recruitment Rules, 1981 with retrospective effect and, as such, the judgment and order of the High court Division is liable to be set aside. He further submits that in the B.C.S. (Fisheries) Recruitment Rules, 1981 there is provision for 100% direct recruitment to the entry level post of 'Upazila Fisheries Officer' and the required qualification is B.Sc. Fisheries (Hon's) degree, but the qualifications of the writ petitioners are General Graduation which is not a professional degree and if the writ petitioners are promoted to the said post there will be serious anomaly in the Department of Fisheries and thus, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

8. Per contra Mr. Faird Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos.24-27, in his submission sup-ported the impugned judgment and order passed the High Court Division. 

9. In the instant case the writ-petitioners-respondents relying on an internal communication that is recommendation dated 17.12.2013 by the Public Service Commission along with some other letters, i.e. inter ministerial communications had filed the writ-petition to implement the said recommendation. 

10. It is by now well settled that an inter-departmental/divisional communication do not finally determine any right or obligation of the parties. 

11. In the cases of Bangladesh Vs. Dhaka Steel Works Ltd., 45 DLR(AD), page-69 and Secretary, Internal Resources Division, Ministry of Finance and Chairman, National Board of Revenue Vs. Nasrin Bann and others, 48 DLR(AD). 171 this Division has held that Inter ministerial/divisional communications made in the process of reaching a decision, uncommunicated to the affected persons, do not create a legal right in their favour.  

12. In the case of Al-Haj Abul Bashar being dead his heirs Hosne-Ara Begum and other Vs. Bangladesh and others, 50 DLR(AD), Page-1 I this Division has held to the effect: "Since no legal or vested right has accrued in favor of the petitioners by mere Inter-Ministerial Communications the petitioners can-not have any legal right to ask for return of the land. Further, the Inter-Ministerial Communications are merely internal policy decisions and guidelines for the various departments of the Government and the same is not a declared policy decision of the Government. Hence, no abuse of discretion or arbitrariness or unfair treatment can be attributed to the executive government, as there is also no lawful obligation on the part of the Government to act or intend circulars and decisions so far as it relates to the petitioners." 

13. In the case of Abdur Rahim Khan and others Vs. Bangladesh and others 1999(7) BLT(AD), Page-313 this Division has also held that: 
"The recommendation of a Cabinet Committee cannot be enforced through a writ for simple reason that it is not law. It is as simple as that. The writ-petition was misconceived at the inception." 

14. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Laxminarayan R. Bhattad and Ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra and Anr. MANU/SC/0287/2003 [2003]3SCR409, held that: 
"A right created under an order of a statutory authority must be communicated to the person concerned so as to confer an enforceable right." 

15. In the case of Sethi Auto Service Station and Ors. Vs. Delhi Development Authority and others (MANU/SC/ 8127/2008 A1R2009SC904, (2009) 1SCC180) the Supreme Court of India has observed: 
"That the internal noting or communications with the DDA (Delhi Development Authority) are of no relevance and consequences till a final decision was taken and communicated to the concerned parties. In the present case though the proposals of other Government Agencies were considered, no final decision was taken and communicated by the DDA to the appellants. As regards the approval by the Technical Committee or other officials, the stand of the DDA was that till a final decision was taken by the competent authority i.e. the vice Chairman and communicated to the appellants, there was no question of any vested right accruing in favour of the appellants, merely on the basis of recommendations of the officials of the DDA." 

16. In the above case it has also been observed to the effect: 
"Thus, the first question arising for consideration is whether the recommendation of the Technical Committee vide minutes dated 17th May, 2002 for re-sitement of appellants petrol pumps constitutes an order/decision binding on the DDA? It is trite to state that noting in a departmental file do not have the sanction of law to be effective order A noting by an officer is an expression of his viewpoint on the subject. It is no more than an opinion by an officer for internal use and consideration of the other officials of the department and for the benefit of the final decision-making authority. Needless to add that internal notings are not meant for outside exposure. Notings in the file culminate into an executable order, affecting the rights of the par-ties, only when it reaches the final decision-making authority in the department, gets his approval and the final order communicated to the person concerned. 

17. In the above case in paragraph 13 it has been observed to the effect: 
"In Bachhittar Singh Vs, The State of Punj ab MANU/SC10366/1962: AIR1963SC395, a Constitution Bench of this Court had the occasion to consider the effect of an order passed by a Minister on a file, which order was not communicated to the person concerned. Referring to the Article 166(1) of the Constitution, the Court held that order of the Minister could not amount to an order by the State Government unless it was expressed in the name of the Rajpramukh, as required by the said Article and was then communicated to the party concerned. The court observed that business of State is a complicated one and has necessarily to be conducted through the agency of a large number of officials and authorities. Before an action is taken by the authority concerned in the name of the Rajpramukh, which formality is a constitutional necessity, nothing done would amount to an order creating rights or casting liabilities to third parties. It is possible, observed that Court, that after expressing one opinion about a particular matter at a particular stage a Minister or the Council of Ministers may express quite a different opinion which may be opposed to the earlier opinion. In such cases, which of the two opinions can be regarded as the "order" of the State Government? It was held that opinion becomes a decision of the Government only when it is communicated to the person concerned." 
 
18. In the case of Jasbir Singh Chhabra and Ors. Vs. State of Punjab and others MANU/SC/0152/2010=(2010)4SCC, 192 the Supreme Court of India has observed that: 
"It must always be remembered that in a democratic polity like ours, the functions of the Government are carried out by different individuals at different levels. The issues and policy matters which are required to be decided by the Government are dealt with by several functionaries some of whom may record nothings on the files favouring a particular person or group of persons. Someone may suggest a particular line of action, which may not be conductive to public interest and others may suggest adoption of a different mode in large public interest. However, the final decision is required to be taken by the designated authority keeping in view the larger public interest." 

19. In the case of State of Urrisha and Ors. Vs. Masco Still Ltd. and Ors. (2013 4SCC 340) it has been held by the Supreme Court of India that: 
"A writ petition shall not be maintain-able unless it having been filed against such order which finally determine any right or observation of parties." 

20. In this particular case the recommendation of the Public Service Commission (PSC) for amending the Service Rules i.e. the schedule of the B.C.S. (Fishery) Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing to appoint 1/3rd to the entry level from the feeder post of 2nd class Gazetted Officer by way of promotion, which approved by the Ministry of Public Administration also, was never finalized by the Ministry concerned i.e. Ministry of Fisheries publishing any gazette notification and further, the said recommendation was never communicated to any of the writ petitioners. 

21. Upon consideration of the facts and circumstance of the present case coupled with the above propositions of law, we have no hesitation to hold that the High Court Division committed grave error in making the Rule absolute directing the writ-respondents-appellants to give pro-motion to the writ-petitioners-respondents amending the relevant Rules with retrospective effect within a period of 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the judgment and also pay them the arrear salary and other benefits. 

22. The High Court Division in making the Rule absolute also held that the writ-petitioners have got the legitimate expectation to be promoted as per the proposed amendment of the Rules. 

23. In the case of Secretary, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock & others Vs. Abdul Razzak and others reported in 71 DLR(AD)395 this Division has held as under: 
"Before applying the principle the Courts have to be cautious. It depends on the facts and recognized general principles of administrative law applicable to such facts. A person who bases his claim, on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, must satisfy that there is a foundation, that is, he has locus standi to make such claim. Such claim has to be determined not according to the claimants perception but in the public interest. 
The doctrine of legitimate expectation can neither preclude legislation not invalidate a statute enacted by the competent legislature. The theory of legitimate expectation cannot defeat or invalidate a legislation which is otherwise valid and constitutional. Legitimate expectations must be consistent with statutory provisions. The doctrine can be invoked only if it is founded on the sanction of law. (Hear statutory words override any expectation, however well-founded. It is open to the Government to frame, reframe, change or re-change its policy. If the policy is changed by the Government and the court do not find the action malafide or otherwise unreasonable, the doctrine of legitimate expectation does not make the decision vulnerable. The choice of policy is for the decision maker and not for the Court. While dealing with public policy in juxtaposition with the doctrine of legitimate expectation, the following observations of Lord Diplock in Hughes Vs. Department of Health & Security (1985) 2 WLR 866 must always be kept in view by a Court of law: 
"Administrative policy may change with changing circumstances, including changes in the political complex-ion of Governments. The liberty to make such Changes is something that is inherent in our constitutional form of government."
 An expectation, fulfillment of which requires that a decision maker should taken an unlawful decision cannot be said to a legitimate expectation. This is based on the doctrine that can be no estoppels or legitimate expectation against a statute (wade: Administrative Law, (2005) pp-376."
 
24. In the said case it has been further held that the legitimate expectation would not override the statutory provision. 

25. In the case of National Buildings Construction Corporation V. S. Raghunathan and others. MANU/SC/ 0550/1998: AIR1998SC2779, the Supreme Court of India has observed as under: 
"The doctrine of "legitimate expectation" has its genesis in the field of administrative law. The Government and its departments, in administering the affairs of the country, are expected to honour their statements of policy or intention and treat the citizens with full personal consideration without any iota of abuse of discretion. The policy statements cannot be disregarded unfairly or applied selectively. Unfairness in the form of unreasonableness is akin to violation of natural justice. It was in this context that the doctrine of "legitimate expectation" was evolved which has today become a source of substantive as well as procedural rights. But claims based on "legitimate expectation" have been held to require reliance on representations and resulting detriment to the claimant in the same way as claims based on promissory estoppels". 
 
26. In the ease of Punjab Communications Ltd. Vs. Union of India and ors. MSNU/SC/0326/1999: [1999]2SCRI033, the Supreme Court of India referring to a large number of authorities on the question, observed that a change in policy can defeat a substantive legitimate expectation if it can be justified on "Wednesbury" reasonableness. The decision maker has the choice in the balancing of the pros and cons relevant to the change in policy. Therefore, the choice of the policy is for the decision maker and not for the Court. The legitimate substantive expectation merely permits the Court to find out if the change in policy which is the cause for defeating the legitimate expectation is irrational or perverse one which on reasonable person could have made. 
 
27. In Jitendra Kumar and Ors. v. State of Haryana and Anr.MANU/SC/819212,007: (2008)2SCC161, it has been reiterated by the Supreme Court of India that a legitimate expectation is not the same thing as an anticipation. It is distinct and different from a desire and hope. It is based on a right. It is grounded in the rule of law as requiring regularity, predictability and certainty in the Government's dealings with the public and the doctrine of legitimate expectation operates both in procedural and substantive matters. 
 
28. In view of the above propositions, the findings of the High Court Division that the writ petitioners have got a right by way of legitimate expectation to be promoted on the basis of proposed amendment of the service Rules, which never attained in its finality has got no legal basis. 

29. In view of the forgoing discussions, we are of the view that the High Court Division committed grave error in passing the impugned judgment and order making the Rule absolute. 

30. Thus, we find merit in the appeal. 

31. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. 

32. The judgment and order dated 01.11.2018 passed by the High Court Division is hereby set aside. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 19.08.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Fist Appeal No. 161 of 1999 and 160 of 1999.)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique CJ. Civil Appeal No.353 of 2015 and Civil Appeal No.167 of 2014 have been heard together and they are being disposed of by this common judgment and order. 

2. The respondents 1 and 2 of Civil Appeal No.167 of 2014 Noor Mia and another as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.119 of 1994 against United Engineers and Planters Limited and others for Specific Performance of Contract in respect of the land described in the schedule to the plaint of that suit. On the other hand, appellants Syed Badrul Haque and others filed Title Suit No.09 of 1994 in the Second Court the then Subordinate Judge, Sylhet for declaration of title in respect of .1321 acre of land out of .6080 acre of plot No.7526 khatian No.1255 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality Mohalla Dupadighir Purbapar and for partition. Both the suits were heard analogously and disposed of by a common judgment. The trial Court decreed the suit in Title Suit No.09 of 1994 in preliminary form and allowed saham in favour of the appellant Syed Badrul Haque and others to the extent of the land measuring an area of .1275 acre. It also decreed Title Suit No.119 of 1994. The Defendant United Engineers and Planters Limited and others preferred First Appeal No.161 of 1.999 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.9 of 1994 and First Appeal No.160 of 1999 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.119 of 1994. The High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and decree, allowed the First Appeal No.161 of 1999 and dismissed the First Appeal No.160 of 1999. Then the Plaintiff Syed Badul Haque and others preferred C.A. No.353 of 2015 against the First Appeal No.161 of 1999 and the United Engineers and Planters Ltd. preferred Civil Appeal No.167 of 1994 against the judgment and decree of First Appeal No.160 of 1999. 

3. Plaintiffs" ease in Title Suit No.9 of 1994, in short, was that the land measuring an area of .6080 acre appertaining to khatian No.1255 and plot No.7526 of Mohalla Dhupadighir Purbapar within Mouza Sylhet Municipality, P.S. Kotwali belonged to their sister Syeda Nazira Banu. She died on 12.12.1965 leaving her three consanguine brothers, namely- Syed Sadrul Huq, Syed Badrul Huq, Syed Shafiqul Huq (plaintiff Nos. 1-3), Syed Nazmul Huq and consanguine sisters Hafsa Begum (plaintiff No.4) and Fatema Begum (defendant No.5). Accordingly, the plaintiff Nos.l-3 and Syed Nazmul Huq each inherited .12 acre of land and plaintiff No.4 and defendant no.5 each inherited .06 acre of land. Syed Nazmul Huq died on 19.09.1974 leaving behind his aforesaid 3 full brothers (the plaintiff Nos. 1-3), sisters, the plaintiff No.4 and the defendant No.5 and mother Mobaraka Khatun. On the death of Nazmul Huq his interest to the extent of .12 acre of land was inherited by his mother Mobaraka Khatun to the extent of .02 acre, the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 to the extent of .0250 acre each and sisters, the plaintiff No.4 and the defendant No.5 to the extent' of .0125 acre each. Syeda Mobaraka Khatun died on 13.11.1982 leaving behind aforesaid 3 sons, the plaintiff Nos. 13, 2 daughters, the plaintiff No.4 and the defendant No.5 and 2 grand daughters (son's daughters), the defendant No.3 and defendant No.4. Thus, .02 acre of land left by Syed Mobaraka Khatun was devolved upon the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 who inherited .0040 acre of land each. The plaintiff No and defendant no.5 each got .0020 acre of land while defendant Nos. 3 and 4 acquired .0040 acre of land. Thus, the plaintiffs nos. 1-3 inherited .1490 acre of land, the plaintiff No.4 and defendant No,5 inherited .0745 acre of land and defendant Nos. 3 and 4 jointly inherited 0040 acre of land. Thereafter, the defendant No.5 transferred .07375 acre of land to the plaintiff Nos. 1-3 by a sale deed dated 18.11.1980. Thus, plaintiff Nos. 1-3 acquired .5275 acre of land while the plaintiff No.4 and defendant No.5 acquired .0745 acre of land. Excluding the land sold by defendant No.5 to the plain-tiff Nos.1-3 she had an interest to the extent .0080 acre of land in the suit land. The plaintiff Nos. 1 to 4 transferred .4619 acre of land to the defendant No.1 by 3 kabala deeds. The defendant No.1 was their monthly tenant of the structures standing in the suit land. The suit land was remaining in ejmali. The plaintiffs through plaintiff No.2 approached the Managing Director of the defendant No.1 on 01.01.1994 to get the suit land partitioned claiming their unsold .1321 acre of land but the defendant no.2 denied their title and to effect partition the same. Under the circumstances, the plaintiffs prayed for a preliminary decree in their favour in respect of .1321 acre of land on declaration of their title thereto. 

4. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 (who are also defendants in Title Suit No.119 of 1994) contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying material allegations contending that suit plot No.7526 measuring an area of .5937 acre which the contesting defendants along with their partners had been possessing as monthly tenants under the plaintiffs by running their business therein. While in such possession, the plaintiff No.1 transferred his interest to the defendant No.1 by a kabala deed dated 12.01.1985. The plaintiff No.2 transferred his interest by another kabala deed dated 31.07.1984 to the defendant No. l. The plaintiff No.4 transferred his share to the defendant No.1 by another kabala deed dated 19.12.1984. Similarly, the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 also transferred their interest by a kabala dated 19.12.1984 to the defendant No. l. By this way, entire area of the land appertaining to suit plot No.7526 was transferred to the defendant No.1 mentioning specific boundaries thereof. By a separate receipt the structures and fixtures standing on the suit land were transferred by the plaintiffs at a consideration of taka 7,70,000/- to the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. After purchase, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 got suit plot No.7526 and mutated in their names opening a new khatian being No.1394 within the knowledge of the plaintiffs and defendant Nos.3-5. The contesting defendants constructed a community centre in the suit land. The plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. In order to make an illegal gain they instituted Title Suit No.09 of 1994 on false and concocted allegations which was liable to be dismissed. 

5. The added defendant Nos. 6 and 7, Noor Miah and Mannan Miah, of Title Suit No.9 of 1994, instituted Title Suit No.119 of 1994 against defendant No.1 United Engineers and Planters Ltd. represented by its Managing Director Abdul Matin Khan, the defendant No.2. Said Abdul Matin Khan (who was also defendant in Title Suit No.9 of 1994) and 11 others alleging that the land described in the schedule 1 of the plaint belonged to the defendant no.1 who entered into an agreement with the plaintiffs to sell .15 acre of land as described, in the schedule -2 of the plaint (hereinafter referred the suit land) at a consideration of taka 52,50,000/- and on receipt of earnest money of taka 5,00,001/-executed a deed of agreement in their favour on 21.11.1993. It was disclosed then that a portion of land of the suit plot was mortgaged with defendant No.13 BSCIC for obtaining loan from it. It was agreed that the plaintiffs of this suit would give a further sum of taka 10,00,000/- to the defendant company by the 31 March, 1994 for redemption of the mortgage and after such redemption the defendants would execute and register kabala deed on receipt of the balance consideration amount from them by 31st December, 1994. The plaintiffs were always ready and eager to perform their part of contract. But in the 2nd week of March, 1994 they came to know that a Title Suit being No.9 of 1994 was instituted against defendant No.1 and others by making the entire land of suit plot for partition and, on the approach of the plaintiffs of the said suit, notice was issued upon the defendants to show cause as to why they should not be restrained from transferring the said land till disposal of the suit. The plaintiffs then contacted defendant Nos. 1-5 and held discussion with them and wanted to know about the specific period when the said suit would be ended but they could not ascertain them anything. In such a situation, the plaintiffs issued a notice through their learned advocate requesting them to execute sale deed within one month of receipt of the notice. On receipt of the said notice, the defendant Nos.1-5 gave a reply to them through their learned advocate holding them responsible for non payment of taka 10,00,000/- on the last date of the month of March, 1994 on a false excuse that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.119 of 1994 instituted the said suit in collusion with the instant plaintiffs. It was also stated in the same reply that the said sum of taka 10,00,000/- having not been paid within the stipulated period, the deed of agreement stood cancelled and the earnest money of taka 5,00,000/- has been forfeited. They refused to enter into another contract afresh. These plaintiffs also found that the defendant Nos. 1-5 construc ted roads around the northern and southern side of the suit land land also closed the western portion thereof by raising a pucca wall and further constructed a massive community center by the east of the a land. The defendant Nos.1-5 had been making preparation to sell out the suit land elsewhere. Under such circumstances, they issued another notice on 27.06.1994 requesting defendant Nos. 1 to 5 to redeem the land mortgaged from the BSCIC and apprise them. But without co-operating the plaintiffs, the defendant Nos.1-5 issued a notice' dated 24.07.1994 that the deed of agreement for sale stood cancelled which thus gave rise to the cause of the suit for specific performance of contract. 

6. The defendant Nos. 1-5 of Title Suit. No.119 of 1994 contested the suit by filing joint written statement admitting that they received a sum of taka 5,00,000/- as earnest money for transfer of the suit land from the plaintiffs and executed an agreement for sale on 21.11.1993 with certain specific conditions entered therein. The plaintiffs breached the terms and conditions of the deed of agreement, consequently, the same stood repudiated and the earnest money of taka 5,00,000/- was forfeited. The plaintiffs were not entitled to any decree for specific performance of contract. So, the suit was to be dismissed with cost. 

7. The result of the title suits and appeals have been stated as earlier. 

8. Mr. Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants of Civil Appeal No.353 of 2014, submits that the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court without adverting to the specific findings of the trial Court as per provisions of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that High Court Division upon misreading and misconstruing the evidence as adduced in Title Suit No.09 of 1994 erroneously reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. He further submits that the plaintiff appellant Nos. 1 to 3 and their two sisters transferred .4619 acre of land to the contesting defendants out of land measuring an area of .59 acre and that they have retained their title and constructive possession of .1321 acre and that the trial Court rightly decreed the suit in preliminary form, the High Court Division erred in law in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

9. Mr, Md. Nurul Amin, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent in Civil Appeal No.353 of 2015, submits that the plaintiffs being co-sharers of the suit land sold their shares to the defendant No.1 by different kabla deeds, thereby, exhausted entire shares, the Appellate Court, upon proper consideration of evidence on record rightly held so and dis-missed the suit. He further submits that defendant Nos.3 to 5 sold the structures of the suit land at a consideration of taka 7,70,000/- with single receipt signed by all of them and that after transferring entire land, the plaintiffs have no subsisting interest in the suit land, the appellate Court rightly reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

10. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, appearing for the appellants in C.A. No.167 of 1914, submits that the plaintiff respondents by their notice dated 30.03.1993 rescinded the agreement for sale deed dated 21.11.1993 and on 30,03.1994, the Court below erred in law in decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract, He, lastly, submits that price of the land as described in the schedule to the plaint, at present, is few crore and that the plaintiff's are going to lose the said land at consideration of taka 50,00,000/- only having no fault of their own as such they are entitled to get solatiam. 

11. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the plaintiff respondents of C.A. No.167 of 2014, submits that agreement executed by both the parties is admitted. The plaintiffs filed the suit for specific performance of contract in time. The plaintiffs filed instant suit for specific performance of contract on the basis of admitted bainanama, learned Courts below upon proper appreciation of materials on record decreed the suit. The appeal should be dismissed. 

C.A. No.353 of 2015 
12. The suit land originally belonged to Syed Sadrul Haq, Syed Badrul Haq and Syed Shafiqul Hague sons of Syed Nazmul Haque and Hafsa Begum, plaintiff No.5. The plaintiff Nos. 1-3 got .1490 acre of land each in their share and the plaintiff No.4 got. 0745 acre of land. Plaintiff Nos. 1 to 4 transferred .4619 acre of land to the defendant No.1 by three kabla deeds. After so transfers, they claimed that they have owned .1321 acre of land of disputed plot No. l. The defendants claimed that Syeda Nazira Banu died leaving Syed Sadrul Haq, Syed Badrul Haq and Syed Shafiqul Haq who got .12 acre of land each and Hafsa Begum, the plaintiff No.4. got .06 acre and defendant No.5 Fatema Begom got .06 acre of land. It is further case of the defendant No.1 that Syeda Nazira Banu had another son Syed Shamsul Haq who died on 12.06.1963. It is the definite case of the contesting defendants that Syeda Nazira Banu's son was Syed Shamsul Haq and after the death of Nazira Banu Syed Shamsul Hay's daughter got the share of Syed Shamsul Haq. In such view of the matter, after transfer of the share by the plaintiffs to the defendant No.1 they have no subsisting interest in the suit land. It appears from the judgment and decree of the appellate Court that it considering the evidence, both oral and documentary, came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs after their transfers have no saleable interest in the suit land and accordingly the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.09 of 1994. 

13. It appears from the judgment and decree of Title Suit No.119 of 1994, that is, the suit for specific performance of contract that both the Courts below upon proper appreciation of evidence on record held that defendants of the said suit contracted to sell the suit land to the plaintiffs upon receiving earnest money. 

14. We do not find any misreading and misconstruing the evidence on record by the learned Courts below. However, Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants in Civil Appeal No.167 of 2014 submits that price of the suit land at present is several crores. In such circumstances, the appellant is entitled to get solatium for the ends of justice. 

15. In view of the facts and circumstances, we direct the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.119 of 1994 to pay a sum of taka 50,00,000/- as solatium along with unpaid consideration within 3(three)months from the date of communication of this judgment and order of this court. The trial Court is directed to hand over the same to the defendant-appellants after payment of solatium and the rest consideration. In-case of failure to deposit the rest consideration and solatium within 3(three) months from the date of communication of this judgment the suit for specific performance shall stand dismissed. 

16. Accordingly, Civil Appeal No.353 of 2014 is dismissed. Civil Appeal No. 167 of 2014 is also dismissed with direction to the plaintiff respondent to pay solatium taka 50,00,000/- (fifty lac) and rest of the consideration to the appellants within 3(three) months from the communication of the judgment and order of this Court to the trial Court with the aforesaid default order. 

End.

parties:

Chairman, First Court of Settlement, Segunbagicha, Dhaka and others ------- Respondents [CA No.202-203/14]

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 19-5-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5864 of 2000 and 6442 of 2008)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, CJ: The delay in filing Civil Petitions for Leave Appeal Nos.1257 of 2023 and 1258 of 2023 is condoned.
2. Civil Appeal Nos. 202 of 2014, 203 of 2014 and Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos.1257-1258 of 2023 are heard analogously and they are being disposed of by this common judgment and order.
3. One Abul Hashem and Monir Ahmed filed Settlement Case No.14 of 1991 (Ka: Si. 18, P.9762(11) in the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka for getting release of the House No.21, Larmini Street, Sutrapur, Dhaka stating that one. Hamidunnessa was the owner of the disputed property who gifted the same to Kaser Ali. Kaser Ali brought Money Suit and got decree and in execution case arising out of the decree, he purchased the disputed property and obtained sale certificate. Kaser Ali died leaving two sons. The petitioners of Settlement Case claimed their title and possession in the disputed land through Kaser Ali. The Court of Settlement disbelieved the documents produced by Abul Hashem and another and dismissed the case by a judgment and order dated 1-10-1993 holding that the disputed property belonged Hamidunnessa and Hasibur Rahman. They had been possessing the same as their own property till December, 1971. Thereafter, they left their house and their whereabouts were not traced. One Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury, claiming himself as son of Hamidunnessa, filed review petition for reviewing the judgment and order dated 01-10-1993 in the said case. The Court of Settlement, by its order dated 10-10-2000, rejected the said application for review holding that in the aforesaid settlement case Hasibur Rahman was not party so the instant review petition was not maintainable. Against the said order dated 10-10-2000 passed in Settlement Case No.14 of 1991 by the Court of Settlement, Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury filed Writ Petition No.5864 of 2000 in the High Court Division and obtained Rule.
4. Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury also filed Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008 in the High Court Division, against the execution of sale agreement and order of allotment in favour of writ respondent No.3 Raihana Shafi by the Government in respect of the disputed land and obtained Rule.
5. The High Court Division heard the Writ Petition No.5864 of 2000 and Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008 analogously and disposed of by common judgment dated 19-5-2011.
6. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute issued in Writ Petition No.5864 of 2000 and set-aside the judgment and orders dated 10-10-2000 and 21-10-1993 passed by the Court of Settlement in Settlement Case No.14 of 1991. It disposed of the Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008. The High Court Division sent back the case on remand to the Court of Settlement with direction to dispose of the case within 4(four) months.
7. Against the aforesaid judgment and order, writ respondent No.3 appellant has filed Civil Appeal No.202 of 2014 and 203 of 2014 in this Division upon getting leave and Government filed Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos.1257 of 2023 and 1258 of 2023.
8: Mr Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appeared for the appellant Raihana Shafi in both the appeals and Mr Sheikh Mohammad Morhsed, learned Additional Attorney-General appeared on behalf of the Government in the aforesaid two leave petitions. On the other hand, Mr ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, learned Advocate appeared for the respondent Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury in all the appeals and petitions. Raihana Shaft claimed possession of the disputed property upon getting allotment from the Government. In fact, the submissions of Mr Probir Neogi and Additional Attorney-General are identical.
9. They submit that the writ petitioner Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury is a fictitious man and the petitioners of the Settlement Court, namely, Abul Abul Hashem and Monir Ahmed, preparing some fake papers and taking the opportunity of the finding of the Court of Settlement that Hamidunnessa and Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury are owners of the property, in question, have filed instant writ petition behind the back in order to grab the abandoned property. They submit that the High Court Division committed error of law in setting aside the order passed in review petition though there is no application of the Code of Civil Procedure in disposing of the litigation before the Court of Settlement. They add that the Court of Settlement rightly rejected the review petition, since the same was not maintainable. Their further submission was that the High Court Division has committed a fundamental error of law in directing the Court of Settlement to proceed with the Settlement Case again at the instance of so called Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury though in Settlement case the provision of order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no application. They, lastly, submit that the High Court Division, in fact, has given new life of the settlement case, thereby, allowed the Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury to ventilate his grievance inasmuch as his claim, by filing before the Court of the Settlement, is hopelessly barred by limitation.
10. Mr ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury in both the appeals and the civil petitions, submits that Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury and his mother Hamidunessa who are the admitted owners of the property, in question, have been and has been living in different places in Bangladesh. In the papers produced by him clearly proved that Hashibur Rohman Chowdhury is a citizen of Bangladesh so he is entitled to get release of the disputed property, the High Court Division rightly remanded the case to the Court of Settlement allowing him to ventilate his grievance and there is no error in the judgment and order of the High Court Division.
11. It is not disputed that the Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury did not file any case in the Court of Settlement for getting release of the disputed property from "Ka" list of the abandoned properties which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-1986 [Ka list in serial No.118 page 9762 (11)]. He filed an application for reviewing the judgment and order dated 31-10-1993 passed by the Court of Settlement in Settlement Case No.14 of 1991 filed by one Abul Hashem and Monir Ahmed. That review application was filed on 10-10-2000, that is, after about 7(seven) years after disposal of the said settlement case and about 14(fourteen) years after the aforesaid gazette notification inasmuch as time limit for filing any settlement case provided in section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 was only 108 days. The Ordinance does not permit third party to file review petition against the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement after disposal of the same.
12. It further appears that Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury, filing Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008, challenged the execution of the sale agreement and allotment of the disputed property in favour of Raihana Shafi by the Government. In this writ petition, he did not pray for getting release of the property from the "Ka" list of the abandoned properties. The said writ petition was disposed of without any specific result considering the prayer made in the said writ petition. That is, Hasibur Rahman Chwodhury accepted the judgment and order passed in Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008. Allottee Raihana Shan preferred the aforesaid two appeals against the judgment and order of the High Court Division.
<u>13. The only question which is to be considered as to whether the High Court Division rightly allowed Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury to ventilate his grievance in the Court of Settlement in the Settlement Case filed by Abul Hashem and another or not. The law does not provide any provision to review a judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement at the instance of third party whose claimed, if any, is barred by the provision of limitation. Section 10 of the Ordinance specifically provides that except as otherwise provided in the Ordinance, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure shall not apply to a Court of Settlement and sub-section (2) of section 10 limits the area of the applicability of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court of Settlement is not a Civil Court and its authority is to determine as to whether the disputed property is abandoned property or not. The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure should be applicable in respect of summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath; requiring the discovery and production of any document; requiring evidence on affidavit; requisitioning any public record or copy there of from any office; and issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents. In such view of the matter a question stands on the way as to the entertainability of the application under Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure for adding the applicant as claimant to get release of abandoned property filed by other party making different pleading. Our view is "no".</u>
14. In the application for getting release of disputed property filed by Abul Hashem and another from the list of abandoned properties there is little scope to get relief by Hasibur Rahman since the source of claim made by them in the said case is quite different. In that application for getting release of the disputed property it is difficult for Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury to establish that he is a citizen of Bangladesh and he was present in Bangladesh and. his whereabouts is known or he has not ceases to occupy, supervise or manage in person of his property. Without amending the contents of the claim made by Abul Hashem and another in the Settlement Case it is almost impossible to get any relief in the said case. It is more difficult for the reason that applicability of the provisions of Civil Procedure Code is very limited.
15. It appears from. the papers produced by Hasibur Rahman Chowdhury that he claimed that sometimes he lived at Keknasar Khabari, Sirajdikhan, sometimes at 28/2 Dakkhin Mukdapara, sometimes at Jouripur Lane, Sutrapur of Ward No.77, Dhaka which created a doubt about his identity and his claim that earlier any point of time he had been living in the disputed property, that is, at House No.21, Larmini Street, Wari, Sutrapur, Dhaka.
16. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances, we find force in the submissions made by of Mr Probir Neogi and learned Additional Attorney-General.
Thus, both the appeals are allowed. The judgment and order dated 19-5-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.5864 of 2000 (heard analogously with Writ Petition No.6442 of 2008) are set-aside. The Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos.1257- 1258 of 2023 arc disposed of in the light of judgment and order passed in appeals.
End.

full_judgment:
Naima Haider, J: In this application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution, Rules Nisi were issued in all the writ petitions in the following terms: Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo No, ভূঃ মঃ/শ-৮/খাজব/৬৬/২০০১/৪৬৮ (৬৪) dated 7-6-2005 (Annexure-C) passed by the Senior Assistant Secretary, Section-8, Ministry of Land, Respondent No. 3 cancelling the Memo No. 8-28-85/1023(64) dated 17-10-1985 as to renewal of long term lease of non-agricultural khas land and the Memo No. ভূঃ মঃ/শ-৮/খাজব/১৩৫/২০১১/৫৮৯ dated 10-5-2011 (Annexure-D) passed by the Deputy Secretary, Section -8, Ministry of Land, Respondent No. 2 imposing new conditions as to renewal of long term lease of non-agricultural khas land should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. The relevant facts leading to filing of the instant writ petitions are briefly, set out as follows:
In Writ Petition No. 9643 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of apartments of the, holding No. 23. Segun Bagicha, namely, "Prestige Homes", proportionality measuring 0.186 acres in Mouza: Kakrail, Police Station: Rainna, District: Dhaka under SA Khatian No. 4(KM)117, SA Plot No. 112 (KM) 22(SA)7, KM Plot No. 122 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land"). The said land was leased out to one Sree Monmonsen Mitro Roy for a period of 30 years by a registered deed with effect from 1-4-1931 to 31-3-1961 who sold the land .to Sreejukto Senehalata Mukharjee vide Deed No. 3777 dated 19-9-1.945. Thereafter Senehalata Mukharjee also transferred the land to Mosammat Amena Khatun vide Deed No. 314 dated 9-1-1998. The tenure of lease was further renewed for further 30 years vide deed of renewal of lease deed No. 1528 dated 16-1-1985. After the death of Mosammat Amena Khatun her heirs owned and executed a General Power of Attorney in favour of Tropicals Homes vide Deed No. 5 dated 6-5-1998. Subsequently, a 9(nine)-storied residential building comprising of 32 apartments was constructed over the land, Present petitioners including the original landlords are the present owners of the said apartments. In the writ petition, the petitioners elaborated on the devolution of title of the Land in her favour and also in favour of the other co-sharers.
3. In Writ Petition No. 9640 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of the land measuring 0.2712 acres proportionately, Holding No. 6 Segun bagicha, knownas "Eastern Villa", in Mouza: Kakrail, Police Station: Ran-Ina, District: Dhaka under CS Khatian No. 3, Plot No. 79 Municipal Ward No. 3, Touji No. 16725 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land"). The said land was leased out to one Pran Kumar for a period of 30 years in the month of April, 1931 and he sold the said land to Anwari Rahmatullah on 22-1-1949 and Anwari Rahmattillah sold the /sand at Safia Begum and Zubeda Begum on 2-5-1950 and they renewed the said lease for a period of 30 years with effect from 29-8-1964. Thereafter they sold the said land with building thereon to Sahera Khatun vide Deed No. 3408 dated 11-1-1969 and she sold the siad land to "Eastern Housing Ltd." vide Deed No. 202 dated 23-1-1990. The Eastern Housing Ltd. subsequently constructed a multi-storied building on the land and the petitioners obtained ownership of the apartments of the building with proportionate land by several deeds. They also mutated their names and possessed the same for time peacefully.
4. In Writ Petition No. 9641 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of the land proportionately measuring 0.29 acres known as "Eastern Ulania" Holding No. 2, Mouza-Kakrail, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka, CS Khatian No. 60, RS Khatian No. 1.57 corresponding to CA Plot No. 211, SA Plot No. 208, RS Plot No. 1441 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land"). The said land was originally leased out to one Sree Birendra Mohan Ghosh for a period of 15 years vide Lease Deed No. 4350 dated 27-11-1946. Thereafter he sold the said land to Miss Nurun Nahar Hady vide Deed No. 3776 dated 8-6-19413. After expiry of the period of lease said Nurn Nahar Hady applied to the Joint Collector Revenue for renewal of the said lease for further period of 60 years and Government of East Pakistan granted lease of further period of 30 years with effect from 1-4-1961 vide registered deed No. 4764 dated 13-9-1961. Nurun Nahar Hady sold the land to Md Shah Humayun Kabir vide Deed No. 3170 dated 18-6-2006. Md Shah Humayun Kabir subsequently constructed a multi-storied building in the land and the petitoners obtianed ownership of the apartments of the building proportionately land by several deeds. They also mutated their names and possess the same for long time peacefully.
5. In Writ Petition No. 9642 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of the land holding No. 9, proportionately measuring 0.2011 acres known as "Eastern Haven" in Mouza-Kakrail, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka, CS Plot No. 80. Hal Plot No. 216/1306, Shabek Khatian No. 14, Hal Khatian No. 732, Jote No. 131, Ward No.3, Sheet No. 20, Collectorate Touji No. 15725, JL No. 5, Municipal Holding No. 80, Now-9 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land"). The said land was originally leased out to one Jotinnoya Sen and he transferred the same to Dr. Md Hossain and Dr. Md Hossain transferred the same to Mis Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. by a registered deed and M/s Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. sold it to Mr Shahadat Ali Khan vide Sale Deed No. 4042 dated 25-3-1958 and he applied to the Government for renewal of the said lease for further period of 30 years and accordingly the Government though the Collector, Dhaka extended the lease for further period of 30 years i.e. upto 31st March, 1991 vide CI (Sadar) Order No. 416(2)1-5/60 dated 17-10-1960. Shahadat died leaving behind wife, 6 daughters and 3 sons.
6. In Writ Petition No. 9644 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of the land measuring 9,31 katha, known as "Excelsia Tower" in Holding No. 6/2, Segunbagicha, Monza-Kakrail, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka, CS Khatian No. 38, SA Khatian No. 39 corresponding to CS Plot No. 339, SA Plot No. 513 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land"). The said land was originally leased out to one Mrs. Mojira Khatun vide Lease Deed No. 619 dated 31-1-1.955 and 2377 dated 28-4-1961. She died leaving behind 3 sons AKM Fazlur Rahman, ATM Aminur Rahman, ASM Sofiqur Rahman and 3 daughters Sahina Eakub, Rowshan Bashar, Kawsar Jahan. Hasina Islam died leaving behind a son Khaled Saiful Islam and a daughter Shahin Eaqub. After expiry of lease they applied for renewal and the Government renewed the period of lease for further period of 30 years. They gave registered power of attorney to "Asset Development and Holding Ltd." for high-rise building. The said company constructed a multi-storied building on the land and the petitioners obtained ownership of the apartments of the building with proportionate land. They also mutated their names and possess the same peacefully for a long time.
7. In Writ Petition No. 9645 of 2014, the petitioners are the owners of the land of Holding No. 5, Segunbagicha, proportionately measuring 29.39 decimals known as "Concord Apartment" in Dhaka Collectorate Touji No. 15725, JL No. 282, Mouza-Kakrail, Police Station-Ramna, District-Dhaka, CS Khatian No. 2, SA Khatian No. 63, RS Khatian No. 629, DP Khatian No. 1143 corresponding to CS Plot No. 78, SA Plot No. 211, RS Mutation Khatian No. 64/4, Jot No. 772, DP Plot No. 6315, Plot No. 1237, DP Plot No. 6315 and measuring 17 katha 13 chatak or 0.204 katha, Dhaka Collectorate Touji No. 15725, JL No. 282, Mouza-Kakrail at present Ramna, Police Station-Ramna under CS Khatian No. 2 and thereafter 98, SA Khatian No. 63, RS Khatian No. 96, DP Khatian No. 1143, corresponding to CS Plot No. 78, SA Plot No. 211, RS Plot No 1437, DP Plot No. 6315, Mutation Khatian No. 63/4, Jot No. 772, Touji No. 15725, JL No. 283 (hereinafter referred to as "the Land").
