case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 24th day of January, 2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2624 of 2005).
full_judgment:
M. Enayetur Rahim, J: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 24-1-2010 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2624 of 2005 making the Rule absolute.
2. The facts, relevant for disposal of the appeal, are that the predecessor of the present appellants as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.81 of 1996 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Meherpur for declaration that the preliminary decree dated 30-10-1989 and the final decree dated 5-11-1989 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Meherpur is collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff and for cancellation the same and also for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the 'Ka' schedule land to the plaint measuring an area of 66 decimals appertaining to SA Khatian Mo..331, CS Plot No. 50 and 51, 41 decimals of land out of RS Plot No. 703 and 25 decimals of land out of 52 decimals land of Plot No. 702 contending inter alia that the land of SA Khatian No. 331 Mouza Bowmanpara, measuring an area of 11.03 acres land belonged to Ratimon Nessa who died leaving behind 5 sons namely-Saifuddin, Nasaruddin, Kasaruddin, Didar Uddin and Khabir Uddin and one daughter Shaharan Nessa; by amicable partition the 'Ka' schedule land was allotted to the saham of Saifuddin who had been possessing the same and died leaving behind one son Zillur Rahman alias Abdur Rahman and one daughter Shakaran Khatun.
3. An amicable partition took place between Zillur Rahman and Shaharan Nessa. Zillur Rahman got 2.06 acres of land in his saham and, thereafter, sold the same by kabala deed dated 19-1-1974 in favour of the plaintiff's wife Arjia Khatun and Khalesan Nessa. Said deed was not executed and registered but a Bainanama was executed on 19-1-1974 and, thereafter, Zillur Rahman @ Abdur Rahman refused to execute and register a kabala deed in December, 1974.
4. Abdur Rahman demanded more money but that was refused by Khalesan Nessa and the plaintiff's wife demanded back the kabala money, and that was refunded and, thereafter, Abdur Rahman wanted to sale out the suit land and a fresh bainanama was executed on 4-2-1981 for transferring the Suit land in favour of the plaintiff and his wife. Thereafter, Abdur Rahman without executing and registering a kabala had transferred the said land in favour of Sara Khatun. Having come to know the said fact plaintiff's wife instituted Title Suit No. 206 of 1991 but mistakenly the plaintiff was not made a party in the said Suit. Thereafter, Abdur Rahman executed and registered a kabala deed on 19-12-1991 and, thereafter, Arjia Khatun withdrew the Title Suit No. 206 of 1991.
5. Further case of the plaintiff is that defendant No. 1 with a view to deprive the plaintiff from the suit property made collusion with her brother Abdur Rahman and instituted a suit for partition being No. 4 of 1982. Thereafter, without serving notices upon the defendant managed to get a preliminary decree on 25-10-1989 and got a final decree on 10-10- 1990. The plaintiff came to know about the said decree on 10-3-1995 and, thereafter, got the certified copy on 27-4-1995 and instituted the suit.
6. The Suit was contested by the present respondent No.1. In the written statement it is contended inter alia that the Suit was not maintainable and was barred by limitation as well as defect of parties. It was the case of the defendant that Rahman Nessa being a co-sharer of the suit holding died leaving behind one son named Didar Uddin and a daughter, Shaharan and predeceased 4 sons and 2 daughters. One of the predeceased sons Nasar Uddin died leaving behind one son and 5 daughters and Khabir Uddin died leaving one widow, 3 daughters and Saifuddin died leaving behind 1 son Abdur Rahim and a daughter Sara Khatun. In this way the defendant became a co-sharer to the case holding and instituted partition Suit No. 4 of 1982. That Suit was contested by Didar Uddin, son of late Nasar Uddin and the suit was decreed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 31-10-1989.
7. It is the further case of the defendant that the plaintiff Abdul Hamid was made defendant No.3 in the said suit and his wife Arjia Khatun was made defendant No.18. The final decree obtained in the said Suit was executed by filing Execution Case No. 1 of 1991 and the decree holder got delivery of possession in the decreed land on 5-5-1991. After the delivery of possession was made in the said Suit the plaintiff's wife Arjia Khatun instituted Title Suit No. 206 of 1991 on 17-8-1991 and the plaintiff Abdul Hamid was a Tadbirkar who sworn affidavit and submitted an application under order 39 rule of the Code of Civil Procedure. The application was contested by the present defendant by filing a written objection. In the said written objection the fact of Title Suit No. 4 of 1982 and its decree was disclosed and the prayer for injunction was rejected by order dated 15-10-1991. Then Arjia Khatun preferred Title Appeal No. 60 of 1991 against the rejection order of the injunction application and that appeal was also dismissed by judgment and order dated 17-5-1994. Thereafter Arjia Khatun withdrew the suit on 12-8-1995 and after withdrawal of the said, a criminal case was filed. The plaintiff does not have any title and possession in the suit land.
8. At the trial, respective parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. After hearing, the trial Court by its judgment and order dated 29-2-2004 decreed the suit.
9. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the defendant preferred Title Appeal No.24 of 2004 before the learned District Judge, Meherpur. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Meherpur, who by his judgment and order dated 9-5-2005 dismissed the appeal.
10. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court, the defendant moved before the High Court Division by filing a revisional application and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.2624 of 2005. A Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing said civil revision by the impugned judgment and order dated 24-1-2010 made the Rule absolute by setting aside the judgments and decrees passed by the Courts bellow.
11. Feeling aggrieved by the judgment and order passed by High Court Division, the successors of the plaintiff filed civil petition for leave to appeal No. 1212 of 2010 before this Division and leave was granted on 22-5-2016. Hence, the present appeal.
12. Mr Md Hamidur Rahman, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that when the plaintiff prayed for confirmation of possession as consequential relief by paying advolarame court fees, the findings of the High Court Division that the defendant obtained possession through process of the court, the instant suit is not maintainable, is not legal.
13. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Judge of the Appellate Court categorically held that the summons upon the defendant No. 3 (present appellant) in title suit No. 4 of 1982 was not served, therefore the High Court Division in absence of any misreading or misappreciation of evidence by the Court's below set-aside the decree and hence committed error of law. The learned Advocate finally submits that when the suit itself for declaration of title and setting aside the decree, Article 120 of the Limitation Act governed for filing of such a suit within 6 years, therefore, the High Court Division Committed illegality in holding that the suit is barred by limitation.
14. Per contra Mrs. Shahanara Begum, learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the respondent No.1 having supported the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division submits that the plaintiff was defendant No.3 in that title suit No 81 of 1996 and the plaintiff's wife Arjia Khatun was defendant No.18 and present defendant Sara Khatun got preliminary decree on 31-10-1989 against one Didar and the decree was made final on 10-10-1990. That final decree was put into execution in Case No. 1 of 1991 and the defendant Sara Khatun got delivery of possession in the suit land through Court on 5-5-1991. So, this suit is not maintainable without seeking prayer for recovery of khas 'possession. The learned Advocate further submits that the judgment and decree passed in Partition Suit No.4 of 1982 bears that the defendant was admitted a co-sharer to CS khatian and she being a co-sharer instituted partition suit where plaintiff and his wife Arjia Khatun were made defendant No.3 and 18 respectively. From the report of Process Server (Exhibit 'Tha' and 'Da') it proves that summons were duly served upon those defendants. She further submits that the fact of filing of Partition Suit No.4 of 1982 was well acquainted with the plaintiff, who came to know about the said decree in 1991 from the written statement filed in Title Suit No.206 of 1991 through his wife so the present suit was filed long after 5 years which was hopelessly barred by limitation, but the Courts bellow failed to appreciate the same and the High Court Division arrived at a correct decision.
15. The learned Advocate finally submits that the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court failed to consider that defendant No.1 has been possessing the suit land for long time and, the plaintiff appellant fraudulently filed the suit which was not maintainable.
16. In the instant case, the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title, conformation of possession and that the primary and final decree dated 30-10-1989 and 5-11-1989 passed in Title Suit No. 4 of 1982 respectively were obtained by fraud.
17. The trial Court decreed the suit, which was affirmed by the Court of appeal below. However, in revision the High Court Division set-aside the judgment and decree of the Courts bellow holding that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and it was barred by limitation.
18. The trial Court and the appellate Court although found possession of the plaintiff relying on the evidence of PW 2 but it appears that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the evidence and record came to definite finding that the defendant entered into the possession of the suit land pursuant to the decree passed in Title Suit No. 4 of 1982 and Title Execution Case No. 422 of 1999. The High Court Division also held that since defendant being the co-sharer in the suit property the suit in not maintainable in its present form without any prayer of consequential relief of khas possession. Further, the High Court Division held that the suit was not filed within a period of 3 (three) years from date of judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 4 of 1982.
19. Upon perusal and consideration of the above findings of the High Court Division, it appears that those findings are based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on records and as well as law. The High Court Division in deciding the issue of limitation has observed:
"It further appears that the fact of filing of Partition Suit No. 4 of 1982 was well acquainted with the plaintiff opposite party who came to know about the said decree in 1991 from the written objection filed in Title Suit No. 206 of 1991 through his wife. The present suit was filed long after 5 years of institution of that Title Suit No. 206 of 1991. The law of limitation provides 3 years limitation for filing a suit for setting aside a decree passed in a suit. In the instant case the Suit was filed after 5 years. So, the Suit was barred by limitation. Both the Courts below measurably failed to decide the question of limitation."
20. The High Court Division further observed that the defendant got delivery of the possession through Court on 5-5-1991 in the suit land but the plaintiff managed to get the suit land transferred by a kabala dated 19-12-1991. Learned Advocate for the appellants has tried to convince us that the High Court Division has committed serious error in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact of the Court's below.
<u>21. It is now well settled that the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction has got the jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact of the courts below, if it finds error apparent on the face of record.</u>
22. In the case of Golam Sarwar vs Md Liakat Ali, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 67, this Division has held that: "Ordinarily, the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional authority should not embark upon the function of the lower appellate court to reassess the evidence on record in reversing a finding of fact. If however, the High Court Division is satisfied that the lower appellate Court has failed to consider any material evidence in reversing a finding of fact arrived at by the trial Court upon assigning proper reason therefore, the proper course is to send back the case on remand to the appellate Court for rehearing the appeal upon proper assessment of the evidence on record. But there may be cases where, in the interest of justice, the High Court Division may also consider the evidence which were not considered by the lower appellate Court, in upholding the finding of the lower appellate Court to maintain the appellate decree."
23. In the case of Chand Biswas vs Abdul Khaleque Sheikh, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 55, this Division has also held that:
"True, the High Court division has interfered with the findings of fact by the last Court of fact but the interference being based on detecting error apparent on the face of the record need not be disturbed."
24. In the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury alias Ahmed Hossein Chowdhury and others vs Md Nurul Amin and others, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 this Division has observed that:
"It is to be stated here that if there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case."
25. Thus, we are of the view that the judgment passed by the High Court Division based on sound principle of law and facts and there is no scope to interfere with the same.
Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
End.

full_judgment:
Md Ali Reza, J: Purchaser opposite party 1 has preferred this appeal challenging the judgment and order dated 16-6-2014 passed by the Joint District Judge, Court No. 2, Magura in Miscellaneous Case 2 of 2011 allowing the pre-emption in part.
2. Respondents as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case 2 of 2011 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Court No. 2, Magura for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
3. The case of the pre-emptor, is that, the pre-emptor himself is a co-sharer in 8(eight) annas share in SA khatian 305 appertaining to Borovila Mouja. His father was owner in possession in SA plots 1203, 1204, 1205, 1272, 1365 of Purbasreekol Mouja and in SA plots 3603, 4072, 4077, 8177 of Sreekol Mouja and in SA plots 81, 83, 120, 323, 405 of Borovila Mouja. He died leaving behind 2(two) sons named Safiuddin Mridha and Golam Sarwar. Thus the pre-emptor is a recorded tenant in plot 119 of SA khatian 305 and heir of other plots. The son and daughters of Golam Sarwar sold the case land in favour of opposite party 1 by the impugned documents dated 14-12-2010 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor came to learn about the sale from the husband of opposite party 1 on 17-12-2010 and got definite knowledge on 30-12-2010 after getting the certified copy. It is further stated that the pre-emptor and his brother purchased the land of SA plot 405 appertaining to SA khatian 280 by kabala dated 16-2-1972. Their father Bazlur Rahman sold the land of plot 323 of SA khatian 351 to Jamanat Ali through kabala dated 24-10-1962. Subsequently the land was purchased by pre-emptor and his brother from Jamanat Ali Molla by kabala dated 4-2-1971. Although Bazlur Rahman sold 20 decimals of land out of 41 decimals from plot 8171 of SA khatian 1180 but he had right, title, interest and possession in the remaining land. Their mother 365 also had title in plot 1262/21365 SA khatian 1647. Besides the pre-emptor is also an heir. in SA khatian 415. Thus the pre-emptor is the co-sharer by inheritance and purchase. The quantum of land owned by the pre-emptor does not exceed the ceiling. Hence the case for pre-emption was filed.
4. Opposite party 1 contested the case. Her case is that this pre-emption is not maintainable and the same suffers defect of party. The case is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The pre-emptor and Golam Sarwar are 2(two) brothers. Golam Sarwar died leaving behind 1(one) son and 4(four) daughters who are opposite parties 2-6. These opposite parties 2-6 do not reside in the disputed mouja. Because of the necessity of sale they requested the pre-emptor to purchase the land. But pre-emptor expressed his inability to purchase the same and told opposite parties 2-6 to transfer the same elsewhere. Then opposite parties 2-6 assigned the pre-emptor to transfer the case land. Pre-emptor then asked opposite party 1 to purchase the land and negotiated and fixed the price and the transaction was done at his instance and, as such, this opposite party 1 purchased the land. Since pre-emptor gave consent to sell and also negotiated the sale his claim of pre-emption is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in plot 1205 of SA khatian 415. Samed Mridha, Hamid Mridha, Amir Mridha, Samir Mridha are necessary parties being tenants in SA khatian 2172. Wazed Mridha is also a necessary party being tenant in SA khatian 1180. Pre-emptor is not a co-sharer because he transferred his interest to some other persons. The pre-emptor knew about the transfer from before. This opposite party 1 has not purchased the case land behind his back. The husband of this opposite party 1 neither asked the pre-emptor to abandon his claim in the case land nor the pre-emptor acquired knowledge of such transfer from her husband. The case of the pre-emptor being false is liable to be dismissed.
5. Learned trial Court framed as many as 4(four) issues:
i. Whether the case is maintainable in its present form;
ii. Whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding;
iii. Whether the pre-emptor has negotiated the impugned transfer;
iv. Whether the pre-emptor can get an order of pre-emption sought for.
6. In course of trial pre-emptor examined 2(two) witnesses and opposite party 1 examined 3(three) witnesses and both the parties adduced documentary evidence in order to prove their respective cases.
7. Trial Court allowed the pre-emption in part by judgment and order dated 16-6-2014 on the finding that pre-emptor is entitled to have pre-emption being co-sharer by inheritance through his parents in all plots except SA plot 405 in which he is co-sharer by purchase. Thus partial pre-emption in 110½ decimals out of 123 decimals is granted.
8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the Joint District Judge opposite party 1 preferred the instant appeal.
9. Mr Taposh Kumar Dutta, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that from a plain reading of the application for pre-emption it is not understood how the pre-emptor became co-sharer by inheritance in the case land. He points out that it was the duty of the pre-emptor to draw a clear picture on point of his co-sharership but the application does not even introduce the BS and RS khatians corresponding to SA khatians covering the land of the disputed sale. He also submits that some of the SA khatians have not been filed to make out a definite case on co-sharership and the same is also apparent from the third schedule of the application. He further submits that the sale by exhibit-Uma(1) dated 4-6-1982 was miscalculated by the trial Court because the transferors were Bazlur Rahman and 2(two) sons of Wakil Uddin both of whom got 1/3 share each. He drives our attention on the case of Abdul Karim vs Nurjahan Begum and others, 38 DLR 361 and submits that the vendors being brother's children the pre-emptor is in loco parentis with them and principle of estoppel is applicable where a case of acquiescence is made out. He finally submits that the trial Court erred in law in allowing pre-emption in part upon wrongful consideration and the impugned judgment being perverse is liable to be set-aside.
10. Mr Md Khabir Uddin Bhuiyan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent submits that since the purchaser has admitted the pre-emptor's co-sharership by inheritance she is now estopped from challenging the same. The documentary evidence available on record clearly indicates that pre-emptor is a co-sharer by inheritance. He further submits that the plea of the appellant relying upon the case of Ahmed Hossain and others vs Basharat Ali and others, 32 DLR (AD) 54 that partial pre-emption is not tenable in the present case is not correct because it is held in the case of Karimunnessa Begum Chowdhurani and others vs Niranjan Chowdhury and another, 43 DLR (AD) 108 that several holdings if are transferred by a single kabala and if it is found that the pre-emptor is co-sharer not in full but in some holdings in that case partial pre-emption is permitted. He then submits that the learned Joint District Judge upon proper appreciation of evidence passed the judgment in accordance with law which does not deserve interference by this Court. He finally submits that since there is no bar in allowing partial pre-emption it will be legal and proper to affirm the impugned judgment.
11. We have heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused the pleadings and evidence on record and consulted with the relevant law.
12. The pre-emption case was filed on 10-2-2011. It is admitted that in major portion of the case land Bazlur Rahman was the owner in possession. He died leaving behind 2(two) sons Shafiullah, Golam Sarwar and 3(three) daughters Sofia, Rezia, Shahanaz. These 3(three) daughters are opposite parties 7-9. Golam Sarwar died leaving behind son Anisuzzman and 4(four) daughters Sahana, Samima, Sahela, Sakila who are opposite parties 2-6 and they are sellers. They sold the case land on 14-12-2010 to Selina Akter who is opposite party 1. Safiuddin claiming co-sharership by inheritance filed this case.
13. Pre-emptor claims that the sale was secretly done beyond his knowledge and he came to learn of the same for the first time from the husband of the purchaser on 17-12-2010. Opposite party 1 purchaser claims that sale was done at the instance of the pre-emptor. It is the definite case of the pre-emptee that opposite parties 2-6 due to necessity of sale requested their uncle to purchase the case land. But pre-emptor expressed his inability and told his nephews to sell to someone else. Then opposite parties 2-6 put the responsibility on the pre-emptor to conduct the sale. Because of this pre-emptor asked opposite party 1 to purchase. He fixed the price. Opposite party 1 transacted money and purchased the case land through pre-emptor. Due to pre-emptor 's consent and negotiation the sale was completed and this case is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The written objection was filed on 19-2-2012. After filing of written objection the application for pre-emption was amended on three occasions on 14-2-2013, 3-3-2013 and 20-1-2014. But this material fact of negotiation by and sale through pre-emptor was not at all challenged and denied in the application which is mandatory under Order 6 Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Material fact introduced in the written objection must be specifically controverted otherwise it tanta-mounts admission and in such a case the party who failed to controvert and deny the fact cannot be allowed to lead evidence to the extent as if the material fact has been challenged by the failing party.
14. Husband of the purchaser as OPW 1 stated in examination-in-chief that opposite parties 2-6 requested pre-emptor to purchase the land. But pre-emptor expressed his inability for want of money and told to sell elsewhere. Opposite parties 2-6 then assigned pre-emptor to sell and pre-emptor then asked opposite party 1 to purchase the land. It was not that pre-emptor did not know the sale and he did not negotiate the sale. In cross he stated that first talk of the sale was held in the house of his neighbor Monwar Khan. Pre-emptor, Monwar Khan, Akter Lasker, OPW 1 were present there Anisuzzaman came when he was informed. The case of involvement and mediation of pre-emptor as made out by opposite party 1 in her pleading and evidence was not at all denied by the pre-emptor. OPW 2 Anisuzzaman who is one of the vendors and nephew of the pre-emptor stated in his deposition that he told his uncle about sale but he refused to purchase for want of money and asked to sell elsewhere. His uncle decided to sell to Mostafa Master. Pre-emptor was present at the time of payment. In cross he stated that talk of sale was held in the house of Monwar Khan and his uncle went to the registry office before him. In the case of Abdus Sobhan Sheikh vs Kazi Jabedullah, 52 DLR 289 it was held that the presence of the pre-emptor in sub-registry office does not amount to acquiescence. We do not agree to this point of view in the present case because pre-emptor's negotiation and presence in the registry office are not challenged and denied in his pleading and evidence. Pre-emptor claims that he had no knowledge about the sale but he did not deny his presence in the registry office. It implies that he had knowledge and took a leading part in bringing about the transaction. In the case of Fazaruddin vs Maizuddin, 1994 BLD (AD) 29 = 44 DLR (AD) 62 it was held that presence of pre-emptor in the registry office does not help pre-emptee to resist pre-emption because in that case pre-emptor went to the registry office to put up resistance to the execution of the impugned sale thus the pre-emptor did not waive his right to preempt. But here in this case pre-emptor went to registry office to encourage execution and his presence in the office is not otherwise challenged or denied by him. OPW 3 stated in examination-in-chief that he was present at the time of talk of the sale. Pre-emptor was also present and fixed the bargain and in cross his statement became more emphatic like OPWs 1 and 2. PTWs 1 and 2 did not make out any case of refusing mediation and even if any evidence had been led to that effect the same would not have borne any importance being beyond pleading.
15. It should be a moral trait of people to keep their word or promise. People's trust is broken if they don't keep their word. It creates disorder and confusion in the family and society. In the instant case the previous act and negotiation of the pre-emptor in assisting and encouraging the sale is proved in evidence. Pre-emptor by his act and conduct induced pre-emptee to purchase the case land and having been so induced pre-emptee altered her position and purchased the land. The right of pre-emption inheres in a co-sharer and is flexible' or amenable to be waived or relinquished by consent, conduct or acquiescence even before the sale actually takes effect. Waiver depends upon consent and the fact that the other party has acted upon it is sufficient consideration. Acquiescence implies that a person abstains from interfering while a violation of his legal right is in progress and it operates by way of estoppel. Estoppel is a complex legal notion and very generic and amorphous rule in the law of evidence. It means one cannot contradict, deny or declare one's previous statement made by him to be false. It means to stop. According to it when any person says one thing at one time and another thing at another time then he is prevented from doing so.
16. In the case of Aklasur Rahman vs Sarafullah, 1994 BLD (AD) 20 = 42 DLR (AD) 189, it was held that the conduct of the petitioner has induced the purchaser appellant to alter their position and the pre-emptor cannot now turn around and assert his right to undo a transaction which is very largely the result of his own creation. But in the case of Fazaruddin vs Maizuddin, 1994 BLD (AD) 29 = 44 DLR (AD) 62, the principle of acquiescence and waiver in resisting pre-emption was refused. Honourable Court found that although the pre-emptor gave oral assurance that he would not pre-empt but evidence shows that he resisted the sale by presenting himself in the registry office which does not constitute waiver or acquiescence. It was held that the right of pre-emption accrues after transfer of the land and statutory right of pre-emption cannot be taken away by mere verbal assurance of the person having such right unless other facts and circumstances clearly make out a case of acquiescence or waiver. Thus this decision implies that in the event of making out a clear case of acquiescence or waiver in pleading and evidence the right of pre-emption would be defeated.
17. In the case of Rokeya Begum vs Md Abu Zaher, 2000 BLD (AD) 90 = 5 BLC (AD) 97 both Aklasur and Fazaruddin cases were referred and it was held that—
"It appears that the learned single Judge on due consideration of evidence came to the finding that the appellant waived her right of pre-emption by refusing to purchase the land transferred at the earliest opportunity and that she is estopped from repurchasing the land. The learned Judge in so holding rightly relied upon the decision in the case of Aklasur Rahman and others vs Sarafatullah and others, 1994 BLD (AD) 20 = 42 DLR (AD) 189. In Aklasur Rahman this division held   "that the right (right of pre-emption) can be waived or relinquished at an earlier date than on date of actual completion of sale under the law or thereafter."
18. In this case pre-emption was refused by majority view. 19. In the case of Dewan Ali vs Jasim Llddin, 60 DLR (AD) 73 = 13 MLR (AD) 198 both Aklasur and Fazaruddin cases were also referred. It was held by our Appellate Division that—
"The view taken in the aforesaid case of Fazaruddin appears to be a better view. Right of pre-emption accrues on the date of registration of the sale deed. The pre-emptive right of purchase of the case land accrued to the pre-emptor only after the case land was sold to the purchaser pre-emptee by its owner and not before. Pre-emptive right does not exist before sale and so it is not enforceable before sale. Any such right before sale is an inchoate and immature right. Hence no conduct of the pre-emptor before sale of the case land refusing to purchase the same or consenting sale thereon to another can constitute waiver, acquiescence or estoppel demolishing his right of pre-emption. The bare requisite for extinction or demolition of pre-emption right lies in the accrual or existence of such right. In the instant case, the facts and circumstances proved on evidence do not establish that the conduct of the pre-emptor amounted to waiver, acquiescence or estoppel affecting his right of pre-emption."
20. Thus from reading of this decision it appears that the conduct of the pre-emptor amounting waiver, acquiescence or estoppel is subject to setting up evidence. This Dewan Ali case was affirmed in the case of Syed Shamsul Alam vs Syed Hamidul Hague, 69 DLR (AD) 339. In Shamsul Alam case it was held that—
"We have also perused the decision reported in 13 MLR (AD) 198 = 60 DLR (AD) 73 wherein it has considered whether the right of pre-emptor extinguishes by waiver, acquiescence and estoppels and found that right of pre-emption arises on the date of the transfer of the disputed land. Therefore, there cannot be waiver of the right before its accrual. When not specifically proved by clean evidence on record, the contention of waiver of the right of pre-emption cannot be accepted."
21. In this case we also find that section 115 of the Evidence Act can be invoked if there is clear evidence in its support.
22. In the case of lqbal Hossain vs Joynal Abedin, 26 BLC (AD) 302 = 10 LM (AD) 143 = 18 ADC 23, Aklasur Rahman, Fazaruddin and Shamsul Alam cases were referred and it was finally held that—
"The right of pre-emption is not a right to the land sold but a right to the offer of the land about to be sold. The right of pre-emption becomes enforceable only when there is a sale but the right exists antecedently to the sale. The pre-emptor has a secondary right or a remedial right to follow the land sold. The right being a preferential right to acquire the interest, which is proposed to be sold, can be defeated by all legitimate methods. If a pre-emptor waives or gives up his right without raising any objection to the sale in favour of third party, the Court may hold that the pre-emptor has already given up his right. From the pleadings and evidence adduced by the pre-emptee it appears that the pre-emptors had voluntarily abandoned their known right. There are cogent evidence reflecting the pre-emptor's conduct which clearly established the abandonment of such right. It was argued by the pre-emptor respondents that the right of pre-emption could accrue to the pre-emptors only after sale of the land by the vendor, and thus they could not be said to have waived it by their refusal to purchase the case land before its actual sale to the pre-emptors. The right of pre-emption can be waived even before sale, by express refusal to purchase the case land or by conduct reflecting clearly that the pre-emptors were not interested in its purchase. It is to be pointed out here that cases of pre-emption are no exception to the rule of estoppel to be found in section 115, Evidence Act."
23. In the aforesaid case pre-emption was refused on ground of principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence.
<u>24. In the case in hand the Joint District Judge did not assign any cogent and rational reason in disbelieving the case of negotiation and assistance of the pre-emptor in conducting the sale. The Court disbelieved the pre-emptor's negotiation on the point that he did not sign in the impugned document as witness and since the case was filed within time the negotiation by pre-emptor is not proved. This finding is perverse and wrong for two reasons. One is Court cannot come to this finding because no case of contradicting the mediation of the pre-emptor has been made out in the application for pre-emption and the next is in the instant case the negotiation of pre-emptor is not relevant to decide the statutory period of time. Our Appellate Division discussed on point of signature in impugned document in paragraph 5 of Rokeya Begum case 12000 BLD (AD) 901 as referred above. The lower Court has to consider that the role of the pre-emptor in bringing about the sale as claimed by the pre-emptee whether is proved or not. In this case pre-emptor even did not bother to challenge and deny such allegation on negotiation through his pleading and evidence. The Court failed to appreciate the act and conduct of the parties prior to sale. The Court failed to consider the primary route for driving the course of this particular case. The pre-emptor has lost his predatory right of pre-emption because of his previous promise and conduct. He led the parties to document to complete the sale.</u>
<u>25. As discussed above and according to the ratio laid down in Iqbal Hossain case we hold that the case of pre-emption is hit by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence thus it is barred under section 115 of the Evidence Act. The trial Court misconceived the law and facts of the case and arrived at a wrong conclusion. We find substance in the appeal. Thus the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order passed by the trial Court is hereby set-aside.</u>
Communicate this judgment and send down the lower Court's record.
End.

Md Ashad Ullah, Advocate—For the Defendant-respondent-opposite party.
