full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and Decree dated 27-4-2015 passed by the Additional District Judge, Brahmanbaria, in Title Appeal No. 165 of 2004 disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming the Judgment and Decree dated 9-11-2004 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Brahmanbaria, in Title Suit No. 226 of 2001 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 226 of 2001 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Brahmanbaria for cancellation of Ewajnama Deed in respect of the suit property along with declaration of title and recovery of Khas possession.
3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the plaintiff's husband was possessing the suit land by way of purchase from the lawful owner. On 10-7-1990 the defendant took rent of the suit house standing on the suit land from the plaintiff's husband. The plaintiff's husband was a contractor and subsequently he became ill in the year 1993. Meanwhile, relationship between Hosen Kha, a classmate of plaintiff's hunband and the defendant was developed. On 3-10-1993 the plaintiff husband died. Before that on 18-9-1993 plaintiff's husband gifted the 1st schedule suit land infavor of the plaintiff in presence of the witnesses. The defendant created a forged Ewajnama Deed i.e. 2nd schedule in respect of the 1st schedule suit land allegedly showing that plaintiff's husband put his signature in the Deed. The adjacent land of Ewaj land belongs to the defendant's relations. The plaintiff's husband never possessed the same, rather in the recent survey DP Khatian No. 739 has been recorded in the name of the defendant. The suit land under 1st schedule. (6 decimals land along with a dry washing plant) which has been recorded in the name of the plaintiff. On 1-1-2001 the plaintiff found that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff and hence the plaintiff constrained to file the instant case.
4. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that Nazrul Islam alias Golam Kibria while owned and possessed the suit land transferred the same to plaintiff's hunband Abu Bakkar on 17-2-83 and 10-3-1983. The defendant got the suit land from Abu Bakkar vide. schedule-2 Ewajnama Deed. Abu Bakar on 20-3-1992 executed a Bainama Deed and died. The Ewajnama Deed was executed with the knowledge of the plaintiff and Pourashava holding number was also opened in the name of the defendant and the defendant is paying electricity bills. Since 1991 the defendant is possessing the suit land and DP Khatian has been prepared in his name. Hence the defendant prayed for dismissal of the suit.'
5. The Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Brahmanbaria dismissed the aforesaid suit vide judgment and Decree dated 9-11-2004. Against the aforesaid Judgment and Decree the plaintiff as appellant preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 165 of 2004 before the District judge, Brahmanbaria which was transferred to the Additional District Judge, Brahmanbaria who disallowing the Appeal and affirming the Judgment and Decree dated 9-11-2004 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 226 of 2001 dismissing the suit and hence the plaintiff-appellant as petitioner moved this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court and obtained this Rule.
6. Mr SM Abul Hossain learned Advocate appearing with Mr Md Golam Samdani learned Advocate submits that the Court of Appeal below being the final Court of fact neither discussed nor even mentioned the name of the PWs and DWs adduced by the parties nor mentioned the exhibits submitted by the parties neither gave independent findings in respect of the documentary and oral evidences and passed the Judgment and Decree in very slip-shod manner causing grave injustice to the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner which cannot be sustained in law. He further submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below miserably failed to consider that this suit being a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession through Court the suit has been filed within time and the Court of Appeal below being the final court of fact ought to have considered the case of either parties in juxtaposition of law. In the instant case, the Court of Appeal below neither discussed the evidences of parties at all nor mentioned the exhibits submitted by the respective parties. Non-consideration of the evidences on record and non-consideration of the exhibits filed by the respective parties independently the judgment and decree passed by the Court of Appeal below cannot be sustained in law. The learned Advocate then submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that the alleged Exchange Deed, Exhibit 4, fraudulently brought into existence covering only 52/ loo decimals of land with construction whereas the area of the suit land is. 65/100 decimals of land with construction, the excess land being not covered by the Exchange Deed Exhibit 4 should have been discussed and a finding in this regard ought to have been given by the learned Courts below the omission of which has rendered the impugned judgment and decree of the Courts below as illegal. He further submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that there cannot be any legally acceptable ground for the exchange of the suit land covered by the Exchange Deed Exhibit-4 situating at the heart of Brahmanbaria town, the value of which according to the purchase deeds of 1983 and 11987 (Exhibits 1 & 2 of 1983 and Exhibit 3 of 1987) standing in the name of the plaintiff's late husband is Taka (40,000 + 30,000 + 12,000) = 82,000 with the village land of Mouza Behair within Brahmanbaria Police Station the value of which is Taka 25,000 as stated in Exhibit 4. Besides this, the Behair Mouza village land of 5 decimals belonging to the defendant has been taken back by the defendant under an unregistered Deed Exhibit 5 in which there is only one witness but according to the section 3 of Transfer of Property Act at least 2 witnesses are necessary for any Deed and, as such, there should have been a finding that there has been no exchange at all of the suit land or any portion thereof under the alleged Exchange Deed Exhibit 4 with the Behair Mouza nal land of 5 decimals. He further submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that the Courts below ought to have come to the conclusion to the effect that the non-suited 5 decimals of nal land of Behair Mouza never came under the ownership and possession of the plaintiff's husband or the plaintiff and in such view of the matter, should have decreed the suit. He then submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that it is the settled principle of law that when both parties in a suit set up their independent claim to any property the onus becomes divided, that is to say, the plaintiff is to prove his plaint case and the defendant is to prove his defence case. He also submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that in the present suit onus being divided the plaintiff has discharged her burden by proving that the alleged Exchange Deed Exhibit 4 has been illegally brought into existences and the plaintiff's husband did not execute this alleged Exchange Deed Exhibit 4 and the plaintiff's husband did not go into possession and ownership of the Behair Mouza nal land of 5 decimals. Besides this, this 5 decimals of land also stands transferred to the defendant Exhibit Chha allegedly executed on 20-3-1992 and hence there has been no exchange of the properties between the parties and the aforesaid Exchange Deed has not been also acted upon and the defendant did not at all try to prove the execution of the suit Exchange Deed Exhibit 4 by the plaintiff's husband and so there has been failure on the part of the defendant to discharge his onus to prove the genuineness of the execution of the Exchange Deed. The learned Advocate submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that if really there would have been actually any Exchange of the properties between the plaintiff's husband and the defendant, the title deeds Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 of the suit land legally ought to have been in the custody of the defendant and on this count also the Courts below ought to have came to the conclusion that there has been no exchange of properties between the parties. He then submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that the entry of the defendant in the suit property as the ejectable monthly Bharatia under the plaintiff and the non-consideration of this aspect and the plaintiff has become the owner of the suit property by way of oral gift from her husband according to the provision of Muslim law and non- consideration of the aforesaid aspect in a lawful way has rendered the impugned judgments and decrees of the Court below illegal. Mr Hussain lastly submits that the Trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that the payment of Poura Taxes, creation of separation of Khatian, payment of rent of the suit land, papers relating to new survey, payment of electricity bill, etc all the papers marked as Exhibits for the defendant during illegal occupation of the suit land by the defendant and during pendency of the suit cannot at all be considered to be anything to confer any title to the suit property and, as such, committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.
7. Mr Md Ashad Ullah learned Advocate submits that the plaintiff is to prove her case by adducing cogent evidence as it is the cardinal principles of law that the plaintiff is to prove her case and the weakness of the defendants case cannot help the plaintiff is getting decree as mandated under section 101 of Evidence Act, 1872. The plaintiff-petitioner totally failed to prove her case and that law declared by the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh to that effect in the case of Golijar Ali Pramanik vs Saburjan Bewa reported in 6 BLC (AD) 41 (relevant para No. 8) quoted as under:-
"8....There may be thousands of defects in the documents of the defence as well as their case but that does not entitle, the plaintiff to get a decree. The plaintiff is to prove his case irrespective of the defence version of the case and from the materials on record it appears that the plaintiff failed to prove genuineness of their documents and also their possession. This aspect of the matter escaped the notice of the High Court Division is the aforesaid Second Appeal and in such circumstances the finding of the High Court Division is wrong and cannot be sustained."
8. He next submits that the plaintiff petitioner as PW 1 in cross-examination clearly admitted regarding ২য় তফসিল দলিল that:
“........ আমি ১৭-৮-৯৬ ইং সনে নালিশী দলিলের সই মহুরী নকল প্রাপ্ত হই এবং ২৪-১১-২০১১ ইং তারিখে মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করি........”
9. Evidence, quoted above, plaintiff petitioner admitted that she obtained certified copy of the Deed on 17-8-1996 and filed the Suit on 24-11-2001 for cancellation of the being Deed No. 6617 dated 23-12-1991. As per Article 91 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 time is 3(three) years for filing a suit for cancellation of the Deed from the date of knowledge. From Exhibit '4' of the plaintiff's exhibits, it is clear that she obtained certified copy on 17-8-1996 and, as such, 3(three) years time to file the suit expired on 16-8-1999 and the present suit filed on 24-11-2001. Consequently, suit is barred by limitation. Trial Court and the Court of Appeal below decided that the suit is barred by law. Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Anwarul Haque vs Iqbal Ahmed, reported in 19 BLC (AD) 253 decided law relating to Article 91 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and relevant para No. 33 quoted as under:
"33. It is evident from the above authoritative pronouncements the Court does not possess uncontrolled and unlimited power in considering an application for amendment of pleadings at any stage of the proceedings and the powers are circumscribed by certain limitations. The Court should not allow amendment only because it is relevant for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy. This is probably because, even if the prayer is lawful, if the party seeking amendment sat over his rights, his rights will be extinguished by lapse of time if the relief is not sought within the period, of limitation prescribed by law. Article 91 of Limitation Act provides the limitation of 3 years for cancellation or setting aside an instrument from the date of knowledge. Such amendment would certainly cause serious prejudice to the defendant because the claim is barred."
10. He further submits that the defendant-opposite party is in possession on the strength of Registered Deed No. 6617 dated 2342-1991. Petitioner as plaintiff exhibited certified copy of the Deed No. 6617 dated 23-12-1991, marked as Exhibit '4' without any objection. Opposite Party as defendant exhibited the original Deed No. 6617 dated 23-12-1991, which marked as Exhibit 'Ka' without objection. Consequently, both parties exhibited registered Deed No. 6617 dated 23-12-1991 as exhibit without objection, executed by the husband of the plaintiff-petitioner and the said document cannot be questioned by the plaintiff side, in view of the law declared by the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Joynal Abedin and others reported in 1993 BLD (AD) 150 = 44 DLR (AD) 162 and relevant para No. 8 quoted as under:
The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was of the opinion that those documents were not admissible in evidence as the originals were not called for. Mr SR Pal, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant appellants, rightly argued that the documents having been filed and marked exhibits without any objection, the question of admissibility of those documents cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time and the Court below, including the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, acted wrongly in not considering those kabuliyats Exhibit. D series and failed to consider the effect of these kabuliyats in the instant case. The learned Advocate, in support of his argument, has also cited the case of Abullah and others vs Abdul Karim and others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205. In that decision it has been held that objection as to formal proof of a document is to be taken at the earliest point of time. In the present case, the document was admitted in evidence is under without any objection from either side..."
11. He next submits that the plaintiff petitioner claimed title of ১ম তফসিল সম্পত্তি by way of oral gift from her husband on 18-9-1993 and the husband died on 3-10-1993. Admittedly opposite party is in possession of the suit land on and from 23-12-1991. Plaintiff failed to prove oral gift dated 18-9-1993, failed to prove that her husband made proposal of the gift to the plaintiff and she accepted the proposal of gift in presence of two witnesses and the husband handed over delivery of physical possession made to her. Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of A. Hakim vs Ahmadul Huq and others, reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 223 decided about gift and paragraph No. 5 quoted a:, under:
"The learned Advocate Mr T.H. Khan appearing on behalf of the appellants has submitted that plaintiff No. 1 has got his house in the suit lands and he has possession therein, there could not be any valid gift unless the donor Abdul Jabbar put the donee in possession of plot No. 4183 whereupon the plaintiff was possessing by constructing huts. One of the essentials of a valid gift under Muslim Law is delivery of possession, and admittedly no such delivery has been made with regard to the portion whereupon the plaintiff has been living and the huts situated thereon could not be said to have been validity given by the gift and, as such the defendants are not entitled to the portion where the plaintiff had been living in the huts situated on the south eastern corner of the bank of the disputed tank in plot No. 4183, the appeal is, therefore, allowed in part with regard to the south eastern portion of the bank of the disputed tank of Plot No. 4183 and the Deed of gift will have no effect transferring title to the donees, namely, defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 10 to the south eastern corner of the tank in plot No. 4183 where the plaintiffs huts are situated. There will be no order as to costs."
12. He lastly submits that A Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh declared law about gift in the case of Rafia Begum vs Afroza Bewa reported in 57 DLR 48 (relevant paragraph No. 11) quoted as under:
"11. For a valid Mohammedan gift there must be (1) declaration of gift by the donor, (2) an acceptance of the gift expressed or implied by or on behalf of the donee and (3) delivery of possession of the subject of gift by the donor to the donee. In case of non-fulfillment of any one of the above three conditions the gift will be invalid. In the instant case there is neither assertion in the plaint nor any evidence that the appellant ever accepted the alleged gift in any manner. There is also no evidence in support of delivery of possession. As found above the appellant never exercised her right as owner of the suit building on the basis of the alleged gift. She used to live there as the wife of its owner and has been continuing to live there even after divorce. Thus the alleged oral gift and appellant's right, title and interest in the suit property on the basis of such gift had not been proved."
13. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties and perused the record.
14. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted the instant suit for cancellation of Ewajnama Deed (Deed of Exchange Exhibit 4) in respect of the suit property along with declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land.
15. From the record it appears that plaintiff's husband was the owner of the suit land and on 10-7-1990 the defendant opposite party took rent of the suit house standing on the suit land from the plaintiff's husband. Subsequently the plaintiff-petitioner claimed title of Yg \54.p1-421 71735.A (suit land) by way of oral gift from her husband on 18-9-1993 and her husband died on 3-10-1993. Plaintiff failed to prove that her husband made proposal of the gift to the plaintiff on 18-9-1993 and she accepted the proposal of gift in presence of two witnesses and the husband handed over delivery of physical possession made to her. Plaintiff as PW 1 in her examination in chief stated “আমার স্বামী মৃত্যুর পূর্বে ১৮-৯-১৯৯৩ ইং তারিখে সকল অনুমান ১০-০০ টায় আমার ব্রাক্ষণবাড়ীয়াস্থ বাসাতে আমার ভাই সৈয়দ মফিজুল ইসলাম এবং আমার একমাত্র ছেলে আবু শামীম মোঃ সাদাত এর মোকাবিলায় মৌখিকভাবে নালিশা সম্পত্তি আমাকে দান করিয়া দখল দিয়া দেন।” but as per plaintiff's case, defendant-opposite party is in possession of the suit land on and from 10-7-1990 and tie plaintiff-petitioner filed this suit on 24-11-2001 for recovery of possession of the suit land and on the other hand the defendant-opposite party claimed that he is in possession of the suit land on the strength of Ewajnama Deed Exhibit-4 dated 23-12-1991 and admittedly on 18-9-1993, the date of Heba, the defendant opposite party was in possession in the suit land. Accordingly the alleged oral gift is not valid.
<u>16. Plaintiff as PW 1 in her examination in chief stated regarding ২য় তফসিল that “আমার স্বামীর মৃত্যুর পর ৩১-৭-১৯৯৬ ইং তারিখে বিবাদীকে আমি নালিশী সম্পত্তির দখল ছাড়িয়া দিবার এবং বকেয়া ভাড়ার টাকা দেবার জন্য বলিলে বিবাদী নালিশা উক্ত এওয়াজ বদল দলিল মূলে নালিশা সম্পত্তির মালিকানা দাবী করে ।”and in corss examination she stated  “আমি ১৭-৮-১৯৯৬ ইং সালে নালিশা দলিলের সই মুহুরী নকল প্রাপ্ত হই এবং ২৪-১১-২০০১ইং তারিখে মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করি।” As per Article 91 of the First Schedule to the limitation Act, 1908 time is 3(three) years for file a suit for cancellation of the Deed from the date of knowledge. But in the instant case plaintiff came to know about the Ewaznama Deed (Deed of 'Exchange Exhibit 4) on 17-8-1996 and filed the aforesaid suit on 24-11-2001 i.e. more than 5 (five) years after. Consequently, the instant suit is barred by limitation.</u>
17. Considering facts and circumstances of the Case, I find no substance in this Rule, rather I find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party.
18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 19. The impugned Judgment and Decree dated 27-4-2015 passed by the Additional District Judge, Brahmanbaria in Title Appeal No. 165 of 2004 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the Judgment and Decree dated 9-11-2004 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 226 of 2001 is hereby up-held.
20. The interim order of injunction is hereby vacated.
Send down the lower Courts record with a copy of this Judgment to the Courts below at once.
End.

lawyer:
Sk. Md Morshed, Additional Attorney-General with Rahima Khatun, Deputy Attorney-General; Md Ruhul Amin and Sandha Ghosh, Assistant Attorney-Generals—For the Appellants. 
Munsur Habib with Simul Sultana Advocates—or the Respondents.
parties:
Secretary Ministry of Housing and Public Works and another -------- Appellants
vs
Md Abu Muzaffor Ahmed and others ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Quddus, J: This first appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 13-10-2015 (decree signed on 19-10-2015) passed by the Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka in Title Suit Number 23 of 2004 dismissing the suit.
2. The appellants instituted Title Suit Number 283 of 2003 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka for a negative declaration to the effect that the defendant (respondent number 1 herein) had not acquired any right, title and interest over the suit land by obtaining fraudulent decree in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 and the said ex-parte decree was not binding upon the plaintiffs as the suit property was an abandoned property. Subsequently the suit was renumbered as Title Suit Number 23 of 2004 on transfer to the Joint District Judge, Arbitration Court, Dhaka.
3. The plaintiffs' case, in brief, was that the property as described in the Schedule of the plaint was an abandoned property. The Government allotted the same to the Police Department on 27-6-1972 under Memo Number 1093. Earlier the suit land was allotted to one Md Zainul Abedin in 1963 on an application dated 10-1-1963 filed by him. Said Zainul Abedin was serving Dhaka Match Factory and had seven minor children at that time.
4. One Mainuddin, a fictitious person applied for renewal of the lease on 1-1-1987 stating that his father Zainul Abedin died in 1978 leaving him as his only heir and successor. At the time of filing the application, his age was 45 years. In the said application it was stated that his mother died before the death of his father. He however managed to get the lease renewed by fraud practice without prior permission of the Government. Defendant Number 1 Md Abu Muzaffor Ahmed, an Administrative Officer of Public Works Department (PWD) identified the signature of Mainuddin and subsequently said Abu Muzaffor claimed himself as owner of the suit property. The basis of his claim was that he entered into an agreement with Mainuddin, who obtained permission to sell the suit property on 19-12-1987 and ultimately transferred it to him. He also got the record mutated in his name on 26-9-1988 under memo number 5696 and filed an application to the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Public Works on 27-9-1988 for handing over the possession.
5. It was stated that Abu Muzaffor had instituted Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka and obtained an ex-parte decree on 8-9-1996 for eviction of tenant and realization of arrear rent. The Government filed Miscellaneous Case Number 65 of 1996 for restoration of the suit on setting aside the ex-parte decree, which was also rejected on 13-7-1997. Thereafter, the Government filed several cases up to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, but failed.
6. It was further stated that Zainul Abedin took loan from the House Building Finance Corporation (HBFC) on 20-7-1964 under Loan Case Number 1778 depositing the original title deed and mortgaging the suit property. He did not approach the HBFC since 1971 and also did not pay any installment, for which the HBFC authority instituted Money Suit Number 613 of 1997 before the District Judge, Dhaka and obtained a decree. The decree could not be executed because neither the original allotee Zainul Abedin nor his heirs were residing in the Country. The suit property was a two-storied building, ground floor of which was being used by a Sub-Inspector of Police and the first floor by a battalion of Ansar. It was explained in the plaint that the original record regarding the suit property was lost and another record was reconstructed and opened on 12-10-1988.
7. Since the original allotee Zainul Abedin was not found in Bangladesh from 1971 and the fictitious person Mainuddin was trying to grab the property claiming him as the heir of Zainul Abedin and was harassing the plaintiffs by bringing several litigations, they were constrained to institute the suit. The cause .of action for institution of the suit primarily arose on 8-9-1996, when the defendant obtained the so-called decree in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 by practicing fraud upon the Court and thereafter in the last part of July 2003 which was still continuing.
8. Defendant number 1 (herein respondent number 1) contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit was clearly barred by the principle of res-judicata, law of limitation and was hit by section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. It was also barred by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The Government of the then East Pakistan allotted the suit property in favour of Md Zainul Abedin in 1963. On payment of salami and lease money, the possession of the property was handed over to him and Lease Deed Number 14438 of 1963 was registered in his favour. While in peaceful possession over the suit property, Zainul Abedin obtained a plan approved by the then Dacca Improvement Trust (DIT) and constructed a two-storied building thereon. He let out the house to the Superintendent of Police, Dacca City in 1967 for accommodation of the officials of Mirpur Police Station. The Police Department was paying him the monthly rent on regular basis. All of a sudden, the Police stopped payment of the rent from August, 1971. He tried his level best to realize the arrear rent, but failed. He died in 1978 leaving behind his son Mainuddin, who inherited the suit property. Accordingly, Mainuddin mutated the record in his name and got sale permission from the plaintiffs' office vide Memo Number SP-172/63/8591 dated 19-12-1987. Thereafter, he transferred the suit property to the defendant Abu Muzaffor in 1988 by sale deed number 6077. This defendant demanded the arrear rent with a request for delivery of possession, but the Police did not pay heed. Having no other alternative, he instituted Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka for recovery of possession and realization of arrear rent. On receipt of summons, the plaintiffs entered appearance, but ultimately did not contest the suit. As a result the suit was decreed ex-parte. The Police Department fought up to the Appellate Division, but failed to set-aside the said decree and restore the suit. Defendant number 1 then filed Title Execution Case Number 7 of 2001 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka which was/is pending. The plaintiffs had no right, title and interest over the scheduled property.
9. On the aforesaid pleadings, learned Judge of the trial Court reframed the issues, namely, (i) whether the suit was maintainable in its present form, (ii) whether it could be declared that the decree dated 8-9-1996 passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 was binding upon the plaintiffs and whether the suit property was an abandoned property, (iii) whether the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree as prayed for. During pendency of the appeal, this Court also framed two issues, namely, (iv) whether the present suit was barred by constructive res-judicata under section 11, explanation 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and (v) whether the vendor of defendant number 1 was the legal heir of original allotee Md Zainul Abedin.
10. In order to prove their respective cases, both the parties examined witnesses and adduced documentary evidence. The plaintiffs examined one Md Aminul Islam as PW 1. He stated that the scheduled property was allotted to the Police Department in 1972. Before that, Mirpur Police Station was housed there. Since a new police station was constructed, the suit property was being used for residential purpose of the police personnel. Earlier it was leased out to Zainul Abedin in 1963 by the Government of erstwhile East Pakistan. In the application for lease, Zainul Abedin stated that he had seven minor children. He paid the first and second installments of the lease money, but did not pay the third and fourth. A person named Mainuddin applied to the Government on 1-1-1987 for renewal of the lease, where he claimed himself as only son of Zainul Abedin and mentioned his age 45 years. He also mentioned that the documents were missing from his custody. At the time of mutation of record in his (Mainuddin's) name, an Administrative Officer named Abu Muzaffor Ahmed (defendant number 1 herein) identified him and attested his signature. The Deputy Commissioner, however, without proper inquiry mutated the record in his name. Mainuddin got a sale permission on 19-12-1987 in collusion with defendant number 1 and thereafter, he transferred the suit property to the defendant. After purchasing the same, defendant number 1 filed an application for mutation of the record in his name and obtained an order of mutation in his favour on 26-9-1988 by practicing fraud. Defendant number 1 then filed an application to the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Public Works for handing over the possession of the suit property. Mainuddin or defendant number 1 was not in possession of the suit property, but obtained the mutation orders by fraud practice. In fact, Mainuddin was a fictitious person set by defendant number 1 for the purpose of grabbing the suit property. He instituted Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 and obtained an ex-parte decree, but no summons in that suit was served. The Government, however, filed a miscellaneous case for restoration of the suit which was rejected for negligence of Government's pleader. The Government approached the higher Court against the said order of rejection.
11. PW 1 further stated that Zainul Abedin took loan from HBFC on 20-7-1964. On his failure of repayment of the loan, HBFC instituted Case Number 613 of 1997 and got judgment in its favour. Since Zainul Abedin or his heirs and successors were not available in the Country, the judgment could not be executed. At present the office of Deputy Commissioner of Police, Mirpur housed in the suit property. It was allotted to the Police Department by order dated 27-6-1972. Defendant number 1 by misusing his official power created the forged document. The original lessee Zainul Abedin or any of his legal heirs did not file any application for release of the property.
12. PW 1 admitted that the suit property was not included in the list of abandoned property. Because of nonpayment of lease money against third and fourth installments, the lease given to the original allotee was automatically cancelled. Mainuddin was not the son of Zainul Abedin, although he claimed so in an application dated 1-1-1987. Defendant number 1 attested the signature of Mainuddin on the said application. He was the Administrative Officer of Public Works Department. No proper inquiry was held on the application of Mainuddin.
13. In cross-examination, PW 1 stated that in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994, they were made parties, but he did not know anything about the suit. It was also not known to him whether the Government pleader was present in that suit or not. There was a miscellaneous case for restoration of the suit. So far he knew that because of negligence of the Government pleader, the said miscellaneous case was also rejected. The ex-parte decree in the suit was obtained by fraud practice. He, however, failed to explain the fraud. He knew that the Police Department approached the High Court Division and thereafter the Appellate Division. The suit property was enlisted as an abandoned property under the President's Order Number 16 of 1972, but subsequently it was not included in the Gazette because of influence of defendant number 1. He denied the defense suggestion that Zainul Abedin and his son paid the remaining installments and also repaid the outstanding loan to HBFC, or that Mainuddin was the son of Zainul Abedin. PW 1 also admitted that after mutation of the record of right, Mainuddin got sale permission from their office. It was not known to him whether Zainul Abedin let out the suit property to the Police Department in 1967. According to the affidavit, Zainul Abedin was 45 years old in 1963 and Mainuddin was 21. PW 1 exhibited bunch of documents including photocopies of the application dated 10-1-1963 filed by Zainul Abedin (Exhibit 1), allotment letter dated 6-7-1963 (Exhibit 2), affidavit dated 2-10-1963 sworn by Zainul Abedin (Exhibit 3), application filed by Mainuddin dated 1-1-1987 (Exhibit 4), application dated 27-9-1988 filed by defendant number 1 to the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Public Works (Exhibit 5), allotment letter dated 27-6-1972 (Exhibit 6), application dated 1-4-1991 filed by defendant number 1 to the Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka (Exhibit 7) and an inquiry report dated 1-9-2002 submitted by the Inquiry Committee of Ministry of Housing and Public Works (Exhibit 8).
14. On the other hand, defendant number 1 Abu Muzzafor Ahmed deposed as DW 1 and stated that Zainul Abedin was a citizen of this Country. He served Dhaka Match Factory, and his only son was Mainuddin. In 1963 he applied to the Government for a plot and the Government allotted the suit plot in his favour on 6-7-1963. Subsequently a lease deed was registered on 21-10-1963 in his favour. Thereafter, he got possession of the same and also got a plan approved by the then DIT. He constructed a two-storied building thereon taking loan from HBFC mortgaging the suit property. His son Mainuddin stood as a guarantor of the loanee and put his signature on the mortgage deed. After construction of the building, Zainul Abedin let out the building to the Superintendent of Police, Dacca City in 1967.
15. DW 1 further stated that Mainuddin got permission to sell the property on 19-2-1987. Before that, he got the suit property mutated in his name. The concerned Ward Commissioner also issued a citizenship certificate in his favour. He (DW 1) got the sale deed registered by Mainuddin on 18-8-1988 and subsequently got the record mutated in his name in the Ministry of Public Works. Thereafter, the Government issued an order dated 23-1-1989 in his favour. He paid rent and taxes to the Government Revenue Office and Dhaka Municipal Authority. The Ministry asked the Police Department to vacate the suit property by a letter dated 20-11-1989. Subsequently, in an inter-ministerial meeting held on 28-4-1992, it was decided that the suit property would be handed over to defendant number 1. After obtaining the decree in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994, the Police Department filed Miscellaneous Case Number 65 of 1996 and lastly filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Number 1364 of 2002 before the Appellate Division, but failed. Defendant number 1 paid the entire decretal money in favour of HBFC and got a money receipt. In total he paid Taka 1,62,000. Thereafter, he filed application for return of the original documents from HBFC and accordingly those were returned to him. He filed Execution Case Number 7 of 2001, where a writ of possession was issued but a Sub-Inspector of Police, Mirpur Police Station prevented him from taking over the possession of the suit property. He denied the suggestion that Zainul Abedin had seven children, or that Mainuddin was not his son, or that he (DW 1) helped Mainuddin getting the lease renewed in his name collusively.
16. DW 1 produced a copy of allotment letter dated 6-7-1963 and adduced in evidence the original lease deed number 14437 dated 21-10-1963 (Exhibit Ka), permission dated 3-2-1964 for construction of building on the suit plot (Exhibit Kha), Letter of Guarantee for loans dated 16-7-1964 executed by Mainuddin (Exhibit Ga), sale permission dated 19-12-1987 (Exhibit Gha), mutation dated 7-7-1987 in the name of Mainuddin (Exhibit,Uma), citizenship certificate dated 5-12-1968 in favour of Mainuddin (Exhibit Cha), sale deed number 6077 dated 18-8-1988 executed and registered by Mainuddin in his favour (Exhibit Chha), letter dated 25-9-1988 issued by the Ministry of Public Works (Exhibit Chha), mutation of record in the name of defendant number 1 vide letter dated 26-9-1988 (Exhibit JO, clearance certificate dated 23-1-1989 (Exhibit Jha), duplicate carbon receipt (DCR) dated 30-4-1989 issued by the Settlement Office (Exhibit Neo), mutated Khatian Number 15420 and rent receipt in the name of defendant number 1 (Exhibit Tta series and Ttha), municipal Tax receipt (Exhibit Da), WASA receipt (Exhibit Na), letter of the Ministry of Public Works dated 20-11-1989 (Exhibit Ta), resolution of the meeting dated 28-5-1992 presided over by the Joint Secretary (Police), Ministry of Home Affairs (Exhibit Tha); letter dated 19-1-1993 and similar letters issued by the Ministry of Home (Exhibit Da series), judgment and decree dated 8-9-1996 passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 (Exhibit Dha series) and the original mortgage deed dated 20-7-1964 executed by Zainul Abedin (Exhibit Bha) etcetera.
17. After conclusion of hearing, learned trial Judge dismissed the suit by the impugned judgment and decree giving rise to the instant first appeal.
18. After the hearing started, the plaintiff-appellants filed two applications, one for additional evidence under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code and another for sending the suit on remand. The defendant-respondent filed two separate written objections against the said applications annexing some documents with a prayer to consider those documents as evidence. We heard the applications and kept it with the record for disposal at the time of disposal of the appeal.
19. Mr Sk. Md Morshed, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the appellants submits that the original allotee Zainul Abedin got the allotment by filing an application stating he had seven minor children (vide Exhibit 1). So it cannot be believed that Mainuddin, who was 45 in 1987, was the only son and heir of Zainul Abedin. The suit property was initially listed as an abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972. As the defendant number 1 had a greedy eye on the property, he had influenced over the matter and managed to misplace all the relevant documents. As a result the suit property could not be subsequently enlisted and published in the official gazette as an abandoned property. As a part of his plan, defendant number 1 set the fictitious Mainuddin and did all the mischiefs to get the property registered in his name. It is a settled principle of law that fraud vitiates everything. So, whatever decree defendant number 1 got in his favour, it would not help him when the fraud has been proved subsequently.
20. As a second line of argument, Mr Morshed further submits that since this Court framed two more issues, the suit should be sent on remand under section 107 of the Code read with Order XLI, rules 23 and 25 thereof. He also submits that if the paper and documents filed with the application for additional evidence is considered by this Court, it would be clear that Mainuddin was not the son of Zainul Abedin.
21. On the other hand, Mr Munsur Habib, learned advocate for the defendant-respondent number 1 takes us through the evidence particularly Exhibits-Ga, Chha, Bha and submits that from a critical examination of the said documents, the signature of Mainuddin put on the Sale Deed dated 18-8-1988 (Exhibit Chha) matches his signature on the Letter of Guarantee dated 16-7-1964 (Exhibit Ga) and Mortgage Deed dated 20-7-1964 (Exhibit Bha). Besides, the address of Md Zainul Abedin, namely, "81, Dania Angul Lane, Dacca" as given in the Lease Deed dated 17-10-1963 (Exhibit Ka), Letter of Guarantee (Exhibit Ga) and Mortgage Deed, and that of the guarantor Mainuddin as mentioned on the last page of the Letter of Guarantee as well as in the Mortgage Deed is same. The father's name of Mainuddin has also been mentioned "Md Zainul Abedin" on the first page of the Letter of Guarantee.
22. Mr Munsur Habib further submits that the plaintiffs stated that the summons in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 were suppressed and not served upon the defendants, but it appears from the ex-parte judgment passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 that the present plaintiffs as defendants appeared in the previous suit and prayed for time repeatedly, but ultimately did not contest the suit. There is no scope to say that the summons were not served upon the defendants in the previous suit. After rejection of the Miscellaneous Case and failure of the Government/Police. to set-aside the decree up to the Appellate Division, when defendant number 1 filed the execution case and a writ of possession was issued, the plaintiffs instituted the present suit which is hopelessly barred by limitation as well as by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. Despite service of summons upon the defendants and making their appearance in the previous suit, they did not contest the suit by raising any claim over the suit property. The instant suit is, therefore, barred by res-judicata.
23. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates and carefully gone through the evidence and other materials on record. The plaintiff-appellants filed the application for additional evidence annexing the photocopies of some documents starting from serial number 9! Of them the first one (Annexure-9!) is a letter dated 27-6-1972 issued by the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development informing the Inspector General of Police that the attached list of houses (it includes the suit property) would be allotted for accommodation of Police Units, Police Out-Posts, Police Officers and Staff in the Dacca City provided the houses were abandoned houses within the meaning of PO 16 of 1972. It is thus clear from the language of this letter that the suit property was yet to allot and the Government was not very sure whether it was an abandoned house. In the said letter, it was also mentioned that the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca was requested to take possession of the houses. It does mean that the Police had no independent possession over the suit property at the time of issuance of the said letter. It helps the defendant number l's case that the Police was a tenant under the original lessee since before 1972.
24. Annexure-10 to the application is a notice dated 7-8-1969, by which the Government asked the original allotee Zainul Abedin to pay the arrear installments with an intimation that in case of his failure to pay the arrear, it would be recovered under the Public Demand Recovery Act. When the suit property was leased out by a registered instrument on receipt of salami and possession was handed over to the allotee, who already paid two installments out of four, and constructed a building thereon taking permission from the Government, the registered deed of conveyance would not be invalidated for non-payment of two installments. The Government would be entitled only to realize the arrear. As a consequence of such non-payment, the lease would not be cancelled, nor would the property be treated abandoned. So, this piece of document would not develop the plaintiffs' case.
25. Annexures-11 series are five receipts showing payment of land development tax against 0.12371/2 acres of land in Jote Number 99/1 one. The tax was paid on yearly basis in 2004, 2012 and 2018-2020. The description of land does not correspond to the schedule of the plaint. Even if it corresponds the suit property, would not make the plaintiffs' case stronger inasmuch the present suit was instituted in 2003, but they failed to show any payment receipt before 2004. It is presumed that the Police started paying the land development tax from 2004 for the purpose of creation of evidence. It is also not clear that without mutation of record, how they could pay the tax in the name of Police. Being post-dated to the institution of the suit, these land tax receipts would also not help the plaintiffs.
26. In this way if we consider the other documents as annexed with the application, namely, Annexures-12, 13, 14 series and 15, these would not help the plaintiffs. Some of the documents rather support the defendant's case.
27. All the annexed documents are photo-copies, but there is no explanation wherefrom the plaintiffs collected these photocopies when they specifically pleaded that the office record in respect of the suit property was lost. No statement regarding payment of land development tax (vide Annexure 11 series) and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit Number 260 of 2003 (vide Anexure-14/B) have been made in the plaint. These documents being out of pleadings are not admissible in evidence. Similarly, the plaint in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 (Annexure-13) has been annexed to be adduced as an additional evidence, but has not been explained why it was relevant to prove what contention of the plaintiffs. In this regard, it is pointed out that the factum of institution of the said suit has not been disputed by the adversary.
28. Moreover, Annexures: 13-15 are photo-copies of certified copies of plaint, decree, judgment, judicial order etcetera. When a certified copy itself is the secondary evidence as defined in section 63 of the Evidence Act, photocopy of certified copy of any judicial record is not ac:missible as secondary evidence where the originals are lying with judicial record and certified copy thereof can easily be obtained by any person. It is not explained in the application, why the plaintiff-appellants failed to obtain the certified copies of these documents. There was no scope to adduce any of these documents in evidence during trial of the suit. In such a position, we do not find any reason to allow the application for additional evidence at appellate stage and, as such, it is rejected.
29. Learned Additional Attorney-General prays for sending the suit on remand as two more issues have been framed by this Court for proper adjudication of this first appeal. This court sitting in appellate jurisdiction is empowered to send back a suit on remand under section 107 read with Order XL1, rules 23 and 25 of the Code, but as a general principle remand should be avoided. Learned Additional Attorney-General does not propose any additional documents to be adduced in evidence for adjudication of the issues number (iv) and (v). Whether the suit is barred by constructive res-judicata being a mixed question of law and fact can be decided on the evidence already adduced in trial and whether the executant of the sale deed in question was the son and only heir of Zainul Abedin, can also be determined by the evidence available on record. It is a settled principle of law that an appeal is continuation of suit and the Appellate Court is empowered to do all things that a trial court can. We, therefore, do not find any reason to send the suit on remand.
30. It appears that in the previous suit, the same property was the subject matter, where the Government represented by the Secretary Ministry of Public Works was made defendant number 2 and the Chairman, Abandoned Property Management Board was 4, the Inspector General of Police was made defendant number 1 and the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs was 3. It further appears from the ex-parte judgment of the said suit (vide Exhibit Dha series) that despite making appearance and seeking time for filing written statement on several occasions, ultimately they did not contest the suit. In the said suit, the plaintiffs ought to have taken the defense or ground of attack which they pleaded in the present suit. In view of section 11, explanation IV of the Code the present suit on the selfsame subject matter between the same parties appear to be barred by the principle of constructive res-judicata.
31. In the previous suit, decree was passed in favour of the plaintiff (defendant number 1 herein) for eviction of the Police in presence of the Government-plaintiffs. The Police filed Miscellaneous Case Number 65 of 1996 for setting aside the ex-parte decree which was rejected for default by order dated 3-10-1997. Thereafter the Police filed a time-barred first miscellaneous appeal before the High Court Division that was summarily rejected by order dated 24-8-2000. The Appellate Division by its order dated 30-3-2003 also dismissed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Number 1364 of 2002. The Government though appeared in the title suit, did not contest the same or challenge the decree in any forum. The ex-parte judgement and decree dated 8-9-1996 passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 thus reached finality.
32. If we still go into the merit of the present suit, we find that the plaintiffs claimed the property to be an abandoned property under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal Order, 1972 (PO 16 of 1972), but failed to produce any single evidence in support of their claim. It also does not appear that the Government formed any opinion regarding the abandon character of the suit property. The buildings in urban area, which were treated abandoned, were subsequently enlisted in the Ka and Kha list of abandoned properties and published in the Official Gazette under the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance LIV of 1985). Such list is a conclusive proof of abandon character of a property, though it is rebuttable. Admittedly, the suit property is not enlisted as an abandoned property and published in the Official Gazette. The plaintiffs also failed to produce any notice for surrendering or taking possession of the suit property as mentioned in section 4 of the Ordinance LIV of 1985 and, as such, there is no scope to claim it as abandoned after 31st Day of October, 1988. Where the property was not enlisted as an abandoned property, question of allotment of the same as an abandoned property did not arise. It has already been discussed that the letter dated 27-6-1972 of the Ministry of Public Works does not show the suit property to be abandoned. It was allotted to the Police provided that it was an abandoned house. From the language of the said letter it clearly appears that the Government itself was confused about the abandon character of the suit property and did not publish it in the Official Gazette under Ordinance LIV of 1985. Under the circumstances, there is no scope to claim the suit property to be an abandoned property.
33. On the other hand, if we go through the evidence of defendant number 1, his title on the basis of a registered sale deed with prior permission of the Government, successive mutation in the name of Mainuddin and Abu Muzaffor Ahmed (defendant number 1), full payment of lease money, issuance of clearance certificate by the Government, repayment of outstanding loan to HBFC and return back of the original title documents, payment of rent and municipal tax, WASA bill etcetera and production of original title documents by defendant number 1 have been proved in support of the defendant's case. The Ministry of Home issued letter and reminders to the Police for vacating the suit property. In cross-examination, PW 1 could not reply whether the Police rented the house in 1967 from its original lessee Zainul Abedin. It proves that before getting allotment in 1972, the Police was in possession of the suit property. In this background, a duty is cast upon the plaintiffs to explain how the Police went into the possession of the suit property, if it was not let out to them by the original lessee. In view of the above, we think that the defendant number 1 has been able to prove his better title.
<u>34. It also appears that after exhausting all the procedures, when the Execution Case was filed in 2001 and a writ of possession was issued by the Executing Court, the present suit was instituted. Initiation of such suit thus appears to be motivated. It is admitted that the suit property was not enlisted and published in the official gazette as an abandoned property under Ordinance LIV of 1985. The Government or any of its functionaries has no lawful authority to occupy/retain any property of the citizens unless it is vested in it. The Police being an agency of the Government and law enforcers, should not be an illegal occupant of a property. If, still the plaintiffs had any case, they could have raised it in the previous suit, which they did not. The miscellaneous case filed by the Government/Police Department was rejected and the Government/Police failed up to the Appellate Division and ultimately the decree of civil court for recovery of possession in favour of defendant number 1 reached finality. At this stage, the Government or any of its. Agencies should not use the law as well as the process of the Court as an instrument of continuance of illegal possession of any property.</u>
35. Learned Additional Attorney-General for the plaintiff-appellants heavily relied upon Exhibits-1 and 3 and tried to impress upon us that the original lessee Zainul Abedin had seven minor children. So attaining 45 years age on the part of Mainuddin in 1987 was a false statement. We have critically examined both the documents, which were photocopies. Nowhere in those photocopies, the age of Mainuddin was mentioned, but in the affidavit (Exhibit 3) Zainul Abedin was described as a man of 45 years of age. PW 1 adduced those photocopies in evidence without producing the originals, but stated that he was holding the same. There was no endorsement of the learned trial Judge that the plaintiffs ever produced those original documents before the Court, or that the learned Judge himself examined the originals. In paragraph 2 of the plaint, it was stated that the original record of the suit property was lost. In such a position, without producing the originals or any explanation about missing of the same and disclosing the source of photocopies, how the photocopies could be adduced in evidence. Even if the application dated 10-1-1963 (Exhibit 1) is taken to be a replica of the original, it is best known to Zainul Abedin why he stated like that. May be for the purpose of drawing sympathy in his favour, but without any explanation offered by Zainul Abedin, it is difficult to arrive at a ready conclusion on such a doubtful document.
<u>36. In order to appreciate the identity of Mainuddin, we have critically examined the original copy of the letter of guarantee dated 16-7-1964 (Exhibit Ga), registered mortgage deed dated 20-7-1964 (Exhibit Bha) and the sale deed dated 18-8-1988 (Exhibit Chha). In all the documents, the signatures of Mainuddin appear to be of the same hand. His father's name in Exhibits-Ga and Chha is written "Md Zainul Abedin". In the letter of guarantee and mortgage deed, the address of Md Zainul Abedin and that of Mainuddin on the first page of the letter of guarantee are same, i.e. "81, Dania Angul Lane, Dacca". If these three documents, of which two are older than 50 years and undisputed, are considered with the citizenship certificate (Exhibit Cha) and oral evidence of DW1, there are reasons to arrive at the finding of fact that Maiduddin was the son of Zainul Abedin.</u>
37. Learned trial Judge considered the evidence on record, observed that the plaintiffs failed to prove the suit property to be abandoned and that the decree passed in the previous suit reached in finality and dismissed the suit. We do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and decree under appeal.
38. Accordingly, the first appeal is dismissed. The judgment and decree passed by the Court below is affirmed.
Send down the lower Court's record.
End.

parties:
Nusrat Sanjida ---------- Petitioner
vs
Chairman, Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) and 2 (two)  others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Ullah, J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents show cause as to why the initiative taken by the respondents to transfer the ownership of the private car of the petitioner, bearing No. "Dhaka Metro-Gha:15-5914" (said car) ignoring her objection should not be declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents should not be directed to stop harassing the petitioner asking to appear repeatedly at the office of the respondent No.2 on the pretext of resolving the disputes of ownership of the said car and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper shall not be passed.
2. The facts relevant for the disposal of the Rule as made out in the writ petition, in short, are that the petitioner by her hard earned money purchased a private car bearing Chassis No. RU1-1012694, Engine No. L15B-3512710. Pearl Colour and got her name registered on 4-5-2017 bearing registration No. "Dhaka Metro Gha:15-5914" (hereinafter referred to as the disputed car). Due to the frequent misbehaviour of her husband at one stage she was compelled to leave the husband's residence keeping her private car, and the documents of the car therein. Without obtaining any permission her husband on 22-2-2018 deposited the requisite money to the bank for transferring the ownership of the car in his name. Having heard such an initiative, the petitioner on 27-2-2018 applied to respondent No. 2 requesting him not to transfer the ownership of the car to her husband's name (Annexure-B). Respondent No. 2 by a letter dated 30-7-2018 asked the petitioner to appear personally at his office on 27-8-2018 to give statements about the dispute of the ownership of the car and accordingly, she appeared therein and explained the total situation and requested respondent No. 2 not to transfer the ownership of the car (Annexure-C). In this connection, the petitioner also made a CD Entry to the police station. Again on 7-1-2019 the respondent No. 2 asked the petitioner to appear in person at his office within 7(seven) days, to explain the ownership of the car and informed that if she fails to appear and explain her position that deemed to be she has had no objection in changing the ownership of the car. She on 10-1-2019 again appeared at the office of respondent No. 2 and put her specimen signature. Thereafter the petitioner on 14-1-2019 sent an application to respondent No. 2 informing that all the documents of the car remained with her husband's house and she did not put her signature on the purported document of changing the ownership of the car and requested not to transfer the ownership of the car (Annexure-E). Again on 29-1-2019, respondent No. 2 issued a letter asking the petitioner to appear at his office within 7(seven) days with a money receipt, import document and other relevant papers in connection with the car. In such facts and circumstances, the petitioner on 9-2-2019 served a legal notice upon the respondents stating the facts that she having repeatedly appeared in the office of the respondent BRTA requesting them not to transfer the ownership of the car. Despite such facts again on 15-7-2019, respondent No. 2 issued another notice asking the petitioner to appear personally at his office on the pretext of resolving the dispute about the transfer of the ownership of the car which manifests the bad intention of the respondents to transfer the ownership of the car to her husband's name and harassment of the petitioner (Annexure-H).
3. The petitioner also filed two applications one is for attachment of the car and another one for a direction for handing over the car to her custody and to withdraw the suspension of the data of the car from the Information System (IS) of BRTA.
4. Respondent No.3, husband of the petitioner contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that he purchased the car from his fund. But the petitioner managed the registration of the car to her name through the backdoor as a result she is trying to avoid the BRTA authority. The BRTA being a statutory authority has lawful responsibility to resolve the dispute in respect of the ownership of the car. The dispute about the registration of the car does not fall within the purview of the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31 and 42 of the Constitution and, as such, the writ petition is not maintainable. Who paid the purchased money of the car is a highly disputed question of fact that cannot be resolved under the summary jurisdiction of this Court. Under section 107 of the Road Transport Act, 2018 there is a provision for review against any order of BRTA and since the petitioner without availing the alternative remedy filed the instant writ petition, the Rule should be discharged.
5. Respondent No. 2, BRTA entered appearance through Mr Muhammad Rafiul Islam, a learned Advocate of this Court who filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, that the BRTA has the authority to transfer the ownership of the car in question and to do its statutory obligation, BRTA asked the petitioner to appear in person and there is no intention on the part of the office of the BRTA to harass or humiliate the petitioner in any way. The BRTA issued a circular under Memo No. 35.03.0000.31.041.2015-1367 dated 26-4-2016 stating the fact that for transfer of ownership of a car legally, the owner of the car should come to the office of BRTA personally and disclose his or her identity and make a signature on the transfer document. Accordingly, the petitioner was asked to appear at the office of the BRTA. Under section 24 of the Road Transport Act, 2018, the BRTA has the authority to cancel the registration of any vehicle and, as such, notices, as issued upon the petitioner to resolve the dispute, was legally served and hence the Rule should be discharged.
6. On the written request of respondent No. 3 the BRTA took initiative to transfer the ownership of the car that deposited the requisite transfer fees to the concerned bank on 22-2-2018. Based on the application filed by the petitioner. BRTA suspended data front the IS system of BRTA temporarily. Following the application dated 27-8-2018 filed by respondent No. 3, respondent No. 2 by a letter dated 7-1-2019 asked the petitioner appear in person at his office to give her statement about transferring the ownership of the car. On the said request made by respondent No. 2, the petitioner on 27-2-2018 and 10-1-2019 personally appeared before respondent No. 2 and put her specimen signature to show that the purported affidavit for transferring the ownership of the car as filed by respondent No. 3 is forged one. On 28-1-2019 the respondent No. 2 asked the petitioner to appear before his office in person to show the import documents but the petitioner neither appears in person nor submitted any document of the car. Respondent No. 2 only took initiative to resolve the dispute of ownership of the car and, as such, he did not harass the petitioner in any way.
7. Mr Khan Ziaur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the car in question purchased by the petitioner from her fund and registration thereof made in her name rightly by the office of the BRTA, and the petitioner being the sole owner of the car without her written consent BRTA cannot take any initiative to transfer the ownership of the car and, as such, the initiative of the respondents taken beyond the provisions of law and Rules ignoring the objection of the petitioner and hence such initiative is liable be declared have been taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
8. The learned Advocate submits further that on two occasions on the request of BRTA, the petitioner personally appeared and made her statements of ally, as well as, in writing and therein requested respondent No. 2 not to transfer the car to her husband's name but the respondent No. 2 did not pay any heed to such request of the petitioner rather repeatedly upon issuing notices tried to harass and disturb the petitioner in the name of resolving the dispute of the ownership of the car and, as such, the subsequent attempt of the respondent No. 2 should be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
9. The learned Advocate next submits that respondent No. 3 without obtaining any written affidavit or document for transfer of the ownership of the car as required by law deposited the transfer fee on 22-2-2018 to the concerned bank for transferring the car to his name and hence the respondent No. 2, BRTA cannot proceed further for transferring the ownership of the car ignoring the objection of the petitioner and, as such, the subsequent initiative as taken by the respondent No. 2, BRTA should be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
10. The learned Advocate again submits that since the car is under the custody of respondent No. 3, this Court may issue a direction upon the law enforcing agency to hand over the car to the petitioner, as she is the lawful owner of the car.
11. The learned Advocate again submits that a direction should be given to the BRTA to withdraw the suspension order from the IS system of BRTA so that the petitioner can run the car without any disturbance.
12. Mr NM Ahsanul Haque, learned Advocate for respondent No. 3 submits that respondent No. 3 paid the purchase money of the car from his fund, however, due to the restriction to get registration in joint name the car was registered in the name of the petitioner and, as such, the BRTA rightly took initiative to transfer the ownership of the car.
13. The learned Advocate also submits that the writ petition involved the disputed question of facts as to who paid the purchase money of the car and the same cannot be resolved under writ jurisdiction and hence, the Rule should be discharged.
14. The learned Advocate again submits that under section 107 of the Road Transport Act, 2018 there is a provision for review against any order passed by the BRTA and, as such, the present writ petition is not maintainable as the petitioner did not avail such alternative remedy and hence the Rule should be discharged.
15. Mr Muhammad Rafiul Islam, learned Advocate for respondent No. 2 has reiterated the facts made in the affidavit-in-opposition as his submissions.
16. We have perused the materials on record and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates from the contending parties.
<u>17. It appears from the facts that due to frequent inflexible and maladaptive patterns of behaviour, the petitioner was compelled to leave her husband's house on 5-2-2018. Maladjustment affects their couple relationship and family life and now they are living at a separate match. It appears from Annexure-A that the disputed car is registered in the name of the petitioner. The husband of the petitioner on 22-2-2018 deposited the requisite money for transfer the ownership of the car without any document from the petitioner. On the written notices, the petitioner appeared before respondent No 2 twice and explained the conduct of her husband and requested not to transfer the ownership of the car and she disclosed the facts that she did not put any signature in any document for transfer of the ownership of the car even though the responder` No. 2 repeatedly asked the petitioner to appear in person. In such facts and circumstances, when the BRTA ignoring the objection of the petitioner took further initiative without any no objection of the petitioner for transfer of the ownership of the car she moved this Court and obtained the Rule. At the time of issuance of the Rule, on 23-7-2019 the respondents were restrained by an order of injunction from transferring the ownership of the car. For transfer of the ownership of a car, BRTA is to confidently sanguine that the initiative to transfer has been taken properly and lawfully. If necessary BRTA can hear the owner of the car and proposed buyer in person. In the instant case, the petitioner on two occasions on the written requests of respondent No. 2 went to his office and made a written objection for not to transfer the ownership of the car. The petitioner expressed that she did not sign in any ownership transfer document. The affidavit for the transfer of the car dated 20-11-2018 is a forged one. Respondent No. 3 deposited the requisite transfer fees to the concerned bank on 22-2-2018 without oral or written consent for transferring the ownership of the car of the petitioner. Therefore, without no objection or written approach of the owner of the car, the BRTA cannot take further initiative to transfer the vehicle in favour of respondent No. 3. The learned Advocate for respondent No. 3 rightly submits that who paid the money is a disputed question of fact and sitting under writ jurisdiction this Court cannot determine such dispute. Accordingly, we need not consider it prudent to find out who paid the money to purchase the car in question. But there is no doubt the car was registered in the name of the petitioner and she is the sole owner of the car until or unless the ownership is transfer lawfully. Had respondent No. 3, the husband paid the purchased money of the car in favour of the petitioner even then the respondent No. 3 cannot claim the ownership of the car as there is no provision for Benami transaction. To the query made by this Court, the learned Advocate for respondent No. 3 submits that his client did not obtain any affidavit or transfer of ownership document from the petitioner. About Annexure-11 an affidavit for transfer of the ownership of the car as filed by BRTA, respondent No. 3 did not know anything. So it is manifestly clear that the petitioner did not file any affidavit for transfer of her car in favour of respondent No. 3. In such facts and circumstances, the petitioner filed a GD Entry No.358 dated 6-2-2019 to the Officer-in-Charge, Ramna Model Police Station, DMP, Dhaka.</u>
18. For the reasons stated above we find merit in the Rule, as well as, in the application filed by the petitioner for handing over the physical possession of the car in her favour.
19. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute.
20. The Officer-in-Charge, Ramna Model Police Station, DMP, Dhaka is hereby directed to confiscate the car from the possession of respondent No. 3 and handover the same to the petitioner within 3(three) days from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment and order.
21. The respondent, BRTA authority is directed to remove the suspension order from its IS system, if not done yet, so the petitioner can run the car smoothly as the owner of the same.
22. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Officer-in-Charge. Ramna Model Police Station, DMP, Dhaka for compliance.
However, there would be no order as to costs.
End.

Shah Muhammad Ezaz Rahman with Mohammad Ayub Ali, Advocates—For the Petitioner.
