parties:
Enayet Hossain (Md) -------- Petitioner
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
JBM Hassan, J: By filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution, the petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi in the following terms: "Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Order No. 15 dated 30-3-2005 and decree dated 30-3-2005 passed by the respondent No. 1, Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj, in Artha Rin Suit No. 300 of 2004 (Annexure-B and B-1) and the proceeding of Artha Execution Case No. 348 of 2005 and the Order No. 25 dated 16-3-2009 passed therein by the respondent No. 1, Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Narayangonj (Annexure-D), should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper."
2. Subsequently, by order dated 1-11-2010 the petitioner also obtained a supplementary Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order No. 29 dated 15-4-2009 passed by the Artharin Adalat, Narayangonj in Artha Execution Case No. 348 of 2005 rejecting an application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
3. Relevant facts leading to issuance of Rule Nisi and supplementary Rule Nisi are that the Manager, Agrani Bank Limited, Kanchan Branch, Rupgonj, Narayangonj (respondent-Bank) instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 300 of 2004 before the Artha Rin Adalat (Joint District Judge), Narayangonj for recovery of loan amounting to Taka 17,59,920.20 as on 31-3-2004 with up to date interest. Ultimately the suit was decreed exparte on 30-3-2005 (decree signed on 30-3-2005) for the aforementined amount with interest till recovery. Thereafter the decree-holder Bank filed Artha Execution Case No. 348 of 2005 for recovery of decretal dues. In the execution proceeding, the mortgaged property was put on auction and the respondents No. 3 and 4 jointly became highest bidders with their offer at Taka 8,60,000. The bid was accepted by the impugned order dated 16-3-2009. There-after, the judgment-debtor filed an application on 15-4-2009 under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("the Code") depositing Taka 7,94,000. The application was rejected by the impugned order (in supplementary Rule) dated 15-4-2009 on the ground that the petitioner did not deposit the required balance dues in accordance with Rule 89 of the Code. In this backdrop, challenging the decree dated 30-3-2005 and the order dated 16-3-2009 passed in the execution proceeding accepting the bid, the petitioner filed the writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi. Thereafter, the petitioner obtained supplementary Rule Nisi challenging the order dated 15-4-2009 rejecting application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code.
4. Mr Shah Muhammad Ezaz Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits as follows:
(i) The principal amount was Taka 4,00,000 while the suit was filed for Taka 17,59,920.20 and thereby, the claim being more than 200% interest on the principal amount, the suit was on the face of it illegal in accordance with section 47 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (the Act, 2003).
(ii) At the time of filing application for setting aside the sale under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code, the petitioner deposited Taka 7,94,000 towards compliance of the requirement (a) of Rule 89 and instantly the petitioner could not deposit in terms of sub-rule (b) of Rule 89. But ultimately petitioner repaid entire liabilities with the consent of the Bank and the mortgaged property was redeemed and thereby the execution case has been concluded setting aside the sale in accordance with Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code.
(iii) At the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi, as per direction of this Court the petitioner paid Taka 2,00,000 and subsequently, adjusted the entire liabilities negotiating with the Bank in accordance with section 45 of the Act, 2003.
(iv) Bid money deposited by the respondents No. 3 and 4 (auction purchasers) are lying with the Court and the possession of the property has never been handed over to the auction-purchasers. Therefore, considering the stage of execution proceeding, there is scope, even after confirmation of sale, to compromise in accordance with section 45 of the Act, 2003.
(v) The Adalat directed to publish auction notice in two newspapers but the respondent-decree-holder Bank did not comply with the said direction and so the property was sold at a very shockingly low price in an irregular manner.
(vi) After confirmation of sale, considering all aspects the Appellate Division has done complete justice returning back the property to the judgment-debtor giving solatium to the auction purchaser and this authority can be exercised even by the High Court Division exercising section 57 of the Act, 2003.
5. In support of his submissions, learned Advocate refers to the case of Md Mitul Mollah vs Abul Khayer Mollah and others reported in 28 BLT (AD) 278; the case of Abdul Malek (Md) vs Md Asaduzzaman Belal and others reported in 67 DLR (AD) 146; the case of Habibur Rahman Miah vs The learned Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat, Pabna and others reported in 28 BLT (HCD) 7 and the case of AB Mannaf Sheikh (Md) vs 1st Joint District Judge Court and Artha Rin Adalat and others reported in 19 BLC 493.
6. On the other hand, learned Advocate for the respondents No. 3 and 4 (auction purchasers) by filing affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit contends as follows:
(a) The suit was filed on 8-4-2004 while section 47 came into effect on 1-5-2004 and, as such, there was no illegality in filing the suit and passing the decree imposing interest more than 200%. Moreover, non application of section 47 of the Act, 2003 in the suit, cannot be raised in the writ petition except for an appeal in the appellate forum.
(b) The sale was accepted on 16-3-2009 and it was made absolute by the order dated 15-4-2009. Long thereafter, by filing writ petition the petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi on 10-5-2009. Therefore, after making the sale absolute, the Artha Rin Adalat being functus officio cannot set-aside the auction sale.
(c) The application was filed for setting aside the auction sale under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code. But the requirement to deposit the entire liabilities as per sub-rule (a) and (b) of Rule 89 having not been complied with, the Adalat rightly rejected the application which does not call for any interference by this Court.
(d) Before filing writ petition, the sale was confirmed and made absolute. But the petitioner did not disclose those facts at the time of filing the writ petition. Due to which the High Court Division at the time of issuance of the Rule directed to pay Taka 2,00,000 and so the petitioner deposited the money at his own risk suppressing the facts in filing the writ petition.
(e) The auction purchasers paid full bid amount in the year, 2009. Thus, after confirming the sale, the respondents No. 3 and 4 took possession of the property and they are now possessing the property mutating their names relating to the purchased property.
7. In support of his submissions, learned Advocate refers to the case of Sonali Bank vs Artha Rin Adalat and others reported in 62 DLR (AD) 231; the case of Sonali Bank, Sadarghat Corporate Branch, Dhaka vs Mrs. Hazera Islam and others reported in 6 ADC 975; the case of Sk. Mohiuddin vs Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3, Dhaka and others reported in 13 MLR (AD) 356 and the case of Feroza Begum vs Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka and others reported in 2016 BLD (AD) 31.
8. Although, the Bank (decree-holder) appeared by filing affidavit-in-opposition but at the time of hearing of the Rule Nisi, no one appears on behalf of the Bank.
9. We have gone through the writ petition, affidavits-in-opposition separately filed by the Auction Purchasers (respondents 3/4) and the Bank. Supplementary-affidavits filed by all the contending parties as well as the cited cases.
10. Three issues have been raised under this Rule Nisi. Firstly, Decre of the artha rin suit has been questioned raising provision of section 47 of the Act, 2003. Secondly, propriety of the order dated 16-3-2009 accepting highest bid has been questioned and thirdly, the order dated 15-4-2009 has also been impugned by which petitioner's application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code was rejected. Therefore, we are addressing those issues in the following manner:
11. To address the first issue we have gone through section 47 of the Act, 2003 which runs as follows:
“৪৭। দাবী আরোপে সীমাবদ্ধতা ।-(১) বর্তমানে প্রচলিত অন্য কোন আইন বা পক্ষগণের মধ্যে সম্পাদিত সংশ্লিষ্ট চুক্তিতে যাহাই থাকুক না কেন, এই আইনের অধীন মামলা দায়েরের ক্ষেত্রে, কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কোন খণ গ্রহীতাকে প্রদত্ত আসল ঝণের উপর দায় এমনভাবে আরোপ করিয়া আদালতে মামলা দায়ের করিবে না, যাহাতে আদালতে উত্থাপিত উক্ত সমুদয় দাবী আসল খণ অপেক্ষা 200% (S00 + 200 = ৩০০ টাকা) এর অধিক হয়।
(2) উপ-ধারা (১) এ বর্ণিত মতে আসল ঋণ অপেক্ষা ২০০% এর অধিক অনুরূপ দাবী আদালত কর্তৃক গ্রহণযোগ্য হইবে না।
(৩) এই ধারার বিধানটি এই আইন বলবৎ হইবার এক বৎসর পর কার্যকর হইবেঃ
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান, ইচ্ছা করিলে, এই ধারা কার্যকর হইবার পূর্বেই, এই ধারার বিধান অনুসরণ করিতে পারিবে ।”
12. Sub section (1) and (2) of section 47 debar the plaintiff to claim in the suit more than 200% interest on the principal amount. But sub-section (3) of the said provision provides that section 47 will take effect one year after the Act came into effect. The Act, 2003 came into effect on 1-5-2003 and so, the effect of section 47 was scheduled to have come into effect on 1-5-2004. But the present artha rin suit was filed on 8-4-2004. Although there is a proviso giving discretion to the creditor-bank for waiving interest as per section 47 within that one year but non exercise of such discretion shall not make the suit illegal. Therefore, we do not find any illegality in claiming interest beyond 200% in the suit inasmuch as the loan was disbursed long back in 1991. Moreover, it is not the forum to raise this issue.
13. To consider the 2nd and 3rd issues as pointed above, we have gone through both the impugned orders dated 16-3-2009 and 15-4-2009. By the order 16-3-2009 the highest bid of respondents No. 3 and 4 (auction purchasers) was accepted. Although, the decree holder bank objected the highest offer claiming low price but the Adalat giving cogent reason rejected the objection and accepted the bid inasmuch as objection was not filed by any Bank's representative in accordance with law and that the highest offer was above the Bank's proposed value. However, the Bank has not challenged the said order before any higher forum.
14. Furhter, the judgment-debtor (petitioner) also did not challenge the said bid or auction by filing miscellaneous case under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) alleging low price or irregularity or fraud in conducting auction. Rather, the judgment debtor (petitioner) filed application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code to set-aside auction sale by depositing entire liability and compensation, which being rejected by the impugned order dated 15-4-2009 has been challenged, which is 3rd issue under this Rule Nisi. Moreover, application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code having been opted and filed, at the same breath, the petitioner cannot file application under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code in view of Order XXI, rule 89 (2) of the Code.
15. To appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates for determining the propriety of the impugned order dated 15-4-2009 rejecting the application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code, let us first read the relevant provisions of Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code which run as follows:
"89. Application to set-aside sale on deposit (1) Where immovable property has been sold in execution of a decree, any person, either owing such property or holding an interest therein by virtue of a title acquired before such sale, may apply to have the sale set-aside on his depositing in Court—
(a) for payment to the purchaser, a sum equal to five percent of the purchase-money, and
(b) for payment to the decree-holder, the amount specified in the proclamation of sale as that for the recovery of which the sale was ordered, less any amount which may, since the date of such proclamation of sale, have been received by the decree-holder.
(2) Where a person applies under rule 90 to set-aside the sale of his immovable property, he shall not, unless he withdraws his application, be entitled to make or prosecute an application under this rule.
(3) Nothing in this rule shall relieve the judgment-debtor from any liability he may be under in respect of costs and interest not covered by the proclamation of sale."
16. Pursuant to aforesaid provisions to file an application, the judgment-debtor is required to deposit 5% of the proclamation amount as compensation for the auction purchaser and also to deposit entire liabilities as mentioned in the sale proclamation. The said amount has to be deposited within one month from the date of sale in accordance with Rule 92(2) of the Order XXI of the Code. Admittedly, the petitioner did not deposit the required amount in compliance to the said provision considering which the Adalat rejected the application by the impugned order dated 15-4-2009. Therefore, we do not find any illegality in passing the impugned order dated 15-4-2009 by the Adalat rejecting the application under Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code.
17. This view of ours finds support from the case of Mohammad Golam Azam vs The Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and others reported in 10 ADC 417 wherein the Apex Court held as under:
"14. The High Court Division came to a finding that there was no scope for setting aside the auction sale without payment of decretal amount and that admittedly the petitioner deposited only 5% of the price of the auction sale and that the petitioner did not pay the decretal amount as mentioned in the proclamation of sale according to law.
15. The findings arrived at and the decision made by the High Court Division having been made on proper appreciation of law and fact do not call for interference."
18. Mr Shah Muhammad Ezaz Rahman, learned Advocate submits that although the requirement of deposit of entire liabilities in accordance with Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code was to be made within 30 days from sale but the present Rule Nisi being pending before the High Court Division regarding the same issue, the petitioner had the scope to deposit money during pendency of the Rule and that during that period the petitioner his adjusted the liabilities and thereby compliance have been made as per requirement of Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code.
19. To appreciate the submission, we have examined Rule 92 of Order XXI of the Code which runs as follows:
"92. (2) Where such application is made and allowed, and where, in the case of an application under rule 89, the deposit required by that rule is made within thirty days from the date of sale, the Court shall make an order setting aside the sale. Provided that no order shall be made unless notice of the application has been given to all persons affected thereby."
20. Rule 92(2) requires deposit under rule 89 within 30 days from the sale. Non compliance of such requirement the application was disallowed, sale was confirmed and thereupon it became absolute in accordance with Rule 92(1) of the Code.
21. We find that the auction bid was accepted on 16-3-2009 and thereafter the petitioner filed the application for setting aside auction sale resorting to Order XXI, rule 89 of the Code but he did not comply with the condition precedent depositing entire liabilities and after 30 days from the sale, as per law the Court made the sale absolute. The sale was confirmed on 15-4-2009 and sale certificate was issued and registered.
22. Thus, while the transaction became closed, the petitioner came before this Court by filing writ petition and obtained the Rule Nisi on 10-5-2009. Therefore, at this stage, it cannot be said that the petitioner got scope to adjust the liabilities availing the provisions of Rule 89 of the Code. Although at the time of issuance of the Rule Nisi this Court directed the petitioner to deposit Taka 2,00,000 but in the four corners of the writ petition, we do not find that the petitioner ever stated that before moving the writ petition, the sale was made absolute and thus non-disclosing the real facts, the petitioner obtained the order to deposit the money and that being so, it was deposited at his own risk.
23. Now at the fag end of hearing, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the auction notice was published in one newspaper instead of two newspapers as directed by the Adalat and the price was shockingly low. But it is not the petitioner's case before us or before the Artha Rin Adalat, because there was no such application filed before the Artha Rin Adalat under Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code alleging fraud or irregularity or shockingly low price of the auction sold property. Further, filing of application under Rule 89 being opted, the application under Rule 90 cannot be filed in view of Rule 89(2). So much so, from the order sheet we find that auction sale was confirmed and made absolute in accordance with Order XXI, rule 92 of the Code. Thereafter, the Adalat issued sale certificate which was ultimately registered before the concerned Sub-Registrar.
24. There are series of decisions of our Appellate Division that after confirming the sale and issuance of sale certificate, the Artha Rin Adalat becomes functus officio and it has no scope to interfere with the sale. We find the cited cases reported in 6 ADC 97; 62 DLR (AD) 231; 2016 BLD (AD) 31; 13 MLR (AD) 356. In all those cases, the Apex Court held that after making the sale confirmed/absolute there is no scope to interfere with the auction sale.
25. Mr Rahman again submits that the petitioner has not yet handed over possession to the auction purchasers and the auction money is still lying with the Court. In the circumstances, the Adalat can interfere with the sale considering the payment of entire decretal dues. The respondents No. 3 and 4 (auction purchasers) claim that they have got the possession of the property without court's interference.
<u>26. Yet, relying upon the case reported in 2016 BLD (AD) 31 the High Court Division in the case of Bank Asia Limited vs Judge, Artharin Adalat, Chattogram and others case reported in 71 DLR 338 held that non delivery of possession to the auction purchaser, is not material in making the sale absolute and closed in the execution case. If the auction purchaser needs possession through Court in that case he can file proper application before the Artha Rin Adalat under section 33(7ka) of the Act, 2003 and in that case the Adalat can pass appropriate order directing the judgment-debtor or possessor or the owner to hand over possession to the auction purchaser. But this position as to non-delivery of possession will no way help the petitioner to question the auction sale as well as to set-aside the auction sale when a right to property was accrued in favour of bonafide purcharer for value long back in 2009.</u>
27. Finally, Mr Rahman submits that since the liability has been adjusted with the Bank and the Bank in the meantime executed a deed of redemption and that auction money are lying with the Court. At this stage, this Court can consider the whole matter within the ambit of complete justice as the Appellate Division held in the cases reported in 28 BLT (HCD) 7; 28 BLT (AD) 278; 67 DLR (AD) 146 and 19 BLC 493.
28. Referring to the case of 19 BLC 493 he submits that exercising the inherent power of the Court under section 57 of the Act, 2003 the High Court Division can give such relief setting aside the auction sale giving appropriate solatium to the auction purchaser. Before addressing on this point let us first examine the section 5(4) of the Act, 2003 which runs as follows:
"৪। The Transfer of property Act, 1882 অথবা বর্তমানে প্রচলিত অন্য কোন আইনে বিপরীত যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, উপ-ধারা (৩) এর অধীন বন্ধকী মামলা ব্যতিরেকে, এই আইনের অধীন দায়েরকৃত কোন মামলায়, আদালত কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ডিক্রী বাদী আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের পক্ষে নিক্রিয় সমান্তির (Foreclosure) প্রাথমিক ডিক্রী হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে; এবং ঋণের বিপরীতে বাদীর অনুকূলে বন্ধকী স্থাবর সম্পত্তি ডিক্রীর ধারাবাহিকতায় নিলাম বিক্রয় হওয়া মাত্রই উক্ত প্রাথমিক ডিক্রী চুড়ান্ত ডিক্রী হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে, এবং বিক্রয় চুড়ান্ত এবং ক্রয় বৈধ গণ্য হইবে এবং অতঃপর উক্ত সম্পত্তি পুনরুদ্ধার করিবার কোনরুপ অধিকার (Right to  redeem) বিবাদী-দায়িকের থাকিবে না।”
<u>29. We find that the property was sold in auction and the sale was made absolute and thereafter the sale certificate having been registered through Court and the purchasers mutated their names. All these events took place in the year, 2009. Thus, the property has been vested absolutely with the auction purchasers with their title. We are surprised, in such circumstances, how the Bank can execute the deed of redemption in favour of the mortgagor when the auction sale has not yet been set-aside. We are of the view that execution of deed of redemption on 29-3-2015 is absolutely a nullity and void ab initio. Because long before the said execution of deed of redemption, the property was sold to the auction-purchasers making the sale absolute and there was no interference at that moment by the higher Court. Moreover, after auction sale of mortgaged property, leaving the auction purchaser. the Bank cannot make any compromise under section 45 of the Act, 2003.</u>
30. Further, section 57 of the Act, 2003 is an inherent power of the Adalat to be exercised for passing necessary order in the absence of any statutory remedy under the Act, 2003 or the Code. But there are multiple provisions both in the Act, 2003 and under Order XXI of the Code for setting aside auction sale on different stage and eventually, when the sale was confirmed and made absolute under the statutory provision i.e section 5(4) of the Act, 2003, that cannot be interfered exercising inherent power under section 57 of the Act. Moreover, in a series of cases, our Appellate Division consistently laid down ratio that after making the sale absolute there is no scope to set-aside the sale, at this stage, we do not have the scope to do any complete justice in aid of section 57 of the Act contradicting the settled ratio of the Appellate Division. We are of the view that complete justice can only be done by the Appellate Division in accordance with article 104 of the Constitution. Therefore, the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is not tenable in the eye of law. To come to this view we have relied upon the case of Sonali Bank, Sadarghat Corporate Branch, Dhaka vs Mrs Hazera Islam and others reported in 6 ADC 975 wherein the Apex Court held as under:
"7. It appears that the decree of foreclosure in favour of the plaintiff attained its finality and the judgment debtor shall have no right to redeem the said mortgaged property. Moreover after issuance of the certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat AM the same court of Artha Rin Adalat Ain had no power to entertain the application of the appellant invoking section 57 of the Aitha Rin Adalat Ain as such power under section 57 is only available when the other provisions of the Ain are not exhaustive. In this case after the certificate issued under section 33(5) of the Ain the decree-holder has already sold the suit property in favour of the respondent No. 8, Md Rafique by registered sale deed and therefore there is no scope to interfere with the bonafide purchase for value."
31. In view of above discussions, we do not find any merit in the Rule Nisi.
32. In the result, the Rule Nisi is discharged. There is no order as to costs.
33. The. Deed of Redemption bearing No. 2912 of 2015 executed by the respondent Bank (Agrani Bank Ltd) on 29-3-2015 in favour of the mortgagors registered with the Sub-Registrar, Rupgonj East, Narayangonj is hereby declared as void ab initio and, as such, is of no legal 'effect.
Communicate a copy of the judgment and order to the respondents at once.
End.

full_judgment:
AKM Asaduzzaman, J: An application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed challenging the judgment and order dated 18-9-2022 passed by the Senior District Judge, Jamalpur in Civil Revision No. 36 of 2022 reversing those dated 4-4-2022 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Islampur, Jamalpur in Other Class Suit No. 127 of 2021 rejecting the application for amendment of plaint.
2. Instead of making a prayer for leave, Rule was prayed for and accordingly this Rule was issued although in the application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no scope for praying a Rule in this way, however since the Rule was issued by this court, and that refraining from making an objection heard this Rule and disposed of by this judgment.
3. On 23-2-2020 opposite parties as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 80 of 2020, subsequently renumbered as Other Class Suit No. 127 of 2021 being transferred before the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Islampur, Jamalpur, for trial against the petitioner and another for declaration of title in respect of 0.19'/4 acres of land as described in the schedule of the plaint.
4. Defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement denying the plaint case.
5. During pendency of the suit on 13-1-2021 plaintiff filed an application for amending of the plaint under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
6. The Senior Assistant Judge by the judgment and order dated 4-4-2022 rejected the said application.
7. Challenging the said order, plaintiff preferred CR No. 36 of 2022 before the Court of District Judge, Jamalpur.
8. By the impugned judgment and order dated 18-9-2022 the District Judge allowed the revision and reversed the judgment of the trial court.
9. Challenging the said order defendant petitioner preferred this application.
10. Mr Mohammad Eunus, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner drawing my attention to the schedule of the plaint and the amendment of plaint submits that in the plaint nature and character of the suit land has been changed. Suit was shown as cultivating land (ভূমি আবাদি নামা) but in the amendment application by inserting the nature and character of the suit land as (নালিশী ভূমি বসত বাড়ীর ভূমি বটে) it has altogether changed the nature and feature of the suit land, which is not permissible under law by way of amendment of the plaint. The learned Assistant Judge has thus rightly found the same and rejected the application but the appellate court has totally failed to consider this aspect of this case and allowed the amendment most illegally and the impugned judgment is thus not sustainable in law. In support of this contention the learned advocate cited a decision in the case of Azmal Khan vs Md Afzal Khan and others reported in 64 DLR (AD) 17. Wherein their lordships has held that:
"The Courts should bear in mind that although section 15 and Order 6 Rule 17 have given a wide power in favour of amendment of pleadings, such power will be exercised where the amendment amounts to no more than a different additional approach to the same fact. An amendment setting up a new case totally inconsistent with the original case set up will not be allowed if it is unjust to the opponent."
11. In reply to this submission Mr GM Mozahidur Rahman, the learned advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that in the plaint RoR khatian has shown as 2291 wherein the land has sought to bear area of 261/2 decimals of land but since it was mistakenly typed, by way of amendment, the plaintiff tried to introduce the fact that the RoR khatian was in fact 2221 instead of 2291 and accordingly the area of the suit land would be 0.19¼ acres instead of 26½ decimals of land as shown earlier in the plaint but so far the boundaries is concerned there is no change it was remain as it is:
“যাহার উত্তরে আঃ মালেক, দক্ষিণে-মজিবর, পূর্বে-জহর, পশ্চিমে-রুবেল গং।”
12. In the valuation statements although by way of amendment it has been sought to be introduced that: নালিশী ভূমি বসত বাড়ীর ভূমি বটে।  instead of নালিশী ভূমি আবাদী নামা শ্রেণীর ভূমি বটে, it causes no changed of the amendment of the plaint, prayer of the suit and the nature and character of the suit remains as it is. The above change of the amendment application does not effect in any way to the right and interest of the opposite parties as such not been denied in the suit by the defendants through any written objection. Revisional court has thus rightly found the same and allowed the application. Since the amendment do not change in any way the nature and feature of the suit and which are very much essential to determine the real question of controversy, the revisional court committed no illegality in allowing the application.
13. In support of his contention, the learned advocate for the opposite party cited a decisions, namely in the case of Krishna Sundar Mujumder vs Chairman, Chowmuhani Pourashava and others reported in 2 ALR (AD) 119 wherein in the schedule of the plaint boundary in respect quantum of the land as shown in the boundary was sought to be amended. In that case their lordships held that:
"Since the area of the suit land has been described in the schedule to the plaint With a wellneated specific boundary of the suit land mere correction in the quantum of the suit land by way of amendment of the plaint keeping the boundary in tact can not and in deed will not affect the right and title of the defendants in their land nor such correction should be considered to alter the nature and character of the suit or the plaint."
14. In the case of Md Awal Molla vs Md Sayedur Rahman (Sayeed) and others reported in 24 BLT (AD) 440, wherein in the schedule there are some short of amendment was prayed for along with addition of some fact in the body of the plaint. In that case their lordships held that:
"We have considered the averment made in the plaint and the proposed amendment and we are in agreement with the Courts below that the amendment would in no way change the nature and character of the suit."
15. Also referred to a decision in the case of Mettu Bhimudu vs Duggirala Pitchayya and others reported in (1946) 1 mu 462. In the said case by the amendment he sought to plead that by reason of the first defendant's death, the whole of the suit property passed to him according to Hindu Law, that the plaintiff had absolute right to obtain possession thereof and that defendants 3 and 4 had no right whatever to the suit property, the will set up by them and the cowle relied upon by the fifth defendant not being genuine. Consequential amendments were also sought in the paragraphs relating to the cause of action and the reliefs prays for. In the case their lordships held that:
"Consequently it was a necessary and just development of his original case that he should ask for possession of the same on the strength of his alleged right of adoption and in doing so I am unable to hold that there is an alteration or variation of the fundamental character of the suit or that it is a case where one cause of action has been substituted for another. There is no new cause of action as the title remains the same and in any case there is no prejudice caused to the defendants."
16. Heard the learned advocate and per-used the impugned judgment together with the application for amendment of plaint.
17. This is a suit for declaration of title. In that suit an application for amendment was sought for by the plaintiff. From the submission of the opposite party as well as going through the plaint and the amendment application it would be noticed that plaintiff sought ROR amendment on some mistakes in the ROR khatian. In the plaint khatian No. shown as 2291 which now would be 2221 instead of 2291, and the quantum of the land would be 0.19¼ acre instead of 26½ decimel as been said earlier in the plaint and in the body of the plaint some fact has been introduced saying that:
“উক্ত প্রকারে বাদীগণ নালিশী ভূমি পৈত্রিক ওয়ারিশ সূত্রে মালিকানা প্রাপ্ত হইয়া নালিশী ভূমির পার্থ দিয়া বর্তমানে পাকা রাস্তা হওয়ায় বাদীগণ উক্ত ভূমিতে রাস্তা সম মাটি কাটিয়া ভরাট করিয়া উক্ত ভূমিতে ২টি বসত ঘর, ১টি রান্নাঘর, ১টি টিউবওয়েল, ১টি ল্যাট্রিন ও বিভিন্ন প্রকার ফজল গাছপালা রোপন করিয়া এবং অবশিষ্টাংশে বাড়ীর আঙ্গিনা হিসাবে ভোগদখল পরিচালনা করিয়া আসিতেছেন বটে ।”
18. In the valuation statements plaintiffs tried to introduce some fact saying that: “নালিশী ভূমি বসত বাড়ীর ভূমি বটে। instead of নালিশী ভূমি আবাদী নামা শ্রেণীর ভূমি বটে ।”
<u>19. Now question raised whether the above amendment, causes any change of nature and character of the suit or thereby defendant would be prejudiced or not. Trial Court tried to say that the above amendment will change the nature and character of the suit but the appellate court held that the above contention will not in any way change the nature and character and, as such, he allowed the application for amendment. In fact by way of amendment plaintiff did not pray for any alternative prayer rather the suit was intact as the suit for declaration of title with the boundary as been stated in the schedule of the plaint wherein it has been said that: "যাহার উত্তরে- আঃ মালেক, দক্ষিণে-মজিবর, পূর্বে-জহর, পশ্চিমে-রুবেল গং।” So when by amendment they identify the suit land through the boundary as been mentioned in the plaint was not change and the foundation of the suit i.e. suit for declaration of title has not been changed.</u>
20. The learned advocate Md Mohammad Eunus appearing for the petitioner try to make a submission that the plaintiffs by amendment tried to claim the property of the defendants, wherein the defendant has got and homestead land of their own whether the plaintiffs claimed the land of the defendants or not, this is a matter to be decided on evidence by the trial court during trial but perusing the application for amendment of the plaint together with the plaint I do not find there is any prejudice and the nature and character of suit will be changed by amendment as been sought for, which causes any interfere by this court. The decision referred to by the opposite party got some reliance namely in the case of Crishna Sundar Mujumder vs Chairman, Chowmuhani Pourashava and others, reported in 2 ALR (AD) 119.
21. Regard being had to the above law, fact and circumstances of the case, I am of the opinion that the revisional court committed no illegality in amendment of the plaint.
22. I thus find no merits in this Rule.
23. In the result, the Rule is discharged.
24. The order of stay granted earlier is hereby recalled and vacated.
Communicate the judgment at once.
End.

full_judgment:
Zafar Ahmed, J: In the instant writ petition, the petitioner challenged the judgment and order dated 3-11-2022 (Annexure-L) passed by the Election Appellate Tribunal, Jamalpur in Election Appeal Tribunal Case No. 21 of 2022 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 14-6-2022 passed by the Election Tribunal, Jamalpur in Election Petition No. 59 of 2022 (Annexure-H) allowing the same and thereby setting aside the election of the petitioner as General Member of Ward No. 5 of No. 7 Merurchar in Union Parishad Election, 2021 held on 5-1-2022 and declaring the respondent No. 2 as being the elected candidate.
2. This Court, on 16-11-2022 called for the records, issued a Rule Nisi and passed an interim order of stay.
3. Challenging the interim order of stay, the respondent No. 2 filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) No. 3404 of 2022, but did not obtain any order of stay. The CPLA was disposed of by the Apex Court on 23-1-2023 directing this Bench to dispose of the Rule on merit.
4. Relevant facts are as follows:
The petitioner was elected as Member of general seat of Ward No. 5 of 7 No. Merurchar Union Parishad under Upazilla Bakshiganj, District Jamalpur in the Union Parishad Election held on 5-1-2022 by a narrow margin of 8 votes by securing 496 votes, while the respondent No. 2 secured 488 votes. In due course the petitioner took oath and went into the office, but the respondent No. 2 challenged his election by filing an election petition before the Senior Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Jamalpur impleading the present petitioner and another contesting candidate as opposite parties praying for inter alia, recounting of ballot papers on the grounds stated therein.
5. The present petitioner contested the election case by filing written objection. The Tribunal framed issues. Each side both examined 3 witnesses who were cross-examined.
6. It appears from the lower Court records (LCR) that on 2-6-2022 the Tribunal heard the arguments of the learned Advocates of both sides and relying on the case reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 236 = 38 DLR (AD) 275 (para 13) passed an order for recounting of the ballot papers holding that the petitioner of the election case (present respondent No. 2) succeeded by adducing evidence in preparing the foundation for recounting. The Tribunal observed,
“এ বিষয়ে পিটি ভব্রিউ ১ জেরায় বলেন, “পি. ও রজব আলীর বিরুদ্ধে আমি অভিযোগ দেইনি সত্য নয়। আমার এলাকার অনেক ভোটার এরকম অভিযোগ করে । নির্বাচন চলাকালে গন্ডগোল হয় তা দরখাস্তে নেই।” পি ভব্লিউ ২ তার জেরায় বলেন, “জীল ভোট দেয় আমার ভাতিজা সাইদুরের ভোট ৷” ফলে প্রার্থীপক্ষের আনীত অভিযোগসমূহের প্রাথমিক সত্যতা যাচাই করার জন্য ভোট পুনঃগণনার প্রয়োজন মর্মে সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হলো ।”
7. It appears from the judgment dated 14-6-2022 passed by the Tribunal and the report of the Serastadar of the Tribunal dated 14-6-2022 that on 14-6-2022 the Serastadar reopened the gunny bags and recounted the ballot papers in presence of the parties with the assistance of the members of staff of the Tribunal and found that the election petitioner (present respondent No. 2) had secured 427 votes, whereas the opposite party No. 1 (present petitioner) had secured 351 votes. The Tribunal considered the report and allowed the election case and declared the respondent No. 2 as elected candidate.
8. Challenging the judgment and order passed by the Election Tribunal, the present petitioner filed 'Election Appeal before the Election Appeal Tribunal, Jamalpur consisting of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Jamalpur and Additional District Magistrate, Jamalpur.
9. It appears from order dated 341-2022 passed by the Appeal Tribunal that it passed an order for recounting of ballot papers by the Serastadar of the Appeal Tribunal as its representative. It further appears from the said order as well as the report of the Serastadar dated 3-11-2022 that on that day the Serastadar recounted the ballot papers. According to the report, the petitioner and the respondent No. 2 obtained 346 and 373 votes respectively. The Appeal Tribunal accepted the report and passed the verdict dismissing the appeal. Hence, the instant writ petition.
10. Mr MK Rahman, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner made his submissions on two grounds, firstly, both the Election Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal did not lay down sufficient foundation based on evidence on record in directing recount of ballot papers; and secondly, assuming but not conceding that there was such sufficient foundation, the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal committed fundamental error of law in delegating the power of the Tribunal to the Serastadar in the matter of recounting of ballot papers. In support of the argument, the learned Advocate refers to case laws which we are going to discuss shortly.
11. Mr Khondaker lqbal Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2, on the other hand, submits that since the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable in the proceedings, the instant writ petition is not maintainable and civil revision invoking civil revision jurisdiction of this Division is the appropriate forum to challenge the impugned judgment and order passed by the Appeal Tribunal. He next submits that ballot papers were recounted in presence of the parties and that the present petitioner did not challenge the recounting conducted by the Serastadar. Moreover, the petitioner made a written application before the Appeal Tribunal for recounting. The learned Advocate further submits that the finding of fact arrived at by the Appeal Tribunal as well as the Tribunal cannot be interfered in writ of certiorari which involves resolution of disputed question of facts and assessment of evidence which is not the function of the judicial review Court.
12. The election in question was held and the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal were formed under the স্থানীয় সরকার ইউনিয়ন পরিষদ) আইন, ২০০৯ (in short, the 'Ain, 2009') and স্থানীয় সরকার ছেউনিয়ন পরিষদ) নির্বাচন বিধিমালা, ২০১০ (in short, the 'Rules, 2010'). Section 23(6) of the Ain states that the judgment of the Election Appeal Tribunal is final. Hence, the instant writ petition is maintainable.
13. With the introduction of the Ain, 2009 the earlier Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 was repealed. There was no provision for recounting of ballot papers by the Tribunal in the earlier election laws and rules. Nevertheless, in the past Election Tribunal used to pass recounting order which was an outcome of judicial decisions.
14. Under Rule 62 of the Rules, 2010 the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal have been vested with the power to pass an order for reopening the gunny bags and recounting of ballot papers. Be that as it may, Rules, 2010 is silent as to the circumstances empowering the Tribunal to pass such order. In other words, the statute law is silent as to the "sufficient foundation" for making the order of recounting. Therefore, we have to consider the case laws decided prior to promulgamation of the Act, 2009 and Rules, 2010 on this particular point of "sufficient foundation".
15. In Nurul Islam Talukdar vs Munsif of the 4th Court at Sadar Chittagang acting as Election Tribunal and 10 others, 28 DLR 375, it was held:
"When the election was held in a peaceful atmosphere and scrutiny and counting of ballot papers were made in an orderly manner, without any objection from any quarter, reports of the Presiding Officers as to due performance of their duties must be accepted. Otherwise, there will be no sanctity of a free election which is a must for running democratic institutions."
16. In Nowsher Ali Molla vs Election Tribunal and Sadar Munsif, Faridpur and another, 33 DLR 344 this Division held that the Election Tribunal acted illegally in declaring the petitioner's election as void and illegal on the basis of the recounting of votes without considering the evidence adduced by the parties. The case was remanded back to the Tribunal to decide on the basis of existing evidence and in accordance with law and to receive further evidence, if considered necessary.
17. In Afzal Khan vs The Election Tribunal and Munsif 3rd Court, Comilla and another, 1980 BSCR 69 = 32 DLR (AD) 186, the Appellate Division held as correct the following views of the High Court Division—
(a) that the counting was not asked for before the Presiding Officer.
(b) foundation for the exercise of jurisdiction of the Tribunal merely for re-counting was not laid.
(c) In the facts and circumstances of that particular case the High Court Division was justified in recounting the votes itself of the other 14 centres.
18. The Appellate Division further observed:
"Normally mere counting of votes may not be a sole issue before any Election Tribunal unless sufficient foundation for such exercise is laid by evidence. In the present case no allegation was made before the Returning Officer specifically regarding the error in counting but this was raised before Tribunal along with the allegation of corrupt practice."
19. The Appellate Division further observed:
"The jurisdiction of counting eminently lies elsewhere and even the Election Tribunal cannot count the ballot papers, unless the recounting becomes a necessary part of the case itself which has been brought on the basis of certain allegations of corrupt and illegal practices. It is well settled that if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal in connection with an election petition which cannot be determined without such recounting, then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recounting the ballot papers provided sufficient foundation has been laid to come to the findings that the recounting is indispensably necessary for adjudication of the election petition."
20. The above-quoted dicta given in 1980 BSCR 69 = 32 DLR (AD) 186 as well the ratio laid down in 31 DLR (AD) 296, 27 DLR 594, 28 DLR 375 and 33 DLR 344 were discussed and considered by a single Bench of this Division in Moulana Abdul Hague vs Faziul Huq and others, 38 DLR 401 wherein the Rule was made absolute and the case was sent back on remand to the Tribunal holding:
"I am of the opinion that the Tribunal should follow the well-settled path of discussing the oral and documentary evidence on record and then dwell on the result of recounting, if necessary. The Tribunal has already reopened the ballot boxes and whatever it has already found after recounting the ballot papers it will discuss after discussing the other evidence on record. The Tribunal, however, is not precluded from receiving further evidence if it considers necessary for arriving at a decision. The petitioner shall also be at liberty to raise the question of limitation and adduce evidence in respect thereof.
The opposite party No. 1 will also be entitled to give evidence to the contrary. The petitioner shall also be entitled to file an additional written objection so as to question the election petition on the ground of limitation."
21. In Syed A Jalil vs Mahbub Alam (Babul) and others, 46 DLR (AD) 96, it was held:
"It is true that before recounting of ballot papers, which are confidential documents, preserved in proper custody, evidence should be led for preparing the foundation for reopening of the ballot papers. But in this case, a number of dates were fixed for recording of evidence, but this petitioner took adjournments twice and himself remained absent once. In these circumstances, the order of recounting cannot be held to be bad in law."
22. In Md Shajahan vs Md Sadeq and another, 1986 BLD (AD) 236 = 38 DLR (AD) 275 (referred by the Tribunal in support of passing the order of recounting), the Apex Court referred to the case reported in 28 DLR 375 (supra) and held:
"It is not a case of benefit of doubt going to a defeated candidate feeling aggrieved like the accused in a criminal case. Here, presumption is in favour of the returned candidate whose election shall not be declared a nullity unless the Tribunal "is satisfied" as laid down in rule 49 that the election has been materially affected by some illegal acts or contravention of some rules."
23. In Md Khalilur Rahman vs Md Alam Bepari and others, 14 MLR (AD) 43 = 14 BLC (AD) 84, the Apex Court affirmed the decision of the Election Appeal Tribunal holding:
"It appears that the Election Appellate Tribunal has considered the evidence of PW 1, 2 and 3 and also considered the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence of OPW No. 1 and 2 and came to the finding that the election petitioner has succeeded in proving factual foundation for recounting of the ballot papers. The Election Appellate Tribunal appears to have applied his mind in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record keeping in view that there was a difference of only one vote between the petitioner and the respondent No. 1 and admittedly 5 ballot papers, which were duly cast during election, wore found missing and on consideration of these facts the Election Tribunal came to the conclusion that it would be proper for ends of justice if the ballot papers are recounted in presence of the concerned parties."
24. It appears from the case laws discussed above that the principle of laying "sufficient foundation" before passing an order of recounting by the Tribunal has emerged through judicial pronouncements and the principle cannot be placed in a strait jacket nor can a 'fit-for-all' formula be laid down. The principle does vary from case to case and, from one fact-situation to another. The case laws have spelt out the broader principle and are indicative of the circumstances constituting "sufficient foundation". Be that as it may, it is now settled that recounting order should not be passed by the Tribunal readily and as a matter of course.
25. In the instant case, the judgments passed by the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal are totally silent as to the facts, circumstances and evidence on record which persuaded them to pass the order of recounting. Before passing the final judgment on 14-6-2022 Tribunal, vide an earlier order dated 2-6-2022 very briefly discussed the evidence on record which, in our view, does not constitute "sufficient foundation". The Tribunal relied on the case reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 236 = 38 DLR (AD) 275 in passing the order of recounting. We are afraid the Tribunal failed to appreciate the true spirit of the reported case and misdirected itself in applying the said case as a ground for passing the recounting order.
26. Rule 62 of the Rules, 2010 has given specific power to the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal to pass order for reopening the gunny bags containing election materials and recounting of ballot papers. Rule 62 runs as follows:
“৬২। সংরক্ষিত দলিল দস্তাবেজ এর প্যাকেট খুলিবার আদেশ ।-(১) নির্বাচনী ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা নির্বাচনী আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল গণনাকৃত ব্যালট পেপার পরিদর্শনের জন্য উহার মুড়িপত্র এবং দলিল দস্তাবেজ সম্বলিত প্যাকেট খুলিবার আদেশ প্রদান করিতে পারিবেন ।
(২) নির্বাচনী ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা নির্বাচনী আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল উপ-বিধি (১) এর অধীন প্রদত্ত আদেশে ব্যক্তি, সময়, তারিখ, স্থান এবং পরিদর্শনের পন্থা নির্ধারণ করিয়া দিবেন।
(৩) নির্বাচনী ট্রাইব্যুনাল বা নির্বাচনী আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল গণনাকৃত ব্যালট পেপার পরিদর্শনের সময় এইরূপ সতর্কতা অবলম্বন করিবেন যেন ভোট প্রদানের গোপনীয়তা প্রকাশ না হইয়া পড়ে।
(৪) এই বিধিতে যেরূপ বিধান আছে সেইরূপ ব্যতীত, কোন ব্যক্তিতে রিটার্নিং অফিসারের জিম্মায় থাকা কোন বাতিলকৃত বা গণনাকৃত ব্যালট পেপার পরিদর্শন করিতে দেওয়া যাইবে না।”
27. In Amizuddin Ahmed vs Election Tribunal, Narayanganj and others, 27 DLR 594, the Tribunal appointed the Pleader Commissioner to reopen the ballot boxes, recount the ballot papers, determine the validity of those and to submit his report to that effect. It was held that determination of the validity of the ballot papers is a mixed question of law and fact and such a question cannot be delegated to the Pleader Commissioner for determination. It was further held that acceptance of the report means the end of the whole matter inasmuch as the Tribunal is left only with the formality of delivering the judgment.
28. Before recounting the ballot papers, the Tribunal must be satisfied that the gunny bags containing the election materials have not been tampered with. Examination of the Presiding Officer is indispensably necessary if the Tribunal finds tampered ballot papers (28 DLR 375) or the Tribunal should advert to the other evidence and take the decision on consideration of other relevant facts (33 DLR 344). The Tribunal must see whether the ballot boxes were kept in proper custody from the time of its dispatch by the Presiding Officer till its final destination and whether the sealed bags containing the ballot packets as well as the sealed ballot packets are intact. In that connection evidence of competent witness including the Presiding Officer concerned should be recorded [46 DLR (AD) 96].
<u>29. The above discussions unequivocally establish the proposition of law that the Tribunal's jurisdiction to reopen and recount the ballot boxes and the ballot papers is circumscribed by various conditions laid down in various judicial decisions of our superior Courts. In spite of the power given to the Tribunal by Rule 62 of the Rules, 2010 to reopen and recount ballot boxes and ballot papers, the position of law has remained unchanged and the judge-made laws are applicable in full force in the matter relating to laying 'sufficient foundation' before passing the recounting order and the procedures to be followed while recounting ballot papers.</u>
30. Reverting back to the case in hand, both the Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal passed the respective orders of recounting without laying "sufficient foundation". Moreover, ballot papers were recounted by the Serastadar of the Tribunal which is not permissible under the law. If the Tribunal is satisfied on assessment of evidence on record that there is sufficient foundation for passing the recounting order under Rule 62 of the Rules, 2010, it must itself reopen the gunny bags containing the election materials and recount the ballot papers with the assistance of Court staff and in presence of the parties, if so present, after giving notice. In so doing, it must follow the procedures laid down in case laws discussed above.
31. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2 points out that the present petitioner made an application dated 21-9-2022 before the Appeal Tribunal for recounting of ballot papers by a Senior Advocate of the Bar or by a person appointed by the Appeal Tribunal who it deems fit and proper. Such application is opposed to the law and does not confer any power upon the Appeal Tribunal to proceed with the matter of recounting ignoring and bypassing the law. Such application is liable to be rejected outright.
<u>32. In writ of certiorari, the judicial review Court has the power to interfere with the finding of facts arrived at by the subordinate Court if the same is based on non-appreciation and non-consideration of evidence on record and the same is opposed to law which has occurred in the instant case.</u>
33. In view of the foregoing discussions, we find merit in the Rule.
34. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgments and orders dated 3-11-2022 and 14-6-2022 passed by the Election Appeal Tribunal and the Election Tribunal respectively are declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect and are set-aside.
35. The election petition is sent back on remand to the Election Tribunal for re-hearing in the light of the observations made above and in accordance with law. The Tribunal is at liberty to receive further evidence, if considered necessary for arriving at a just and proper decision. The Election Tribunal is further directed to dispose of the election petition within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of the records in his Court.
Send down the lower Court's records at once.
End.
